div.head: 2 MqDOUGALL'S Pategt SELF-RAISING FLOUR /otOCENjoRR. The Examiner, WOMEN'S CHAT. WOMAN'S REALM. THE BLACK DICESS-FASIIION-HOME. I MOTOR CAR. By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.
div.p: 2 MqDOUGALL'S Pategt SELF-RAISING FLOUR /otOCENjoRR. The Examiner, WOMEN'S CHAT. WOMAN'S REALM. THE BLACK DICESS-FASIIION-HOME. I MOTOR CAR. By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.

Princess Margaret's Futirfe Home.—The Royal Wedding has brought Sweden and Norway prominently into notice, and it is probable that that event will induce many to devote their summer holidays to a visit to those shores. Sweden does not present the wonderful beauties of landscape which Norway possesses, but it is not lacking in beautiful scenery, and Stockholm, its capital, ranks as one of the finest cities of Europe. The Royal Palace there provides apartments for the King and Queen, and the Crdwn Prince and Princess, but in summer the Swedish Court removes to Drotningholm. Tbs Castle of Sofiers.which haslbeen presented to Prince Gustav Adolf, and Princess Margaret, was the King's favourite residence, and he has described its picturesque and romantic surroundings iii some of his poems. It is situated on the coast of Southern Sweden, and com- mands beautiful views on the narrowest part of the Sound. The quarrel between Sweden and Norway will unfortunately prevent Princess Margaret from visiting the latter country, and enjoying its beautiful scenery, -unless perhaps some happy chance should give her the opportunity of playing the part of peacemaker between the two kingdoms. The Summer Holidays.—lt is no doubt well to think out plans beforehand, but it is possible to be too fussy, and in many families this leads to slot of worrying and discussion over the summer holidays. They are con- sidered and discussed so long before the time comes, that such topics as where we are to go, what we are to do, and wear, become wearisome, and, in holidays as in everything else, the realisation of what we have so long looked forward to, rarely comes up to anticipation. As a rule the most enjoyable holidays are those which come spontaneously, or are only thought about a few days before the time comes to start. In the case of large families, more elaborate arrangements are perhaps Tte c ess ar y , but it is a mistake to allow these to become a source of worry and anxiety, and there is much to be said for the plan that where suitable opportunities present themselves, members of the family should make their own holiday arrangements independently of the ' others, and spend the vocation in the way that seems to them the most enjoyable. Ireland as a Holiday Resort.—lreland is steadily increasing in favour as 1i holiday resort, and the fact , that the newly. married Royal couple are spending a , portion of their honeymoon there, will tend to increase 1 its popularity in this respect. Princess Margaret of ' course knows Ireland well, and was more than once a visitor at Glenveagh Castle, Mrs. Adair's magnificent seat, which is situated in one of the wildest parts of Donegal. She also knows Adare Manor, Lord and Lady Dunraven's place near Limerick. This is one of the most beautiful and interesting of the Irish houses though lacking the grandeur of Lismore Castle, and the wild scenery of the Donegal mountains. People who know the beauties of Irish scenery are never tired in its praise ; but lack of enterprise has prevented Ireland from being generally better known to holiday makers. Of late , years however there has been a great improvement in ; travelling facilities and hotel accommodation, which , are the two features . most in. need of attention in ;

.... Ireland to encourage holiday visitors. A Society Wedding.—A fashionable wedding which -was of great interest to a large number of the leading I families in Society, was that of Lady Alexandra Acheson, ! and Captain F. W. Stanley, which took place in London last week. The bride is the daughter of the Earl and I Countess of Gosford, whilst Captain Stanley is the /onngest son of the Earl and Countess of Derby. The King and Queen and several members of the Royal family sent presents, Lady Alexandra—as her name indicates being a daughter of the Queen' and a grand- daughter of the Duchess of Devonshire, by the letters previous marriage with the seventh Duke of Man- chester. Lady Louisa Montagu, the second daughter of that marriage. became Countess of Gosford in 187fi. After the wedding. the Duchess of Devonshire and the Countess of Gosford gave a reception at Devonshire House, when the presents were on view. These numbered betwten tour and five hundred, making a magnificent display, the list of donors including almost all the leading people in Society. In spite of sundry accidents and protests, the fashionable world has not given up the practice of throwing rice after the happy couple, and there was evidence of this at the Stanley wedding and also at the recent Royal wedding at Windsor. The Baroness CederstrOm.—Adelina Patti, now the Baroness Cederstrom, does not spend much of her time in this country, hut she has been lately staying in London, and was interested in the King of Spain and the Royal wedding. She was born in Madrid some sixty-two years ago, and made the acquaintance of the King of Spain when be was quite a small boy. She was received by the youthful King in London, and was also present at tfle Royal wedding, King Edward paying her the compliment of chosing her seat in the nave of St. George's Chapel. Her brother-in-law, Baron Rolf Ceder- strom, who is attached to the suite of one of the Princes of Sweden, was also present. That, of course, gave the Baroness an additional cause of interest in the wedding, but besides this she is on terms of intimate friendship with the King and Queen, and is, in fact, possessed of some of the most magnificent presents from almost

every Royal personage in Europe. • The Flower of the Moment.—Marguerites, from the tiny field.variety, to quite huge specimens, abound at all fashionable milliners, and many of the new fabrics shew designs of Princess Margaret's name flower. The marguerite again appears embroidered upon linens, and is hand-painted upon chiffons, while parasols, and hand- kerchiefs also show designs of this popular flower. In the morning and afternoon, the buttonhole of "daisies " is correct, while for evening wear corsage knots and bouquets of marguerites are quite a craze, and this state of things will doubtless continue until the London season is past and gone. - Concerning Elbow Sleeves.—To the woman possessed of pretty arms, some handsome bracelets and a goodly dress allowance, the fashion for elbow sleeves is a de- lightfel one, but unless these advantages have fallen to one's lot, it is wiser to leave it alone. Scraggy arms, or those all too generously porportioned, are not pretty to look upon, yet exhibitions of one extreme or the , other this season, have been plentiful to a very painful degree. Another mistake many women are making is the wearing of four-buttoned gloves with their elbow sleeves. The long frills, in the majority of instances, almost reach to the tops of the gloves, still when the arm is raised the effect is anything but pretty or desir- able. If the long rucked glove is an impossibility,then the long semi-transparent sleeve should be added, for outdoor wear, good hraclets are almost a necessity with the elbow sleeve, but where these are not available, the black velvet band, caught together with a jewelled clasp, or fastened with some pretty ornament, is not to be despised. Ribbon Toilettes.—Some ef the most beautiful dresses seen at Ascot were entirely of narrow glace or gauze ribbons, bound together by means of open-stitch silk embroidery, or fine cobwebby lace. Mounted upon a slip of taffetas,and an underdress of chiffon,and trimmed with a profusion of lace, the effect was very beautiful, but needless to say such a toilette is a costly affair. According to an authority on the subject, gowns built of very narrow velvet ribbons, caught with open stitch embroidery are being prepared for early autumn wear. The amount of ribbon required for such a toilette runs into ninny hundreds of yards, moreover the time required by modistes to weave it together is considerable, and this alone creates a tremendous item in the account. Hair Fever.—People subject to hay fever are recom- mended to refrain from taking country walks or expos- ing themselves to sun and dust, at this tiine of the year, but the general experience of those who habitually suffer from this distressing complaint is, that staying indoors or in town, does not save them from this annual infliction. There are great numbers of people in London who never go near field or meadows, but who are always more or less ill with hay fever during June and July. It is one of those minor ailments about which the doctors appear to know least, and in the case of a great many individuals, it would seem that it must run its course, and can neither be prevented or rured. Women it is thought suffer more than men, which suggests that tobacco smoke is to some extent a preventive, and it is well known that sternorrium, or anti-astrornatic cigarettes are in most cases an alleviative. There are scores of so-called remediec, but what may be partially effective in one casels ineffective in others, and the specific for the malady has yet to he discovered. ' MADGE.

The way in which the fashion of jewels changes was curiously. exempl.fied in one of Princess Margaret's wedding. pesents. It came from Princess Friedrich Karl, and is said to have been one of tip. gifts presented to her on her marriage. It is a bracelet of large, square emeralds set in gold, heavily chesed and wrought in a chain pattern. There is one large diamond from which an emerald pendant is hung. No jeweller of the present day would ever dream of setting emeralds without diamonds, says a lady writer in the Globe, especially such la-go, -fine stones as those in this handsome bracelet. The green looks hard against the gold, like a man's coat against a collarless neck. Put the bracelet belongs to a period when heavily-di...signed gold ornaments were worn by even the highest ladies in the land.

CHAPTER XVlll.—Conttnued:

Then, as he moved his hands from his lips she caught sight of the ring.. With her mind full of dark passion she had not noticed it before.. It was not a very noticeable thing, for the opal had worn dull and lustreless. But now her woman's curiosity prompted her to glance at the. token which seemed so precious to a man about to die. She saw it, and stepping forward a pace, saw it still more clearly. Then she gave a cry of horror, and the revolver dropped to her side. Jordison saw his chance and sprang at her, but she was too quick, and he recoiled from the muzzle of her weapon. He did not notice how it trembled in her hand. •

'That ring," she said slowly, . trying to speak in a calm voice, "where did you get it? Who are you? Where did you get that ring—the opal ring I mean," and she -looked hard at his face, trying to read from it another face that always looked out on her from the past. • But time and penal servitude and misery and despair, and the wrecidng of mind and soul can do much to' change the features of a man. Jordison was silent. He saw no reasons for gratifying a woman's curiosity at a moment like this. He was still thinking how he could get the better of his adversary. "You will not speak," she replied. "Then I will speak for you. Your name is John Porteous, and that ring was given you by Marie de la Mothe."

The words fell on Jordison's ear like a clap of thunder. He moved forward an& stared at, the speaker. But the black mask hid everything he ,wished to see from his view. For more than a minute he stood thus, as though turned to stone. The revolver was still pointed at his heart. ' " Are you not John Porteous ? " she con- tinued, "answer me. You are, very near to death. Tell me the truth."

"I was John Porteous," ha replied mechani- cally, "and who are you ? " "I am the Countess of Heatherstone," she said, "but because you are John Porteous; and because you kissed that ring on your finger, I cannot kill you. Go ! " And she pointed to the window. He did not move. "Go ! " she cried, "or I may repent. I hear the voice of ray son crying out to me." She lowered the revolver and he moved towards the window, passing close to her. He knew well enough now who she was, and why the face of the young Lord Overcliffe had recalled someone in his past life. Then suddenly the dev I took possession of his heart, and he 'did the foulest deed of his life. He turned suddenly upon her, pinioned her arms to her side, took both the weapons from her, and flung her. from him, so that she staggered back against the wall. For a moment he looked at her, then he sprang at her throat. She screamed horribly. "You are Marie de la Mothe," he cried, "and I have sworn to kill you. lam not so merciful as you." Then his madness went from him as suddenly as it came to him. He released his grip and looked at her with a ' kill Nw, for
,u n,
' No," he said, "I cannot yo l now, you have given me my life. God has punished you. lam glad your son is dead. lam glad that_____" he seized her hood, and tore it from her face.

Then he stepped back and broke intp peals of laughter. She tried to hide bag awful features in her hands, but he tore them away and still laughed. She moaned like a dying animal. There were voices and sounds in the passage. Jordison locked the door leading into the other room, and returned to her again and once again tore her hands* from her face. ' "The beautiful Marie de la Mothe," he said, looking closer into her eyes. The wretched woman shrieked and shrieked again. Then she caught the switch of the ,electric light and the room was plunged into darkness, and she sank in a heap to the floor.

div.head: WASHING FROCE.
div.p: A WASHING FROCE.

It is quite within the bounds of possibility to obtain a really smart summer frock, in some light cotton or other washing material, for a very small sum of money, provided that the dress is made at home, and the cost of the making thus saved. It is always wisest to choose a simple pattern that will not be difficult of achievement. An intricate model often so severely tries the temper and powers of the amateur that by the time it is finished it is hopelessly tumbled - looking, and the owner is heartily tired of the sight of it. Our sketch shews a pretty dress, carried out in some pleasing tint of crash, which can he procured for 61d. a-yard. Ten yards will be required; one yard of embroidered

rauslin,from is. to is. 60. a-yard ; half a dozen pretty enamel buttons costing about is. ; and three yards of ribbon, at 41d. the yard. The bodice is made like a blouse, having three stitched box-pleats over each shoulder, the central panel being of the embroidery. The back is arranged in correspond- ing box-pleats all across. The sleeves, with their single puff, end in long, tight embroidery cuffs. Crash is not a material that can be gathered, so we suggest that the skirt be made to fit round the hips, with a box-pleat at the back; and two groups of crossway bands, put on to represent tucks, form the ornamentation for the lower part of the skirt. The neck and waist are smartly finished with a tie and belt of the ribbon; the latter may be made of two widths of ribbon joined together to make it wider. Thus it will be seen that our dainty summer dress has only cost 10s., including the cotton with which it is sewn.

div.head: DISAPPEARING DRESS.
div.p: A DISAPPEARING DRESS.

One scarcely knows whether or not to regret the disappearance of Quaker dress, writes "Miranda." At the recent conference of the Society of Friends it was noticed that only three or four. female members attended in the quaint bonnets aforetime worn by old and young alike, while most of the present generation were actually attired in fashion- able gowns and floral headgear. Nor is it the women members alone who have yielded to the temptations of modern dress. Where nowadays are to be seen youthful Quakers in the long dark coats, amazing hats and sober neckties of their grand- fathers : While one can sympathise with the young people who see no reason why they should wear a uniform in order to express their religious views, it is impossible to quite help some feeling of regret that another picturesque style of garb is fast disappearing from our midst, since there are now so few forms of distinctive dress. Giat's FROM

The little frock shewn in the sketch is constructed on the most simple and practical lines, consisting of a blouse bodice and a plain, well•gored skirt, the hem being stitched with several rows of stitch- ing. It would look equally well in navy serge or in any of the stronger washing materials, such as linen. Brown holland would make up prettily, relieved by a collar of white linen spotted with red. The collar is cut in square tabs back and front,

and is neatly turned in at the neck. The blouse is arranged in box-pleats, and sewn on to a band at the waist, supplied with buttons, to correspond with buttonholes made in the waistband of the skirt. The blouse is fastened down the front by large pearl buttons. The bishop sleeves are drawn into tight-fitting cuffs of the spotted linen, a belt of that material completing the costume.

div.head: WHY THERE ARF FEWER BABIES.
div.p: WHY THERE ARF FEWER BABIES.

When we teach our daughters Latin verses and conic sections, not to mention cricket and hockey and bridge; when we abolish chaperons and countenance latchkeys, and admit them to offices and professions, it is pretty clear, says Truth, that we are manufacturing "bachelor girls"; and when we have manufactured any number of bachelot girls, it is not surprising if we find that babies are not as plentiful as they used to be.

div.head: To-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: To-DAY'S RECIPE.

VEAL FRITTERS—AN-Ds -TO-MATOES.—Chop lb. of lean veal, Vb. of fat bacon, and put both in a mortar; round them together, with one raw, fresh egg, a dessertspoonful of picked leaves of thyme, the juice and grated rind of a lemon, a dash of nutmeg, and pepper and salt to taste. Roll the mixture into small balls, and flatten them. Dip each one into a well-made, rich batter, and fry them in heated lard. While they are cooking, squeeze a little juice from a lemon over them, and drain them free from all fat on kitchen paper. Place on a well-buttered baking-tin two large tomatoes, cut in halves; dust each piece with pepper and salt. Fill a forcing bag and pipe with the batter, and use it to screen the tops of the tomatoes neatly. Set them in the oven, so that they will be ready as soon as the veal critters are comteu. Arrange the fritters around the tomatoes on a hot dish; garnish them with little tufts of waterers', well washed aDhl drained.

div.head: CHAPTER XIX AN INQUISITION
div.p: CHAPTER XIX AN INQUISITION

Jordisan heard the crash of breaking doors, as he slid swiftly down the ladder to the garden. He threw the ladder to the ground., called out to Lipp to follow him, and, looking back as he ran across the lawn, he saw the Countess's apartments flooded with light, and two figures leaning out of the window. A second later they disappeared. He was glad he had remo/ed the ladder. He had gained at least a minute's start. Fortunately the night was dark and rather foggy, and when the two men reached the park, and the rustle of bushes or crunch of graverno longer gave a clue to their pursuers, they breathed more freely. They saw a half a dozen lanterns moving rapidly to and fro behind them, and heard men calling out to one another. Their pursuers would have nothing to guide them ui their search, and the park was a large place. When at last they reached the spot where the motor stood, under the shadow of a great Cypress tree, they could only see one light, and that was several hundred yards to the north, and close to the road. They started the machinery and the car glided silently away to the south. .It was the opposite direction to the way they wanted to go, but Jordison was determined to take no risks. If the man who carried that single light caught sight of a motor, he might draw unpleasant but correct conclusions.

It took them; an hour to reach the Red House. Jordison had to drive slowly, for he was driving without a head light, and they had to traverse a series of narrow lanes, in places half a foot deep with mud and loose stones. When he had Tun the motor into the shed, he went over to the stables, unlocked the door of the harness room, and lit the lantern. Then he poured himself out a stiff glass of whiskey and water, and ate a thick chunk of bread with a slice of cold bacon laid on it. When he had finished this frugal meal, he went out and, locking the door behind him, made his way up a flight of stone steps to the small loft which he had appropriated as his bedroom. He lit a pipe and began to undress. The bed looked cold and unattractive by the light of the lantern. He began to think it was scarcely worth while taking off his clothes' It would be daybreak in another three hours. He put on his waistcoat again, ; and taking down a heavy fisherman's jersey from a peg on the wall, thrust it over his head and struggled into it. Then he flung .himself down on the outside of the bed, and tried to go to sleep. He was thoroughly exhausted both in mind and body. But sleep does not always confer favours where they are most wanted. Jordison closed his eyes, lit pipe after pipe to soothe his brain, but he could not sleep. The events of that night had stirred his mind into a seething whirlpool of thoughts. To many a man the recollection of how close he had stood to death, and how providentially he had escaped, would have come to the surface, but to Jordison, one great aentral thought floated clear above everything else. He had found Marie de la Mothe. There was not a single discordant thought of kindness in the black mass of hatred that heaved and tossed in his brain. He did not remember that she had lost her only son, that she was afflicted by a terrible disease, and that, to use her own words, she had found a living deaths He did not remember that she had spared his life because he had kissed the ring she once gave him. He only saw the treachery of the past, those long years of hell in a convict prison, years in which she bad risen from a somewhat dubious existence to a position second to few held by a woman in England. The man's moral nature had broken down. He was incapable of dis- cerning between good and evil. He only saw the latter, and he resolved that Marie de 12 Mothe must die. That would be an easy matter to arrange. The only .s*ifficultv haci been overcome. She had been found, and a chance meeting had revealed what the ex- penditure of many hundred pounds of good money had failed to unearth from the secrets of the past. • His thoughts were broken by the clankiny

div.head: June 24, 1905.
div.p: Saturday,

of metal in the stables underneath. It was followed by a stifled moan. Then there was silence, and then a loud rattle of iron as though some beast were trying to break loose /from its chains He flung himself ofrthe bed and kicked on• the floor with his heavy boots. He was answered by another moan. He muttered an oath, and taking a lantern, made his way down the stairs to the open air, and unlocked the stable doors _

He entered and, closing the door behind him, walked to the far end, and threw the Light of his lantern into a loose box. There, in one corner on a heap of straw, crouched a man. His hands were fastened together with a pair of handcuffs. One of his legs was chained to a ring in the floor. A thick piece of cord was fastened round his neck, and passea through one of the supports of the manger. His mouth was gagged. He could neither stand up nor lie down with comfort. He crouched in a sitting position, and leant his head against the side of the stall. Jordison unlatched the door of the loose box. As he entered, the man tried to rise, and his chain rattled. Then he sank back with a moan, and pointed to his mouth. Jordison placed the lantern on the floor and swinging the man round by his shoulders, stood behind him and unfastened the gag. , 'Well, Mr Holme," he said, walking back space or two," have you decided to speak ? " "Water, for God's sake. Give me a drink of water."
. "I told my servant to give you some this morning." "I have drunk it. There wasn't more than half *a tumbler full. You have been giving me salt meat."

"That shall be remedied to-morrow," Jordison replied, with a grim smile. "You shall not have any meat to-morrow, and you can have as 'much water .as you want. There's plenty itt the creek." "Salt water," said Holme, in a low voice. "You devil. By God, if I could be free for five minutes. If you and I were alone in here man to man—just for five minutes, I would not ask a. second longer. If you are a man, and have any grievance against me, let me go, and tackle me like a man. If you get the best of it, you can kill me." • "I could kill you just as easily now," Jordison replied. "I have no grievance against you, Mr Holme. But I have a pur- pose in life. There's something I wish to find out, and you can tell it to me." "I can tell you nothing." "You do not know what is in store for you," Jordison said. "I think you will speak one of these days. Salt water is a poor diet for a healthy man." "You cowardly cur," said Holme. Then he broke into a string of blasphembus oaths, reviling Jordison, and even reviling the God who had delivered him into Jordison's hands. Jordison stepped forward and kicked him brutally. Holme (lid not utter a sound, but suddenly rising to his knees, stretched out his wrists and struck with all his strength. The iron handcuffs just missed Jordison's kneecap, as the latter sprang back out of reach. Ther he laughed. "Savage, eh," he said with a sneer. "I think we can tame you." Holme sank back on the straw and glared at hint like a wild beast. _ _

"Why are you not reasonable," Jordison continued. "You will be bound to get the worst of it. It is hot much I ask of you. You have only to tell .me all you know about Arthur Sferious." "I will tell you nothing," Holme replied, doggedly. " You cannot look me, in the face, and say you know nothing," Jordison said sternly. I can see that you are lying. If I thought' for a moment that you spoke the truth, I would let you go." " No, you would not let me go," Holme replied. "You dare not after what has hap- pened." He referred to his own imprisonment. He did not then know that Jordison had .far stronger reasons for keeping him from com- munication with the outer world. He did not know that William Outen was dead.

Jordison bit his lip with vexation. He saw now that he had made a mistake. Only the hope of release would extract any information from Arthur Holme. And Holme realised that whether he spoke or not, there was no hope of release. lie Would therefore keep his mouth shut. Jordison hastened to remove this impression. "I shall certainly let you go, Mr. Holme," he said, after a pause. ' I shall of course ask you to give me your word of honour not to say anything of what has occurred. But I shall certainly let you go." Holme looked up keenly into the dark fierce face. "You lie, you scoundrel," he said," I shall never leave here alive with your consent. I shall not speak." " Ttere are ways of making men speak," Jordison replied grimly. "You might come to think of death as something very sweet indeed. You might even be induced to speak by the offer of death. But I will give you one more chance. Do you know if Arthur Sterious is in England ? " Holme was silent. "How did his watch get into the creek; where we found it ? " Holme was still silent. "What connection had you with Richard' Behag when you were in Valparaiso ? " Still Holme did not answer. "Do you know anything about Behag's death that is not known to the police in Valparaiso ? " ' Holme shrugged his shoulders, but still did not reply. "Do you yoour itiknrohwarawhßetehhearg, itorwabos both, Arthur defrauded the 'firm of Sterious dr Co., and do you know what cause of quarrel there was between Behag and Sterious ? " At last Holme spoke. "I have heard all these questions before," he said quietly," you are wasting your breath and time, Mr. Jordison." "I will do so no longer," Jordison replied. "I will gag you and leave you to think over them till the morning. Are you going to let me gag you quietly, or must I use force. You know it has to be done. It would not do for anyone to hear you." • I refuse to be gagged until you have given me some water." --

"You shall have all you want tc-morrow." " For God's sake, give me some water— just a wineglass full." "Not a single drop till to-morrow. Now, are you going to let me gag you quietly." "Come and try it," Holme replied, rising to his knees. In a second Jordison was upon him, and had borne him to the ground. Holme dashed his fists in the man's face, and the blood streamed down his fingers. He fastened his teeth in his hand and bit out a piece of flesh. Both were powerful men, but the con- test was too unequal. In less than a minute Jordison had choked Holme into insensibility with the rope that was fastened round his neck. Then he forced open the mouth, in- serted the gag and secured it tightly. When this was done he rose to his feet, and looking down at the prostrate figure began to fill his pipe. Then he pulled out his match- box, but his fingers shook with the struggle Ile had just gone through, and the box fell to the floor. He stooped down, gathered up the matches, lit his pipe and went out of the lor.se box, locking all the doors after him. In less than half an hour he was asleep.

An hour afterwards, Holm-e partly recover- ed his senses. He was semi-delirious, and gurgled inarticulate sounds in his throat. ' Lights flashed before his eyes, and strange i noises vibrated n his ears. He had dreamt 01, running water in ht swoon, and stretched out his hand to find the water jug. He found nothing but a single .wax match. He turned it round and round in his fingers. Then he laughed horribly:—the laugh of a maniac, stifled by the gag into a low sobbing moan.

lust as he haa setttea his neact comtortaoty on his pillow, and was dozing off to sleep, he noticed a strange smell in the room. He raised himself up on his elbow and sniffed. It was undoubtedly a curious smell, but he did not realise for a few seconds what it was. Then, as he thoroughly roused himself, he recognised the faint pungent odour. It was the smell of something burning. He jumped off his bed and lit his lantern. The light showed a faint grey haze in the room He searched carefully for the cause but found nothing. _ .

Then- suddenly a low stifled cry broke the silence of the night. It, was followed by the loud rattling of chains, and then by another cry, longer and louder than the first. In 'a flash Jordison realised where the smoke came from, The stable was on fire underneath him.

He rushed from the room and roused Lipp from a heavy sleep. Jermy snored beside him and Lipp raised a brawny arm for a rude awakening. But Jordison stopped him.. " Let him be," he said hurriedly, " two are quite enough, and if by any chance • we cannot put the fire out, well—" He shrugged his shoul- ders, and Lipp understood. Jermy was a constant menace to both of them.

Lipp thrust on a jersey and a pair of trou- sers, and followed his master down the stairs. When they got outside the smoke was pouring through the stable windows, for there was not a pane of glass in any of them. Within they could see the dull red glow lof fire, and as they neared the door they heard a long and horrible scream, and the clank of chains.

"Quick, Lipp," cried Jordison, handing him the key. "He must be saved at any cost." Lipp did not wait to fumble with the key, but burst the door open with his shoul- der. A volume of flames and sparks flew out, and the two men shrank back from the open- ing. There was another scream, and a hoarse cry for help and the noise of chains being tugged and shaken. He is alive, and has got his gag off," said Jordison, hurriedly. " I expect the fire has not reached him yet. The loose box is made of iron. If he is alive we can live there, too. There's the window. Quick." They ran to the 'window at the far end: Jordison tore away the wooden framework with his hands and climbed into the stable. The air inside was comparatively free from smoke, but was hot as the blast of a furnace.

In five minutes' time Jordison reappeared and thrust a limp form through the window. A loose chain dangled from one ankle, and a loop of rope was still round the drooping neck. The hands were crossed close together in the iron clasp of the handcuffs. Lipp took the burden from. Jordison and laid it. on the grass.
"Alive" he said gruffly, hut without the faintest show of interest.

"Yes," said Jordison, coughing and gasp- ing for breath, • but pretty well choked. I couldn't have stood another minute of it. One end of the place is like a furnace. tincic those handcuff's and work his arms a bit to put some air into his lungs. He is safe enough at present." Lipp unfastened the handcuffs, and tried the process recommended for the resuscita- tion of (11 .ning men. It was, as might have been expected, singularly unsuccessful. • Holme neither sighed nor opened his eyes. "Go down to the creek," said Jordison, "and get some water. lam going to see' what I can save. We shall be burnt out to-night. No, stay,, you had bqtter come and help me. He is not dead. He can shift for himself. Put on the handcuffs, take him down to the house, and chain him by the legs to some- thing—a bar_of the cellar window' will do." These words had a sudden and unexpected result. Holme, who had been shamming un- consciousness, eprang to his feet, dashed one fist in Lipp's face, and the other in Jordison's stomach, and sent them both sprawling. Before they could recover themselves, he had caught up the loose chain in one hand and started down the slope towards the creek. Holme was a young and athletic man, and tith the 50 yards start he had obtained, he reached the creek before his pursuers, in spite of his weakness and the chains encumbering his progress. He gained the creek, and plunged through the mud till the water reached his wai,t. Then he struck out for the opposite bank. The weight of the chain became painfully apparent, and he could barely keep his head above water. But he was a powerful swim• mer, and he struggled through the incoming tide to a point nearly too yards above the place where he had entered the water. As he felt the soft mud under his feet once more, he breathed a sigh of relief. From the opposite bank came the report of a pistol, and a bullet sang to the left of him. He flung himself down in the mud and waited. Five more shots went over his head, and then he heard the squelch of mud and the splashing of water. He rose from his soft, but malodorous bed, and reached the bank. The splashing ;of water continued. Then he heard a voice cry out that the current was too strong to keep a foothold, and another giving the order to go back. Neither of his pursuers could swim., and for a while he was beyond their reach. On the opposite bank the stables of the Red House flared fiercely, and he crept on all fours from the lurid and unwelcome light. He knew that so long as he was a mark for a rifle his life was in danger. Foot by foot he crept out of the glare into the darkness. He realised that Jordison and Lipp would not give up pursuit but endeavour to-intercept him before he could reach a place of safety. But now all the advantage was on his side. He knew every inch of the creeks and rnaishes, and before the eastern sky showed grey with the coming dawn he had threaded his way westwards, had swum the creek again, and was moving across the park to Heatherstone Hall. His chain clanked at every step he made. " It was the only refuge at hand, the only shelter where he could find any human beings to protect him. ' But as he crossed the lawn his senses reeled, and his strength gave Way, and he fell in a heap on the green turf. And there the gar- deners found him in the morning, delirious and crying out for water, too weak to move an inch from the place where he had fallen. The men went indoors with the news, and a crowd of servants gathered on the lawn. They talked volubly, but were uncertain how to act. Lord Heatherstone was not yet down. Lady. Agnes was with her stepmother. The whole household were already in a tumult after the events of the previous night, most of which had now become public property. Lady Heatherstone's maid was the only per- son who had any definite ideas. She rashly jumped to the conclusion that the prostrate man had some connection with the attempted burglary of the night before. The chain on his ankle suggested to her mind an escaped convict, and who more likely than an escaped convict to be connected with robbery and violence. She voiced her opinion in shrill tones, and the men, most of whom were, or had been, in love with her, applauded her perspicacity. Certainly, no one recognised Arthur Holme in the huddled and dripping figuer that lay at their feet. His clothes were torn and blackened with smoke. His face was bleeding and smeared with soot, his beard and moustache were scorched into a filthy mass of shrivelled hair. The black mud of the creeks plastered him from head to foot. He was dressed in a rough jerseebuy and a pair of old serge trousers, is feetH were bare, and his ankles were sore and bleed- ing where the chain had chafed them. They resolved to leave him and send for the police. Two of the gardener's picked up the chain and held it in their hands, in case he should attempt to escape. He did not move, but now slot then he cried out for water. The womenkind were tor giving the poor wretch something to drink. The men, backed up by Lady Heatherstone's maid, decided to do nothing without Lord Heatherstone's per- mission.

div.head: [ALL RIGIITS litsEuvr.D.] WIIAT IS A GENTLEMAN?
div.p: [ALL RIGIITS litsEuvr.D.] WIIAT IS A GENTLEMAN?
THE REV. E: J. HARDY, M.A. (Author of" How To Be happy Though Harried," sta.).

Two great novelists have answered for us he question " What is it to be a gentleman ?" Thackeray replies as follows: "It is to be honest, to be gentle, to be generous to be brave, to be wise, and, possessing all these qualities, to exercise them in the most graceful outward , manner. He should be a loyal son and a true husband; his life should be decent, his bills should be paid, his tastes should be elegant, his aims in life lofty and noble. He should have the esteem of his fellow-citizens, and the love of his fireside; he should bear good fortune, suffer evil with constancy, and through good or evil always maintain truth.' Dickens, in " Barnaby nudge "has contrasted a gentleman in sorrow and persecution and a. cad in sensuality and sloth; liaredale who lived up to his rule that no man should deviate from the path of honour and Chester, who never did an "ungentlemanly" action, according to his own definitions, and never did a manly one. In the same social position, no two men could be more unlike. Haredale, severe in his self-re- straint, was tender in his compassion for others and always ready to help them ; Chester, never denying himself an indulgence, was piti- less and vindictive.

The true gentleman is tested not in a yacht, but in a lifeboat, not on parade, but on active service. When Lord Roberts was speaking of the conduct even of the private soldiers under his command in South Africa, he said that they behaved like gentlemen. They had learned self-restraint, they had learned to suffer and be strong. And if the officers were not as well educated in a technical sense as their critics think they should have been, at least they showed that they knew how to. die like gentlemen and make no fuss about it:
THE SIGICIFICANCR OF DRESS.

At one of the oldest social clubs of Oxford the qualification for membership was to be bees notary bent vestitus, moderate dacha which Means, of course, that the new corner must be well born, well dressed, and moderately, not oppressively learned. " The apparel oft proclaims the man " and still more the gentleman. One of the right sort acorns to wear false fronts or cuffs or mock jewellery, or indeed any lie. The ideal gentleman never over-dresses. His dress is like himself unassuming and in harmony with his doings and surroundings. People call him a well-dresesd man but no one remembers what on any particular occasion he weirrs. Refinement in dress is generally associated with refinement in manners. The innate sensitive feeling which rejects the unbecoming in the one will be /prick to avoid it in the other; it will regulate dress and carriage, spirit and speech. Gentlemen do not now use "language " such as they did in days in which a Primate said to a Premier, " It may save time, my lord, if we assume before we commence our discussion that everybody and everything is damned." . Mere was a time, we are told when before an election to a fellowship in All Soul's College at Oxford was made, the selected persons were invited to dine with the electors ; a cherry pie formed part of the meal, and he who ate it most like a gentleman got the fellowship. It is said that the reason why those who were to be called to the Irish bar used to have to eat dinners in Inns of Court in London was because it was desired to see if they understood the management of their knives and forks. A true gentleman is not greedy. At breakfast in a,country house an elderly lady was asked what she thought of the man who had taken her into dinner on the night preceding. She replied that he was not a gentleman. "Oh grandma, why do you think so P" asked a youth from Oxford. " Because," was the reply he scooped all the oysters he could find out of the sauce and appropriated half of the forced strawberries at the dessert." Up- on this someone at the table remarked that the old lady should not speak in that way of one who lift so little to be wished.
TRH INSIGNIFICANCE OP ANCESTRY.

In China long nails on the angers are con- sidered as gentlemanly as they are slovenly in England because they show that the possessor of them does no manual labour. The Cli4iese notion of a gentleman is very much what tsed to prevail in Ireland, where a gentleman was one who never did anything for himself or for any- one else since he came into the world.

The term " gentleman " is sometimes only given to one who is said to "know his grand- fathers" but the man who has this knowledge, only differs from the man who has it not, in this, that the former knows that many of his ancestors deserved to be hanged while th 3 other remains in blissful ignorance of the probable fact. To a British snob an American said, "Sir, my .family began where your's ended." Two servant maids were discussing a new lodger who had come to a boarding-house. " He's a very nice man" one said to the other " but he's not a gentleman" and then gave her reason for . thinking so. "Yesterday morn- ing," she said "I was carrying up a heavy buciret of coal and he took it and carried it for me and you know no gentleman would do that." This is just what one of God Almighty's gentle- men would do. " Bear ye one another's bur- dens " said St. Paul " end so fulfil the law of Christ,"—the law that is of Him who has been called " the first true Gentleman that ever breathed."
AN AMERICAN DEFINITION.

The term "walking gentleman" is some- times given to a man who does nothing but walk about and amuse himself, but a very different name should be given to this sort of character. An American young lady asked an Englishman who was travelling in the States what his father was to what business or pro- fession he belonged. "To none," was the reply; " but I suppose that you have none of that class of people ?" " Why, certainly," re- plied the 'lady "we have lots of them ; they are here called tramps." A man who does not do his share of the world's work, either with bead or with hands, is a thiet or tramp rather than a gentleman. Even the South Sea Islanders who , murdered Bishop Patterson understood • that every true gentleman is a worker' When the bishop first went amongst them he surprised them by being ready to put his hand to any- thing. Ile would do a bit of carpentering, wash up the things after meals, teach the young blacks to wash and dress themselves. Other. white men seen by the natives were lazy, and wanted to put all the work on. them, so to dis- tinguish the bishop from these they called him "a gentleman gentleman," and the others "pig gentlemen." Two working men were discussing the other day what it is to be a gentleman. One said that money made -a gentleman. " But," • said the other, "if you saw a donkey laden with gold and were told that it belonged to him, would you say that he was a gentleman ?" Of the same kind is the error of associating gentle- manliness with Money-giving ;. which in many eases is no better than snobbishness. When Sir Walter Scott visited Ireland, and went to see St. Kevin's Bed, near Glendalough a Mr. Phu), kett, who accompanied him, told the female guide that the visitor was a poet. " Poet ?" said she ; " sortie bit of him but an honourable gentleman • he gave me half-a-crown !" So cabby thinks that anyone who gives him double his fare is " a real gentleman." Others, deceived. by appearances, fancy that clothes make a gentleman. A friend of mine told me that coming over in a steamer from Ireland, he heard two men talking of a third. " Who, ol what is he r' one of them asked. " I don't know," was the reply, " but he is a gentleman: he always wears a tall hat." • A GENTLEMAN VENELRED.

One certain 'mark of a true gentleman is that he respects and controls himself. The phrase "as ,drunk as e lord." noints to the time When publie opinion did not expect torus mat gruh., men to control their passions, but happily this state of things has ceased. No one would now si.ty " As drunk as a.kentleman," for if a unui drinks he is not considered a gentleman. " Once a gentlenm always a gentleman " a true saying. Wellington used to say of (korge IV. that no one could act the part Of gentleman better than he could for ten minutes. This sort of man, even though he be a ',King, iF.• an amateur gentleman, that is, one who only playsat the thing, rather than a real one. Manners of the right sort etumot be put off any more than can the skin. A true gentlenian is : gentle not only to his superiors, but to those who are considered below him in the social scale ; not only to strangers but in the privacy of his home to his wife, his children, his ser- vants, yes, even to his horse, his dog, his eat. The love and admiration." says Kingsley.

" which that truly brave ana loving man, utr Sydney Smith, won from everyone, rich and poor, with whom he came into contact, seems to have arisen from the fact, that without, perhaps having any such conscious intention, he treated rich and poor, his own servants, and the noble- men, his guests, alike; and alike courteously, considerately, cheerfully, affectionately, so leaving a blessing and reaping a blessing where- ever he went." The Christian gentleman in this way respects the image of God in every man,. and treats all his inferiors as well as all hia. equals and superiors as he himself would like to- be treated. When Pope Clement XIV (Gan- ganelli) ascended the Papal chair, the ambas- sadors of the several states represented at his Court waited onl him with their congratulations. When they were introduced and bowed, he re- turned the compliment by bowing also; on which the master of the ceremonies told his Holiness that he should not have returned their salute. "Oh, 'I beg iyour pardon," said the Pontiff, "I have not been Pope long enough to fortet good manners."
THE TREE GEN'TLEMAN.

Having seen what a gentleman is not, let us now ask ourselves what he is. He is a man who is gentle in thought word and deed. He is. a good son, .husband, father, friend, and is. generally true and just in all his dealings. "He back-biteth not with his tongue," as the fifteenth Psalm says, " nor doeth evil to his neighbour. but notketh much of Ahem that fear the Lord." 'What a good description of a true gentleman is that which St. Paul gives in the thirteenth chapter of his First Epistle to the Corinthians, " Charity or love suffereth long and is kind." It has been said that the test of good manners, is to be able to put up pleasantly with the bad manners of others. Charity " euvieth not; " charity " vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Snobs unduly depreciate others and unduly ap- preciate themselves. Charity " doth not behave itself unseemly " that is to say, a true gentleman studies the feelings of others, and tries not to give pain. Charity " seeketh not her own; " only vulgarians are grasping. Charity "is not easily provoked." The word "easily " has no place in the text and was inserted by some copyist who did not understand. He is a foolish and vulgar person who is easily provoked, touchy and prone to take offence; the Christian gentle- man is not provoked at all or if he is he manages to hide it. " Charity thinketh no evil, and re- joiceth not in iniquity." The Christian gentle- man turns a deaf ear to scandal, and puts the best construction possible upon people's actions. Sometimes we are surprised to find people with no advantages, of birth, money, or position ex- hibiting in their manner the sympathetic tact and delicacy of feeling that belong to real gentle- folk. They may well be called God Almighty's gentlemen for it is He who has made them what they are. We hear much now of schemes for refining and beautifying the lives of the dim millions, but nothing can really do this except true religion. Christianity aims at making them all gentlemen in the proper sense of that much- abused word. H anyone says that it is absurds to expect the masses ever to attain to such re- finement and elevation, we reply by asking,—ls it absurd to expect that they may become Christian and if Christian can they be anything; else than true gentlemen and gentlewomen?

Noisy Scenes. Mr. R. A. Naylor, Unionist cendidate for Carnarvon Boroughs, held a meeting at Pad!hell on Tuesday night,. the other speakers being Mr. Greaves Lord,of Liverpool and Mr. David Williams, barrister, of London. Major Gough presided. Mr. Greaves Lord spoke on ihe licensing question and and the fiscal policy, and Mr. David Williams,who spoke. itiVelsh, dealt with the education controversy. Mr. Naylor then addressed ,thA meeting, and appealed to a. crowd of Radicals present to allow him to speak with- out interruption, and said he was quite prepared to answer any questions put to him. The speaker was continually interrupted, and was unable to proceed with his address, and the chairman appealed to the inter— rupters to give" fairplay "to the speaker. The meeting became more and more riotous,and several persons were ejected by the police. Mr. Naylor, failing to get a hearing, resumed his seat amidst laughter, and dictated the remainder of his speech to a reporter. The meeting broke up in confusion.

He sprang from the ground three times, and foil ''neon- scions. Lord Tollemache removed him to his home in a motor car, and he remains in a serious c .ndition.

I have received quite a number of letters during the past week from my little readers, and sone of them have been good enough to tell me of their school life, and others of the various pet animals they keep; all this interests me very much. lam glad so many of you work hard at 1303001; we are often told that our school days are the happiest, still I often think that the bothers children have over their lessons are real troubles to them. .Never mind, all of you do your best and the difficulties will soon pass away. I am afraid I vdas rather lazy when I was at school, and I did not study French as I should have done. The consequence is I now very often wish I could speak and undeittand the language, as when I go on the Continent it makes it very awkward for me. I hope that all my nephews and nieces who have the oppor- tunity will try to leant French, so that when they are grown up they will not be handicapped as I have been. I have sent a postal order for ss. to Wilfrid Tibbett, who sent in the first correct solutions to puzzles in the paper pub- lished June 2nd, These were very neatly written.

ELSIE'S PET. ' Did you ever see a Bullfinch? It is such a pretty bird. One day little Elsie was very good, .• and Mamma gave her a present. It was a sweet little Bullfinch, in a cage. He could whistle a tupe. Elsie loved him very much, and she liked to listen to him. Besides, he was very clever. He soon learned to know Elsie and when she called, "Bully! Bully!" and chirruped to him, ' he would put his head on one side and look so knowing! If she took a seed between her rosy lips and held them near the cage, Bully would look first one way and then another, with his .• bright eyes, ar.d hop, hop, hop,—until he came , quite near, and then he would give a quick little peck with his beak, catch the seed, and eat it up! Oh, he was a bright little bird! Every evening, when Elsie went to bed, Mamma opened his cage and let him fly all over the room; and then she did tiot shut him up .for the night, but let Master Bully perch where pleazed. Sometimes he would settle himself • YPon the table, or,the bureau—standing with his u_right eyes shut and his head under his, wing. • ;but every morning he woke up at the same nour; just as the clock was striking seven. He 'would perch on little Else's pillow and peck, Peck, peck at her soft cheek till she awoke! (To be continued.)

THE LITTLE •MOON. 0, Mamma, look! the little moon Makes just the letter C, And if it had another .line, 'Twould make the letter ...And if there was another moon, put opposite just so, 'Twould make another letter there, and that would be an 0. - ' I think it's funny that I see my letters up so high; thought they only were on blocks, but there they're in the sky. I seem to see them everywhere, whenever I'm at play; •I lay my drumsticks on. my drnin, and there's the letter A. At dinner, when I sit and play with knives.and forks, I see . All kinds of letters round my plate, T, V, X, Y, and E. ,When Bridget:s good, and lets me have the clahes-pin. on the floor, I make H, I, L, 31, and N, and lots of letters more. I\IY papa looks-for hours and hours at letters in a book, With not a picture there at all at which I care to look. I think that letters are quite nice for little boys like me; But why a Man should care for them, I really cannot ''see. • A LITTLE CALLER. Long, long ago, she ambled to town, her flaxen curls bobbed up and down, Her best blue ribbons fluttered gay, and she had some Calling-cards of her own— Long, long ago, the people cried, "There rides the sweet little Arabella, he goes for to make a wedding-call, to-day, on the Prince and Cinderella!"

MOTHER IS-"GOAL."
"The weather is cross," the children say, "Or else forget it's a holiday." Down in torrents the cold rain pours, NO chick or child may peep out of doors.
Good little scholars, the school week througli, On Saturday pant for something to do. And when the fun begins to flag, What is so fine as a game of tags
Over the carpets go nimble feet, Boyish laughter peals loud and sweet. "Mother is goal!" the racers cry. To mother in turn the racers fly.
Dear little sons, in life's real race, When hardest you struggle to win your place, Pressed by pursuers that mean you ill, "Mother is goal," be your watchword still.

div.head: FLABBERGASTER.
div.p: THE FLABBERGASTER.
(Continued from last week.)

"Well, dear me," exclaimed the Jester, as it began to get dark. "Fancy, no one being able to guess the answer, and it's so easy, too," and everybody began thinking again until it came on pitch dark, and they couldn't see to think, nd then the King said that they had all better go to their Royal bye-byes, and try and dream what the answer was; and, if nobody guessed by dinner-time thc following day, then they wokid all give it up. Well, the next day came and everybody was full of excitement as to what the answer would be; so, when they were all stated, the King arose, and offered a magnificent jewel to anyone who had been able to find out "why was a mouse when it spins," but everyone remained 60 quiet that you could have heard a gun go off if anyone had pulled the trigger. "What," shouted: the King, "no one able to find the answer ? What a lot of noodles you are, and it's so easy, too." Of course, the King didn't know himself, but then, Kings don't know everything. Then his Majesty called the Court Jester before him, and re- quested an answer to the riddle, whereupon the Jester, addressing the King, said: "MY Liege, the answer to the riddle can only be given in a Lertain way. It will, be necessary for every per- son to hand me a key, with Which to cross their hands. They must then gaze into‘the palm until the sounding of the Palace gong, when the answer will appear in brazen letters upon the wall of a certain room which must be sought tor."
"Let it be so," said the Xing. (To be continued.)

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

INCREASED POSTAL FAClLlTlES.—Additional postal facilities are to be provided at Stockton Float') as a snb-otlice is to be opened at the shop of Mr: J. Whitley, grocer, &0., Walton-road. Mr. Joshua Whitley will be in charge of the Office which will be opened each day (Sundays excepted) from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., on and from July Ist for money order, postal order, annuity and life insurance business.

ANNUAL SCHOOL TREAT.—The scholars attending the Baptist Sunday School, Hill Chile, had their annual treat on Monday when Frodsham was visited. The outing proved to be a successful one, the drive to Frodsham being exceedingly enjoyable. Buns and milk were provided on arrival and immediately the pleasures of the day were indulged in. Tea was served at four o'clock, and though two or three heavy showers descenied and a thunderstorm took place, the pleasures of the visitors were not marred, as there is ample pro- vision for shelter on Mersey View. After tea races, &c., were indulged in, and many useful prizes were given to the successful competitors. Soon after eight the home journey was commenced and Warrington was reached about ten o'clock.

EXHIBITION OF GAS COOK ERS.—Messrs. Fletcler, Russell and Co. have this week held an exhibition of gas cookers in the Hall Cafe, Victoria-square, and throughout the week the Cafh has been attended by large numbers. One of the principal attractions was the lectures delivered each afternoon by Mts. H. M. Young on cooking. Mrs. Young is well known in the district and her lucid and practical demonstrations of the advantage of cooking by gas were followed with great interest. A variety of cookers were well &s- -played and attracted much attention and favourable comments. There was also an excellent display of incandescent gas lighting, pendadta, &c. The cookers may be hired or obtained on the five years' hire-purchase system from the Warrington Corporation at low half- yearly rentals, and fixed sree up to 35 feet of piping.

div.head: ALLEGED PERJURY BY A WARRINGTON MAN.
div.p: ALLEGED PERJURY BY A WARRINGTON MAN.

Prisoner Committed to the Assizes. Walter Cross, builder and contractor, formerly of Warrington, and latterly of Stalybridge and Ashton was on Wednesday at the Stalybridge Police Court, charged on remand with having coumitted wilful perjury on a statutory declaration made by him in November. 7903. lie was also charged on four other counts with having committed acts of misdemeanour under the Bank- ruptcy Acts by obtaining goods of the value of more than ZCI without declaring the fact that he was an undischarged bankrupt.—Mr. J. H. Garside Ives prose- cuted on behalf of the Treasury, and Mr. J. Bradbury, solicitor, Ashton, defended. Mr. Ives said the perjury cons i isted of false declara- tions made by Cross n November, 1903, before a magis- trate. The charges arose out of certain conveyancing ; proceedings. Cross had built some property in Han- over-street, Stalybridge, and Mr. Itawlinson, of Cockbrook wished to buy a portion for £.250. He (Mr. Ives) was acting for Rawlinson, and certain statements were made to him by Cross He would be fair. Mr. Bradbury (for the prisoner) : You will have to be fair before you have done. Mr. Ives then read to the magistrates the statement signed by the prisoner. It stated that the prisoner Cross had never been adjudicated a bankrupt, that he had never had a receiving order made against him, nor had he ever filled his own petition, nor taken advantage of any Acts for the relief of involvent debtors. That declaration was signed by Cross, and he (Mr. Ives) could not imagine anything more sweeping in its char- acter than that. Cross was an undischarged bankrupt ,at the time, and an undischarged bankrupt could give a title to any real estate. Mr. Allen Howard, solicitor, gave evidence on oath ; He stated that in November, 1903, he was acting for ' I Cross. He told Cross that a Walter Cross, of the firm ,of J. and W. Cross, builders, Warrington, had boon adjudicated a bankrupt. He also asked the prisoner if he had over been in Warrington. lie replied that he had, but he was not the Walter Cross the bankrupt. He also stated the bankrupt was at the time in the Potteries, and that he (prisoner) had lost money through the ; bankruptcy of J. and W. Cross, and worked as a foreman at 'Warrington, occasionally helping J. and W. Cross. Witness then asked the prisoner it he was prepared to make a statutory declaration to the effect that he had never been a bankrupt, and Cross replied that hej was prepared to do so. Witness then saw Mr.l Ives, and the statutory declaration was prepared and ; signed by the prisoner. The declaration was explained to the prisoner. Witness asked the prisoner to• go to Mr. Simpson, a magistrate, and make the declaration before him, and the prisoner left and returned in a few minutes, the document then bearing the signature of Mr. Alderman Simpson, J.P. The business regarding the purchase of the property by Mr. Rawlinson was then proceeded with, and a deposit of £5O was paid. A few days later the prisoner told witness that the Walter Cross who was adjudicated a bankrupt had got his dis- charge. Mr. Ives afterwards made a statement to witness as a result of which the deposit money was returned, and the transaction declared "off." After further evidence, prisoner was committed for trial at the Assizes.

div.head: GLEANINGS.
div.p: GLEANINGS.
PLANT WITH NEVER-OPENING FLOWERS.

In the report of the South African Association for the Advancement of Science, Dr. Schonland describes a plant 'which bears nothing but oleisto- gamous, or never-opening flowers. Hitherto it has been asserted that all the numerous species which bear these curious blossoms always produce normal flowers as well. The plant which is thus asserted to be unique in bearing only cleistogamons flowers is Anacampseros Papyracea. Dr. Schiinland has watched it for years, and has seen nothing but these never-opening tlOwers, which reg,ularly produce seed. The,majority of the species of Anacampseros have very showy flowers, and yet Dr. Schouland thinks they are never visited by insects. It seems to be established that cleistogamous flowers are always fertile, while in some instans the showy normal flowers on the same plant scarcely ever bear seed. This is the case, for example, with the sweet violet.

div.head: POWER OF VEGETATION.
div.p: THE POWER OF VEGETATION.

A remarkable instance of the power of growing vegetation is afforded by the Alpine soldanella. Its flowers actually bore, or, rather, melt their way through the hard snow. Sometimes, indeed, the flower opens before it reaches the surface, so that it actually blooms in a little hole in the snow. Usually, however, it reaches the surface and hangs out its pretty violet bells above the snow, looking. as if stuck into it. This power of growing through the snow is due to the heat developed by the vege- tative process. When the plant begins to send up its flower-stalk in spring the heat of the developing bud melts out a cavity above it. The elongating stem pushes the bud into this cavity, and it on melting more snow. This continues tin it reaches the surface. The melted, or partially melted, snow slips down, and freezes again round the stem, which it thus encloses tightly. By careful obser- vation it has been found that the temperature of many flowers is several degrees above that of the surrounding air. This seems to be most marked in the case of an Italian species of. arum, in which the temperature may rise to over 100deg.Fahr., while outside it is only 60deg.Fahr.

div.head: STRUCTURE OF CRYSTALS.
div.p: THE STRUCTURE OF CRYSTALS.

Dr. A. E. H. Tutton, F.R.S., in his researches zoncerning the relationship between the external form, internal structure, and physical properties of :rystals, and the chemical composition of the sub- stances composing them, has shewn that the :rystals of a series of so-called isomorphous salts are not so absolutely identical in external form as was supposed. They exhibit analogous faces arranged according to the same scheme of sym- metry, but the interfacial angles are slightly different in the various salts of the series, and the differences are definite functions of the atomic weight of the interchangeable metals which, by combination with the same acid, give rise to the series. Further, the whole of the optical and thermal properties of the crystals, and also the dimensions of the molecular structural units com- posing then), follow the some rule of dependence on the atomic weight of the metal present. The interesting fact is revealed that there are very large interspaces within the crystals, probably b oth of an inter-mob cular and inter-atomic nature. In other words, a crystal is not the solid substance it appears to be to our senses, but rather a marvel- lously organised 'structure within whose dimen- sions, defined by the exquisite geometrical shape, the amount of actual matter is small compared with that of free space unoccupied by matter. This is not a question of the relatively very gross cavities revealed by the microscope in imperfectly- formed crystals, which are generally filled with air, mother-liquor, or other included material, but of interspaces infinitely more far-reaching in character, bound up with the crystal's own fundamental constitution. SATURN'S TENTH SATELLITE.

Prefessor Pickering, of Harvard University, has discovered by photogn.phy a tenth satrllite of fi.tnrn. It is about 200 miles in diameter, and no 'es round Saturn in a direction agai.;st The hands of a watch, seen from the north, in twenty- ono days six hours. The plane of its orbi, is considerably inclined to that of the "rings."

div.head: SUN'S CENTRE OF ATTRACTION.
div.p: THE SUN'S CENTRE OF ATTRACTION.

Our sun, with its family of planets, has a proper rrration of about five miles a second, and moves over a space of 157,G0D,000 miles annually, its approximate course being direc'ed to a point near the constellation Hercules, and unquestionably revolving around some great centre of attraction. Nadler, the astronomer, has asserted that the star Alcyone, in the Pleiades, is the great centre of attraction.

div.head: PLATING IRON WITH CADMIUM.
div.p: PLATING IRON WITH CADMIUM.

Plating iron objects with cadmium is the interest- ing new metallurgical achievement of a German chemist. The bath is prepared by dissolving cadmium-chloride in water, precipitating with sodium-carbonate solntion, and dissolving the washed precipitate, while still moist, in a solution of potassium cyanide in water. Cadmium anodes are used, with a current of four or five volts. The deposit, after buffin,g,. has the same colour as tin, but is harder.

div.head: WONDERFUL NEW LIFE-SAVING PRODUCT.
div.p: WONDERFUL NEW LIFE-SAVING PRODUCT.

Half a ton of the curious vegetable produce known as kupok reaches Amsterdam yearly from Java. It is a yellow, wadding-like material, which covers the seeds of the Eriodendron, a rapid- growing tree of the Malaccas, and its fibre is re- markable as being much lighter than cork, so that it will support in the water thirty-five times its own weight. The fibre, however, resists all attempts at spinning or weaving. It is silky, only about an inch long, and is made into thin rings. The claim is made that kupok never decays. A 100. mass will support a man in water, and the substance is expected to become useful for life- saving apparatus; and is even looked upon as the probable future stuffing for all ships' beds.
-- SUGAR FOR CONSUMPTIVES.

Sugar ranks high amongst the heat-producing substances, and it is also a powerful producer of nervous energy. It is recommended by two foreign medical authorities, in the British Medical Journal, to avert the wasting of consumption. It should be given in considera:ble doses-100 to 500 grams per diem, in addition to the amount consumed in ordinary diet, the rule being from 5 to 12 grams per kilogram of body weight. Under this treatment excellent results were obtained, 8 to 15 kilbgrams weight being put on in sonic cases in the course of two or three months. The excessive sweetness may be partially masked by giving it well diluted with milk or coffee, or by adding some bitter tincture. It might take the place of codliver oil where this drug 4 badly borne.

div.head: BLUE LIGHT AS ANESTHETIC.
div.p: BLUE LIGHT AS ANESTHETIC.

Professor Redard, of Geneva, who applied music as a tranquillising influence on persons under alms- thetics, has discovered that blue light falling on the eyes, even when closed, affects the nerve centres and produces sleep, either by a hypnotic or anesthetic action. Violet and green, but not red wid yellow, rays have a similar, but weaker, effect. The method of applying the rays for dental opera- tions were described to the Swiss Odontological Society, at a meeting in Lausanne. An electric incandescent lamp of blue glass, with a reflector, concentrates blue rays on the closed eyes of the patient, who is enveloped in a blue veil. The lamp is held about six inches from the eye, and in two or three minutes produces sleep. The subject wakes when the light is withdrawn, and is said to feel no pain during the sleep, or ill effects after- wards. Many patients have been sent to sleep in this harmless way.
