MR. BALFOUR has THE ARMY STORES abandoned the idea SCANDAL. of a Parliamentary

Committee, and has decided to appoint a Royal Commission to inquire into the Army scandals. This meets with general approval. But the Prime Minister was vastly indignant on Wednesday because Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN intimated that the House of Commons had an inquiry of its own to make, quite distinct from the inquiry of the Com- mission. The responsibility of the officers cen- sured by the Butler Committee is one thing, and the responsibility of tha War Office is another. Mr. BALFOUR says the distinc- tion is absurd, We will pot it in the words of his own supporter, the "Pall Mall Gazette ":—"There are several' acts of apparent neglect of the public interest upon which no further evidence is required beyond that which is avail!ple in Pall Mall and at the disposal of Ministers who are themselves members of the House of Commons. The responsi- bility of the officers and the responsibility of the War Office are separate and distinct, and this is no reason why discussion of the one should be delayed for the more complete elucidation of the other." That is the commonsense of the matter, and nobody would say that our contemporary is biased. But Mr. BAISOUR stormed at the suggestion of any debate on the subject. He accused the Opposi- tion of wanting discussion first and inquiry after. What the Opposition wanted, as their leader said, is to prevent the Government from sheltering I themselves behind the inquiry, and it is only too evident that Mr. Bersouß is seeking that very cover. He would like to prevent any debate on he blunders of the War Office. He does not admit hat there were any blunders, and that the War Office is in any way incriminated. " We cannot

take the Prime Minister's view that the War Office is not arraigned," says the " Pall Mall Gazette." But on Wednesday Mr. BaLroua tried a new shift. He was indignant at the idea that the Royal Commission should inquire into the conduct of the Government; but when he was asked by Mr. BLARE if he would make this part of the reference he said that the Commission would follow the established practice. Whether the established practice would prompt the Commission to take evidence from Mr. ARNOLD-FousTER and other Ministers is doubtful, but at any rate the Com- mission cannot thresh out the facts of the case so well as the House of Commons. As the "Pall Mall gazette" says, all the evidence as to their responsibility is within reach. Mr. Bardrourrt had the courage to say that every possible precaution was taken to prevent the waste of stores. Confronted by Mr. LOUGH with the fact that after peace was declared nearly fifty cargoes ot stores were despatched to South Africa, Mr. BALFOUR replied that it was more economical to send them on their voyage, because the contracts had been made and the freights paid. It was more economical to send them to South Africa, where they were sold for next to nothing, and by an arrangement border- ing on idiocy, were even bought back again at ephanced prices! What is to be said of a Minister with this conception of economy ? If the cargoes had been kept in this country, it stood to reason that they would have had a better market, unless there were people at the War Office absolutely determined to make the worst bargain for the taxpayer and to waste the national property. Mr. BALFOUR should be called upon to justify his statement about those superfluous cargoes in debate. We do not want that and kindred matters referred to the Commission. They bslong to the House of Commons. This is a manifest attempt to ,burke discussion with regard to the responsibility of the Government, and the attempt must be defeated at all hazards.

That ,ever-active organization the Progresaive Lanour League began an open-air campaign on Wednesday evening, and if the workingmen of Warrington are not ere long well educated on the political questions of the day, it will certainly not be the fault of the members of the Lague. The enthusiasm and unanimity of the meeting were indeed full of encouragement to the workers in the Progressive cause, and the readily-accorded resolu- tion of thanks to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman for his action in connection with the War Office scandals was a fitting tribute to a worthy leader. llr. J. Howes, in a characteristically vigorous address, succeeded in bringing home to his hearers the enormity of the scandals which have aroused indignation throughout the land. It is useless for the Government to contend that they cannot be held responsible. The electors know otherwise and the revelations of the past few days will only stiengthen their desire to be rid of the present blundering administration. In a thoughtful address on social reforms, Mr. Crosfield showed that it is not the intention of the Liberal party to appeal to the conntry solely :on a negative policy, but that there is a programme of urgent home reforms —headed by the taxation of land values—which it will be their constant endeavour to carry through.

The march of events along the road to interna- tional amity and universal peace is becoming increasingly rapid, notwithstanding the fact that a terrible war is at present proceeding in the East. Naturally, the position of this country is affected very considerably by the changes which are taking place in the relationships of the powers with one another. The possibility of invasion or of the offensive combination of two European powers against us is becoming more and more remote. The" Manchester Guardian "points out that our improved relations with the United States are such as to render warfare between them and ourselves exceedingly improbable, while " our agreement with France should it endure, ought to have enacts much more far-reaching. Until recently the pro- fessed policy of equality with the two next most powerful navies was directed against France and Russia. The Russian navy has now disappeared ; France is our friend; the two next most powerful navies after Germany's are those of the United States (with whom we have disowned naval rivalry) and of Japan, who is allied with us. Politi- cal changes have, in fact, made the old formulm about the two-Power standard and the like meaningless shibboleths. No new mechanical formula has arisen to take their place, and it will be pure gain if one is never found.", We have therefore arrived at a status zn quo which should have proper weight in the considera- tion of such proposals as are put forward by the National Service Lcague. The fears of those who are fearful seem likely to be rendered ground- less: by this quickening change of international relationships. If we are at peace with all the world and and allied to the strongest naval and military posers there can be little need for the introduction of so constitutionally revolutionary a measure as compulsory national service. A radical and really menacing change in inter- national affairs alone would justify such a drastic change in our defensive policy. Fortunately the tendency is all the other way, and we may still hope to continue a "nation of shop-keepers" with out imperilling our existence.

Though hastily arranged, the reception accorded to Bro. David Houghton. the newly-elected Grand Master of the Order of Druids, on Saturday even- ing, lacked nothing in enthusiasm. It is a high honour to members of friendly societies in War- rington that one of their ' most active workers should have been chosen to preside over a groat Order for the ensuing year, and Bro. Houghton was fully deserving of the congratulations so freely extended. Penketh was agog with excitement, and the scenes attendant upon the Grand Master's triumphal return will live loug in the memories of the inhabitants. Bro. Houghton's triumph is distinctly a personal one. Only a fortnight prior to his election he was under a cloud—an expelled member deprived of all benefits. On appeal, how- ever. the Board of Management acquitted him on all charges and authorised his complete re-instate- ment. This was followed up at the Crewe Con- ference by his almost unanimous election as Grand Master of the Order. Never,we think, had a public man a more complete vindication. His enatnies will surely "for ever after bold their peace."

The state of mind of suicides is a question on which Mr. Coroner Brighciuse holds strong views and he impressed them upon a Warrington jlry with such effect on Monday that the uncommon verdict of " Felo.de-se " was returned. We entirely agree with the Coroner that the question is worthy of more serious attention than it gener- ally receives. The returning of " amiable " ver- dicts of " Suicide whilst of unsound mind" is in many case. a purely formal and perfunctory matter, and it certainly behaves jurors to weigh with the utmost care the evidence submitted before arriving at a decision. Of course, it is a common belief that a person must necessarily be of unsound mind to take his own life, but according to Mr. Brighouse this is bad reasoning. The law assumes every person to be of sound mind until the contrary is actually proved, and while it is to the ordinary mind difficult to conceive that a sane individual would put an end to his existence, many cases unfortunately point to that being the fact. We cannot agree with the Coroner that verdicts of "Polo-dc-se "would have the effect of diminishing the number of suicides, for it is hardly probable that a person contemplating suicide would pause to consider what the verdict would be.

Free bathing for the school children has now been secured, and on the afternoons of Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday the baths will be open to the use of the juveniles—and possibly to the exclu- sion of everybody else. This is perhaps unavoid-

able so long as the bathing accommodation of the town is so limited in extent in comparison with the number of inhabitants. While the baths were confined to the use of ticket-holders and people who paid at the doors the accommodation was not only adequate but excellent. The arrangement with the Education Committee however makes a vast difference, and the Baths Committee will, we imagine, ere long be faced with the problem of dealing with an influx of bathers over and above the number which can be comfortably accom- modated. Should this be the case it will not be a matter for regret—increased bathing facilities can only conduce to an improved public health. The Committee may not welcome the added responsi bility which will probably be forced upon them but they have meekly handed themselves over to the Fates and will have to take what comes with all the philosophy at their command.

Having secured provision for the admission of school children to the baths on such reasonable terms, the Education Committee is evidently inclined to go further. An endeavour is now to be made to obtain a reduced charge for the male and female pupil teachers in the service of the committee. This would be excellent for the teachers concerned but it opens up a rather wide question. The" pupil teachers" can aflord to pav their 6d. like less privileged and humbler folk, and if any concession is made to them we imagine there will be some justifiable grumbling. Apprentices and other "minors " might reason- ably consider themselves entitled to preferential treatment on the same lines. Unless they are going to teach the children to swim we fail to see where the pupil teachers take precedence of other young people. The Education Committee must be careful how it cuts prices in the bathing 'market in the fullness of its generosity.

How long will Japan retain this notion of the worth- lessness of the individual life in comparison with the importance of the future social organism ? Will it survive contact with civilisation ? H. W. Massing ham in the " Westminster Gazette."

* * * We hear there is every likelihood of the school children who make free use of the Corporation baths being relegated to the second class plunge bath, better known as "the twopenny." Users of the first class bath will welcome the intimation. * * * Mr. J. Bruce Glasier, speaking at Bridge Foot, on Sunday evening last remarked that the workingmen of this country were not as well educated, and were in a worse condition than the Greek slaves were 2,500 years ago.

15* The Corporation Investigation Committee is par- t, suing its inquiries into the allegations against certain Councillors, and a further sitting has been held this. week. The nature of the proceedings is, of course, kept secret and the report to the Town Council will be awaited with interest. * 55 The annual excursion in connection with the Women's Liberal Association takes place on Monday next. This year the Zoological gardens, Belle Vue have been selected for the outing. There has been e great demand for tickets and the picnic promises to be as successful as was the one last year to Chester. Mr. Seddon was sixty on Thursday. At eighteen he emigrated as a steerage passenger from St. Helens to Melbourne, where he worked for some years in the engine-rooms of the Government Railway workshops- He afterwards started a public house in New Zealand: took part in the discussions of the niggers who drank at his bar, and became a champion of their claims. They made him a municipal councillor, and, thus started up the ladder, " Diggw- Dick" progressed until he became Premier of New Zealand. *s* To lay sixteen foundation stones sounds like a big afternoon's work, but the Wesleyans of Stockton Heath, assisted by outside friends, accomplished the feat on Thursday. With such a broiling sun, tile' little processions round the site and the customurY ceremonies involved no small ..physical :effort. More: over, there were at least sixteen short speeches, ioa the proceedings wound up with the laying of bricks by school children. *s* There was an amusing little incident at a War- rington inquest on Monday, The last recorded act of a wire weaver who committed suicide was to chalk ou a wall : " Manchester Cup —Airship nap." "Ai Airship won !" exclaimed Coroner Brighouse in quite a triumphant note. Then with a hasty " I beg your pardon, gentlemen" he explained that lie had chanced to notice the sporting ne.vs in his paper on that par- ticular day.

* * * The much-maligned motorist is beginning to hit back. At a meeting of the Society of motor manufacturers and traders in London,Mr. H. Sturmey,said motorists were not the only offenders on the high road. "Pedestrians; were the greatest nuis.ince. The pedestrian was the chartered libertine of the road. All users of the road, even drivers of handcarts and pedestrians, should carry head and tail lights at night." It is certainly the case that some late prowlers might be illuminated with advantage.

* * * Lord Rosebery believes in celebrating his red-letter days in a fashion which gives enjoyment to others. 01 Thursday he gave a treat to the inmates of the Epsoscl Workhouse in celebration of his having won the DerbP 1 This is no new kindness on his part for he similarly' i entertained the inmates on the occasion of bis,l marriage, the birth of Lord Dahneny, his two previous Derbys, the relief of Ladysmith, the marriage of Ladrii Peggy Primrose, and the coming of age of Lottl Dalmeny.

* * * Pwllheli; is getting tired of its tongue-twisting name and wishes to revert to Porthely, the ancieu title of the place in the days of the Black Prince. Th° old-time spelling coincides almost exactly .with the present-day pronounciation of Pwllheli. A conv mittee of the local council has been appointed to report on the matter, and if the change is carried out it will be a boon to holiday-makers. We can quite believe the story that a Mayor of Pwllheli was once, in attending a Lord Mayor's banquet in London, pi 4 among the foreign guests!

*-* * Pwlheli, which is one of Arr. R. A. Naylor's three homes and is also in his constituency, seems to be getting rather inhospitable. On Tuesday; Mr Naylor attempted to address a meeting there in furtherance of his candidature but was denied a hearing by the demonstrative majority of Radicals present. The questions introduced by the speakers, were licensing. fiscal reform, and education. Possibly the audience wanted to hear more about the army stores scandal. Naturally Mr, Naylor and his friends would be die" inclined to talk about so unsavoury a subject.

- * * * The police buildings are neither completed nor pail for. At the Local Government Board inquiry la 4 Friday for the borrowing of another 14,500 the Inspector was by no means satisfied with the particu- lars furnished. Councillor Pemberton made a deter- mined protest on the ground that money had been improperly expended and that the architect's specifica- tions had been exceeded. Finally the Inspector ' adjourned the inquiry, which is somewhat of a. triumph for Councillor Pemberton. On July 11th the Inspector will go into the matter again. By that time perhaps both he and Cuuncillor Pemberton will have obtained a satisfactory statement as to extras alto deductions, which seem to have been responsible for numerous variations from the contract an' specifications. . .

* * * A month ago the School Management Sub-Committee, having drawn up a scheme for the imparting 0f physical instruction to the children in the elernentarY' schools, decided that there was no necessity for another interview with the Gymnasium Committee. The latter body thought otherwise, however, and in a polite resolution, intimates that "they nre not in a position to name the terms upon which they, will allow the use of the Gymnasium . . 'wit/ they have had a further interview with the sub-conel" mittee." Accordingly, the latter committee 1134 climbed down and will meet the Gymnasium Com- mittee to discuss terms. Thus far at least is tile dignity of the Corporation and the Education Cote' mitt ee maintained.

Personal Mr. Thomas Birchall, J.P., is lying seriously ill at Ls residence, Holly Bank, Frogliall-lane. On inquiry -on Friday morning we were informed that he had passed a much better night and had rallied slightly. We are pleased to report an improvement in the -condition of Mr. J. Monro, chief brewery manager for Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, who for some time , has been lying ill at his residence Fir Grove,Latchford. He has throughout the week made a steady improve- ment and is now out of all danger. The Rev. Morley "ite'venson, M.A., principal of the , Warrington Training College, has been appointed by the Bishop of Liverpool to the Hon. Canonry of Liver- lopol, vacant by the resignation of Canon Willink, M.A., late Vicar of St. Helens.—Candn Stevenson has brought the Training College to a high state of efficiency. Darin" his rule at the Training College ' the chapel attached to the college has been built, at a cost of £1,500 ; the Practising Schools, at a cost of S-4,000 ; -Fairfield Hall converted into a hostel, and the Mount Schools purchased and thrown into the college. Walking Day. Preparations for the great children's festival next Friday, are in full swing and given fine weather the success of the day's proceedings is already assured. The Mayor has issued the usual order closing the streets along which the processions will pass to vehicular traffic between the hours of 9 and 12.30. PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LS.NCASHIRE.—AdVt. Sunday School Anniversary. • The Anniversary of the Buckley-street Sunday School will be celebrated to-morrow by the holding of Special services in the morning in the church, and in the afternoon and evening in the Parr Hall. The preacher will be the Rev. J. Humphreys (of Leeds). In the afternoon selections gill be given by the Apollo Choir, Miss L. Fairhurst and Mr. H. Berry. Old Workhouse Inmates' Death. Henry Dutton, aged 78 years, died at the Workhouse 431:1 Monday. He had been an inmate for about four Years and had been in a delicate state of health nearly • the whole of that time. • H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE Toxic cures Sleeplessness. —(Advt.) garden Fete at Padgate. The annual garden fete in aid of the parochial funds , connected with Christ Church, Padgate, was held in the vicarage grounds on Thursday afternoon. Favoured With splendid weather the fete was largely attended and was in every way a success. , The proceedings 'were formally opened by Mrs. Frost, Grappenhall. Ilumorous competitions for ladies and gentlemen had • been organised, and received a fair share of patronage, and musical items rendered by Miss Turner's Mando- , line Band afforded much enjoyment. Death of Miss Pickavance. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Miss Mary Ellen Pickavance, eldest daughter of the late Mr. and Mrs. E. Pickavance, 16, Winmarleigh- : street, who passed away on Wednesday in her thirty- sixth year. For some years the deceased lady had i been n a delicate state of health,but in January of this year her condition become more serious,and she gradu- alb' sank. Heart disease was the cause of death, Miss Pickavance had been a teacher at Wycliffe Sunday .chool for about twelve years, and was much esteemed • by the scholars and her fellow-teachers. She was also 'a Member of the Wycliffe Ladies' • Working Society. The funoral takes place at the Cemetery this (Satur- , day) afternoon at 2.30. %%Rife Church Renovation. There was a good attendance at a meeting which 'was held on Thursday evening in the Wycliffe Memorial buildings, of the members of the church, to consider the question of the renovation of the church. he Rev. J Yonge presided. Mr. George Wallington taoved that a scheme for the re-decoration of the church be proceeded with, remarking • that it was -quite necessary that the work should be taken in hand, and that it <was the general opinion of Wycliffe People that an attempt should 'be made to have it 'completed as early as possible. His motion was eecombd by Mr. W. Beswick, supported by Mr. Ziba ~.-Ll•rmitage, and unanimously agreed to. A representa- 'lre committee was appointed to solicit contributions flcl afterwards report ti the church and receive Instructions with regard to putting the work in hand. 'tie hoped that a good response will be made to the anneal for funds so that the woik may be commenced l'a/iy next spring. Wintery Funeral. With full military honours, the remains of the late ill'ivate F. Sinclair, of the 2nd South Lancashire vecBiment, were laid 'to rest in the Warrington 4orttetery on Saturday. The deceased, who was about _ :years of age, had served 21 years in the Regulars, dad passed through the whole of the South African nPaign. He was stationed at Orford Barracks, but ,rnwent to Fleetwood a short time ago for a course of _usketry. Here he became ill, and died from heart lisease. The coffin was met at Bank Quay Station by theoi • unteer Band, and a detachment of soldiers ;Zorn the Barracks, Lieutenant Robson and Captain ularke Jervois being in command. As the cortege Inceeded to the Cemetery the band played the _uead March." The service was conducted by the •v •B. Percival, vicar of St. Peter's. At the condo- three volleys were fired over the grave and the IvLast Post " was sounded by the buglers. Wreaths ere sent by the South Lancashire Depot, the King's Iti:erpool Depot, the officers of the South Lancashire Pot, D Company (to which Private Sinclair belonged), 'ma also one from Fleetwood.

Mrs. Hicks,the founder of the Oldham Society, will give an address.

The Howley Boating Fatality. A vocal and instrumental recital was given at the Parish Church on Thursday, the proceeds of which were devoted to the fund for the relatives of those who were drowned in the recent boating fatality at Howley. Mr. F. M. Darby was at the organ and instrumental selections were also given by Mr. R. H. Pearson. Vocal items were contributed by Messrs. J. H. Draper and T. Humphreys. There was a large congregation. "PREMIER" CYCLES at 12 guineas with change speed gear Sze.' imequalled.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Rector's Irishman's Rise. The Rey. W. G. Krocker, Rector of Oughtrington, Lymm, was presented by the parishioners with a cheque and pictrire of the church, by Albert Pollitt, on leaving for his new living. The Rector, in reply, said parsons were supposed to ba fond of loaves and 'fishes. [At Hindley he had twice as much salary as there; he was going to less, and might end in the workhouse. (Laughter.) I "PREMIER" CYCLES at 9 guineas for Best Grade, unsurpassed.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55,Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Motorists in Trouble at Lymm. At Lymm Sessions, on kVednesday, James Bolus, The Elms, Patricoft, was summoned for the dangerous driving of a motor car on Church Brow. Replying to Mr. 'Browne, the defending solicitor, the police.wit- nesses admitted that they were about a hundred yards away at the time and that there was no traffic on the road ; also that many people volunteered to give evi- dence for defendant. The case was dismissed. Arthur Cross, Liverpool-road, Eccles, was summoned for driving a motor tricycle to the public danger near Lymm. Defendant, who denied that the machine could go 20 miles an hour, was fined fr:i.s and costs. Stockton Heath Tramways. Colonel Von Donop, Board of Trade Inspector, visited Warrington yesterday (Friday) morning for ' the purpose of inspecting the recently completed Light Railway No. 1, from Stafford-road to Victoria Square, Stockton Heath. The inspector and, members of the Town Council hoarded a car which was in waiting and the journey was completed without a single hitch, Colonel Donop appearing satisfied with the work. The service will be open to the public in the course, of a day or two. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH•CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt.

Trade Defence League Formed. " A meeting of Warrington tradesmen was held at Toft's Assembly Room on Tuesday evening for the purpose of forming a local Defence League: The ' need for such a league has long been felt, and at Tues- day's meeting there was a large attendance, over which Mr. NV. Roberts presided. It was decided to take steps to combine for mutual protection, and a strong com- mittee was elected. Mr. Woolhouse was appointed hon. secretary pro ten. Along discussion took place upon Ivo at was described as the unfair competition from the market, and the matter was referred to a sub- ' sequent meeting. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC aids Digestion.— (Advt.) Newton's New Water Tower. On Saturday afternoon by the kind permission of Mr. Surtees, water engineer, the members of the IBuilding Students' Association visited the water tower in course of erection at the Waterworks, Newton-le- Willows. They were met by Mr. Surtees and Mr. Cook,the contractor's agent. The whole building is on the Hennebique system of ferro-concrete. A circular tank 72ft, in diameter and 12ft. Gin, deep, to hold ' three hundred thousand gallons of water is carried on 28 e -damns braced with horizontal ties. The height' of the tower is one hundred and eight feet to the ' highest point. The work is being carried out by Messrs. william Cubit and Co., contractors,of London, who have on the site machinery for screening, and crushing the aggregate, and for mixing the concrete, all of which were set in motion for the benht of the visitors. Great care has bean taken in selecting the materials for the work. The gravel for the concrete is brought from Walney Island and is of a very hard composition Extensive tests have been carried out at the works by the engineer, to find the most suitable mixtures for obtaining waterproof concrete, and slates five inches thick have been made, which at three weeks after mixing, allowed no water to pass through under an hydraulic pressure of 801 b per square inch. The re- sisting properties of this material are also of a very agla order. Recent tests with a ferro-concrete parti- tion wall, 4 inches in thickness, shelved, with a fire made in one chamber ton white heat that an adjoining room had an increase of temperature of only &F, The , cost in most cases comes out cheaper than brickwork whilst its maintenance is considerably less. The care- ful way in which Mr. Surtees and Mr, Cook explained the various methods and details was much appre- ciated. • _
- ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WAT ERS.—Advt.

Re-Unlon of" Old Blues." There was a large gathering of" Old Blues " at the Warrington Blue Coat School on Sunday evening when the fourth annual re-union and special service took place. The occasian is always looked forward to with. pleasure, as affording a welcome opportunity for the renewal of old associations, and on Sunday there was an attendance of between sixty and seventy old scholars at the institution. They were cordially wel- comed at 5.30 by Mr. and Mrs. E. Rose. The chief item of interest to all who had visited the institution of late was the extension of the grounds belonging to the school, which has been effected by the purchase and pulling down of the old property on the north side of Oliver-street, thus making the boy's play- ground about twice the size it was, and also adding considerably to the open space in front of the school.— Service was held in the chapel at 6.30, commencing with the hymn" Heavenly Father send. Thy blessing on Thy children gathered here." Other items in the musical portion of the service were the anthem, "Con- quering kings their title take "(3. H. Maunder), the anthem" 0 Lord God of Hosts " ((I. E. Lyle), and Nunc. Dimittis (Watscm). The service, which was acknowledged by all present to have been remarkably well rendered by the children, was brought to a close by the singing of the hymn, " Lord dismiss us with Thy blessing," the words referring to those who Would meet again here no more, appealing with considerable force when it was remembered that several who were present on the last occasion had since been called to their rest. Mr. S. Millett officiated at the organ. A considerable number of the members of the Brotherly Society were present, amongst whom may be mentioned Councillor Forshaw (the president), Mr. Short (gie secretary), Mr. Moss (the treasurer), and Messrs. Rowe, ! Walker, and Dobson (members of the committee).

div.head: NEW WESLEYAN CHURCH.
div.p: NEW WESLEYAN CHURCH.
FOUNDATION STONE LAYING AT STOCKTON HEATH. --- Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfield.

Thursday was a memorable day in the history of Wesleyan Methodism at Stocktoa Heatl., for, under ideal conditions, the ceremony of laying the founda- tion stones of the new Wesleyan Church and schools which are to be erected at the corner of Heath-street and Walton-road, took place. The afternoon was brilliantly fine, and it was little wonder that a large and representative gathering assembled. The pro- vision of the new church and school will supply a long-felt want in the village. For nineteen years the old building had sufficed for the holding of services, but for some considerable time it had been evident that the accommodation was quite inadequate. A scheme to supply the defici- ency was inaugurated, and it was decided to erect the new building on the site of the old church which has just been pulled down. The building when completed will be an ornamental structure comprising a church 44 feet by 31 feet with a schoolroom behind about 60 feet by 30 feet. In addition there will be three vestries and a convenient basement in which a kitchen range and boiler will be provided. The whole building will .be surrounded by a boundary wall and ornamental iron railings and gates. The structure will be faced with St. Helens grey bricks ornamented and relieved with red pressed bricks and red terracotta heads,sills and string bands and copings, &c. At the corner of I , the building there will be an octagon tower carried up to some considerable height and having lourve openings in the upper portion to be used as an extract ventilating shaft. Ornamental tracery windows will be fixed in the main gable and the transept gables glazed with cathedral tinted glass. The internal , woodwork will be in pitch pine stained and varnished. I The building will be warmed by hot water pipes and; radiators. Due attention has been paid to the ample ventilation of the church and school The church is designed to seat 270 'persons and the school will accommodate 300. Additional accommoda- tion can be obtained if required by means of a gallery to be fixed over the front entrances, access being gained thereto by means of staircases- from the sall vestries at the front of the church. The work is being carried out by Mr. Harry Fairclough, builder, of War- rington, from the design 'of Mr. S. P. Silcock, F.R.1.8.A., architect of Warrington. The total cost of the scheme is estimated at £1,500 and towards this amount £6OO had been subscribed before Thursday's
ceremony. ' LAYING THE FOUNDATION-STONES. SPEECHES BY THE REV. G. H. CARNSON AND

It was not their purpose to endeavour to oust any other church or denomination of any name or class. Their work was to follow their own people in the first place, because they had a number of members who had left the town to live in Stockton Heath and who would, in winter at any rate, find it too far to go to Warrington churches. div.head: WIRRAL SHOW. Mr. J. Gould's (a—iimm) Successes.
div.p: WIRRAL SHOW. Mr. J. Gould's (a—iimm) Successes.

end of their labour was not the erection of the Church but the bringing of men and women to Christ. (Applause). The Rev. J. Gunnell said the new building stood as a witness for God. Every age had its special difficulties, and the dfiliculty with which the church was confronted in the present age seemed to be the spirit of materialism. He was much afraid that the very ideas of God was far away from the minds of many of our fellow country- men with whom weeks and months passed without a thought of God. (Hear, hear.) The age seemed to him to be given over to the love of pleasure, and the time and money spent in pleasurable exercises was really fabulous. They would not be so cross-grained and dis- agreeable as to deny their fellow caeatures a fair amount of pleasure and recreation. Recreation was necessary, but there were far too many who seemed to give themselves absolutely to pleasure. (Hear hear.) Then there was the desire to make money and when they sawl the sordid spirit to which many seemed to be actuated in their pursuit after wealth, they could not fail to be impressed by the spirit of materialism which was prevalent. (Hear, hear.) He regarded the erection of that Chrititian sanctuary as something which would lead to prevent that spirit spreading, as the building could not fail to suggest to every thinking mind the great source of all life. The building would be a witness for the recognition of the Christian Sabbath. A great tendency of the modern times seemed to be the shameless desecration of the Sabbath and the most lamentable neglect of publie worship OR the part of very large section of English Society. (Applause.) He did not think that at the present moment there was the same coarse and brutal materialism which existed a century ago. We were more refined and cultured, but there was still that love for pleasure,and a forgetfulness of Divine things. He would like to see the Sabbath held in higher esteeem by Christian people. He wished the scheme a happy and successful consuniation at an early date. (Applause.) Mr. Stringer expressed his pleasure at the successful day whine they had had. He would leave wish them three thoughts; • hat they should take a living interest in their work, and that they should take a willing and a prayerful interest in their church for that is the secret of all spiritual success. (Applanse.) Mr. Parker on behalf of the Warrington Free Church Council wished the Stockton Heath Wesleyans God speedlin their work. They did not wish as free church- men for any denominationalist to sacrifice in any wiy his principle. They could, all stick to their principles but let them get rid of their prejudices. They wanted to see things in their broad proportions by the telescope of faith and then they would not be anxious to use the micioscope to see the differences which existed between the various religious bodies. He hoped and trusted that they and their sister churches in Stockton Veath would be on terms of most cordial good feeling. He trusted sincerely that the church would be blessed with a great spiritual history. (Applause)• The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees etpressed his pleasure at the financial success which had attended their efforts. To be all right financially was not however by any means all. They must see that the spiritaal life of the church was maintained. If the spiritual life of the church went down the blame could not be attached to any one individual but put equally upon every member of the church. (Hear, heir). They must see Vsat the flame of God's love is kept -continually burning and that their church was kept 'healthy and progressive. Power to do good was not in their circumstances but in themselves. (Applause). The Chairman announced that he had received a dona- I tion of £2O from Mrs. Garnett, and .£lO from a friend I who desired to remain anonymous.

div.head: LIBERAL ACTIVITY.
div.p: LIBERAL ACTIVITY.
ENTHUSIASTIC; OPEN-AIR MEETING. The Story of the War Offica Scandals. MR. A. /I CROSFIELD ON SEIAL REFORMS.

It was a testimony to the increasing enthusiasm in the Liberal cause in Warrington tbat such a large and enthusiastic audience assembled at the open-air meet- ing organized by the Progressive Labour Leap's, and held near Arpley station on •Wednesday evening. The gathering was one of the most successful of its kind ever held, and was characterized by complete unanimity. In the absence of the Rev. H. Dunnico, the chair was taken by gr. Edmund Osborne. The principal speakers were gr. A. H. Crosfied;.who dealt more particularly with social reforms, and Mr. Joseph Howes whose addre93 was devoted to an exposure of the War Office scandals. Others present were Messrs. S. Wright, J.P., C. Jackson Hohnes,J.P. J.A. J. gorton,T. Bames,and J. Howes, jun. (registra- tion agent.)

div.head: CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.

The CHAIRMAN announced that a telegram had been received from the Rev. H. Ginnie() stating that he was detained in Blackpool. They would that night, continued err. Osborne, have put before them another phase of the contemptieole manner in in which the Government was treating them. They had fortunatalv income respects but unfortunately in others, had to deal with the present Government for some years. The Government had treated the country with a great deal of what he (Mr. Osborne) believed to be contempt. They had fought entirely against the interests of the workingmen of this country, and he was satisfied that so long as the Government was in power so long would they have disorder and dissatis- faction reigning amongst them. The army scandal which had for the last two years been perpetrated by the Government was one which ought to make the blood of every , true English:nen boa. Men who had been placed in honourable positions, and to whom the working classes had been taught to look up and admire, were dragging the coantry dovfn into degradation by their filthy and contemptible methods. They were satislied to take the money and to abuse the rights bestowed upon them. They took money for the South African war and spent it in a dishonourable manner. Men were making vast fortunes out of that country and yet they had been trying to blindfold the working classes of England. They had almost grown tired of denouncing the Government,— they had done so many things that would have been better undone—and it behoved workingmen to take the earliest opportunity of turning them out of office. While he (Mr. Osborne) was a member of the Progres- sive Labour League, he was probably more progressive than many others. He believed in the nationalization of the railuays, canals, and the lant (Hear, hear.) If ' they Could only get hold of those things they would do some good. The only wey to do it was by the work- bagmen themselves insisting that the reforms should be carried oue. What was morally wrong could no.: be politically right. (Applauee.) Mr. S. WRIGHT proposed a vote of thanks to g;r Henry Campbell Bannerman for the services he was rendering in exposing the scandal in connection with the South African stores contracts. He desired.he said, to impress upon his hearers the necessity for their taking a greater interest in politics to realize the power which was placed in their hands. Mr. Cr ostield, the prospective Liberal candidate, had expressed his views upon labour matters and had satisfied those who had taken an interest in trade union matters that he was sound upon labour matters. He had promised to support Mr. Shackleton's Bill for the protection of trade union funds. (Applause.) As Trade Unionists tbey were not trying to kill capital but were trying to raise themselves and to secure better remuneration for their labour. They wanted bett M conditions under which to live.better houses, and the abolition of slum property. (Applause.) How could they get those things while taxation was being heaped upon them by the present Government ? —taxation which practically reduced their wages 20 or 30 per cent. (Applause.) Mr. T. BARNES seconded. Bye-election after, bye- election, he said, was showing that the present govern- ment,had the entire disapproval of the country,he asked them to do all they could to return Mr. Crosfield at the next general election and thereby to help to clear out thepresent despicable Conservative Government.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND SOCIAL REFORMS.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND SOCIAL REFORMS.

Mr. A. H. CaOSFIELD, who was very warmly greeted, thanked the meeting for thair friendly reception. That was not the first time he had had the privilege of addressing Warrington audiences in the open air, because they had some very fine meetings last summer, but he had never seen so representative a gathering as the pre- sent one, and he thought it augured very well for the increasing interest which it had been suggeSted that workingmen might with advantage take in the public affairs of this country. (Hear. hear.) Recall- ing the meetings of last year, some of them believed they were then, if not on the eve of an election, at all events within measurable distance of one. It seemed that if a cat had got nine lives, this Government and its astonishing Premier that we had in England must have a great many more lives--(laughter)—because they seemed to escape many a time by the skin of their teeth. (Hear, hear.) They thought they had nearly done with the Government last year, but it was alive and kicking still. (Laughter.) What it VMS here for goodness only knew. (Laughter.) He had the honour to be aidres3ing a great number of ths members of the Progressive Labour League and his faith in the future of

div.head: WARRINGTOi POLITICAL HISTORY.
div.p: WARRINGTOi POLITICAL HISTORY.

..... _ was stronger on account of the forces which that Leegne could exercise and which it had exercised in the town than anything else connected with our local politics. (Hear, hear). ,He knew very well the opinion of the members of the Progressive Labour League but it was not only -they who were telling the people that this Government • lagged supertlaous on the stage." (Hear, hear). Everybody almost in the other party was saying that. The Conservatives themselves would tell themall over the place that it was high time we had a change, because the Government had

LOST ALL MORAL AUTHORITY and all standing in the country and there was no doubt that their friend the man in the street siznbly looked upon this Government, as everybody looked upon it, as a sort of sorry joke. (Hear, hear.) He would grant them that Mr. Balfour had afforded a certain amount of entertainment. As a man who danced on the tight rope, as a juggler, or as a conjuror, he beat anybody et a circus. (Laughter and a voice: "How about Joe?" Well he thought the Premier beat Jae too. (Laughter.) So long as they regarded the Cabinet as a sort of Parlia- mentary circus—and it was not altogether an inapt com- parison, because very many of the members of that Cabinet simply bad to dune as the Premier told them —they might find a little amusement in it. But although theyhad in Edgland many people who regarded politics as a means for some little excitement or for braggadocio rhodamontade, it was only the small percentage of so called society that was oontent to take politics in that way. The great mass of the ceople of this country remembered that, after all, the English House of Commons had been called and was the mother of Parliaments, and we in this country were not satis- fied that that old and honoured assembly, which in its day and within its measure had done a great deal for the cause of progress, should be degraded and that it I should be treated, if he might not say with contempt, at any rate with a measure of

CYNICAL INDIFFERENCE that ill became the Premier of our country. (Applause.) Many of those present could carry their political memories back a good deal further, he was happy to say, than he could. But most of them probably had a very vivid recollection of the high tone which, when leader of the House of Commons and Premier of this country. Mr. Gladstone always in- troduced into his statemansitip. (Applause.) They remembered that in his day our time-honoured assembly, the mother of Parliaments, was a worthy example to her children all over the world. Those were two of the reasons why they would not have their Parliamentary institutions treated as a joke. But the great reason why people said it was time to put an end to this farce was the simple and honest remon that we had in this country—although England, he was glad to say, was the happiest land in the world—a great many people who were looking to Parliament to help to

div.head: IMPROVE THEIR ENVIRONMENT
div.p: IMPROVE THEIR ENVIRONMENT

and to give theta a better chance in life. (Applause.) There was no humbug about that. They knew Parlia- ment was not going to give them a Utopia. They knew there were limits to what Parliament could do, but they also knew that Parliament could to an enormous extent improve the opportunities of the less-fortunate people in this land and by wieer and Tester taxation help to bring about in the future a wiser and better distribution of wealth. (Applause). They really did not know what this Government was about— what it was here for. They knew, however, that if it were not for the Septennial Act the Government would be sent to the right about to-morrow because it really seemed to exist only for the purpose of marking time,ana killing time and blocking the way and, worse still, it was raising obstacles in the path of those who would have to follow and who, as they hoped, would help to move the old world a little bit further on its journey. (Hear, hear.) Part of the work the Liberal party had got before them he would like to briefly touch upon. He did not know what measures would be first undertaken when the new Government came in, but Mr. Wright, without directly touching upon it,had indirectly touched upon the measure which, whether it was first in time, was at arty rate first in importance for them to deal with. He (Mr. Crosfield) had often in Warrington sub- mitted that they ought really to make a determined effort to get that great question of
THE 'FIXATION OF LAND VALUES dealt with—(hear, her)—end he could not help think- ing, as Mr. Wright spok?, how many questions there were of vital importance to the health and well-being

of the people which depended npon that reform being carried through. (Applause.) They had heard a great deal about the unearned increment—well, the best way of dealing with the unearned increment was by the taxation of land values. He had on other occasions alluded to the extremes between wealth and poverty which had become a perfect evil in the United States and which tended to become exaggerated to too great a degree in England. He sub- mitted respectfully that with all due regard to just claims of private property in which both j workingmen and capitalists had a ut and legitimate interest, by means of the taxation of land values' the extremes that he had alluded to between great wealth and great poverty could be modified with great advan- tage to the State. (Applause.) More important per- haps than economic .questions was the effect that that measure would have in bringing about that long talked- of need in this country namely, the _

BETTER HOUSING of the masses of our people. (Hear, hear). Mr. Wright had alluded to that and he (Mr. Crosfleld) agreed with him that that reform was the foundation of all true progress. (Hear, hear.) They had heard much lately about the physical degeneration of the English people. He was thankful to think there had been a little bit of exaggeration—(hear, hear)— but unfortunately it was true that while amongst the well-to-do people of England the physical standard was probably gradually and steadily rising, amongst the more unfortunate of our fellow-countrymen, who aver% crowded together in unhealthy and pernicious slums, there was a physical deterioration going on, and it was ' high time that we stopped it. (Applause.) Therefore if they encouraged cottage suburbs in the neighbourhood of the great towns, and if they reduced the pressure upon the tenements in the centre of towns, they at . once began to stop that terrible increase in land values in the centres of towns; they gave municipalities the oppor- tunity to put up more property, to widen the great arteries of traffic, to give them good tram accommoda- tion and enable workingmen, whether by tram or by cheap trains, to get to and from their work, which was an absolute necessity for millions of people whose work lay in the heart of these great ininstrial centres. (Applause). That to his mind, whether it came first in order of Parliamentary business—he was afraid it would not—or whether it came later, was tha greatest thing they could help to carry through for this country because when they got that reform they got a gradually rising standard of health, happiness, comfort and res- pectability. (Hear, hear.) He would add that as they got that rising standard of respectability and well- being, so THE CURSE OP THIS COUNTRY 'that Mr. John Burns had spoken so forcibly about—the unfortunate tendency towards sottish habits and an excessive indulgence in liquor —would inevitably diminish. (Hear, hear.) Another result which in importance was second to none was this: When men and women, as Morley had put it, got that opportunity of learning to be happier and happier in better ways, did they (his hearers) think those people would be satisfied without a gradually rising standard of culture, civilization and education? He would like to read an extract from a book he was reading recently, written by one of the broadest-minded and best Liberals in the country. Education like temperance would fol low in the wake of land reform, but he (rr. Crosileld). would say in the meantime that the temptations toward' excessive drinking could be lessened by clearing out a lot of the shady'drink shops that were not wanted-While be had never been 1 faroar of tryiny, te trust teetotal- ism down the throat of anybody, while he recognized that" one man's meat was another man's pohon," while he was not a teetotaler by any means, still be had never in this town or anywhere else recommended young men to begin tippling.(Hear,hear.)Speaking to the younger men present, and perhaps as a sportsman to some who were sportsmen, he was sure the great majority would and that they were quite as well off on teetotal lines while they were young. They would save money which many of them could ill afford to spend on liquor and they would be just as capable both for athletic p owess and for their basineis without liquor as with it. The

div.head: LIQUOR QURSTION
div.p: LIQUOR QURSTION

was a great question. He had often exprokssel his views in Warrington and his hearers knew them. They were not extreme views, but such as they were, he respect- fully stood by them. (Applause.) They wanted to extend the ares, continued Mr. Crosfield, in which it would be impossible for a man to enter decent society, whether it was rich or poor, unless he exercised reason- able moderation in taking intoxicants. (Hear, hear). By the reforms he had mentioned they would get that grand spread of culture and the enlarged circle of interests which always followed an improved stanclard of civilization and with that there came the

div.head: KEENNESS FOR, EDUCATION,
div.p: KEENNESS FOR, EDUCATION,

the thirst for knowledge, the desire amongst the people to raiss not only themselves, but their children in their future careers. This was what the writer he desired to quote had to say about the subject :—" In all the long list of practicable reforms there is none, perhaps, which promises a larger increase in the real greatness of our country than the raising of educational ladders no which the clever children of indigent parents may climb to the higher levels of service. . . . Anieducated man has interests more wide, pleasures more numerous and more worthy, than one who is ignorant: he stands on a higher level ; he is able to lead a finer life ; and if the object of our policy is to eKtend op?ortunities for right living, we find a direct means to the end in extending opportunities for education." (Applause.) He (Sir. Crosfield) was very happy to close his remarks with a quotation which, he ventured to submit, was so well worthy the attention and consideration of them all. The motion which he had the honour to support referred ta the honest and faithful service that the Liberal party had received from the leader of the Oppo- sition—Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman. (Applause). He believed that everyone who had watched the stalwart fidelity with which, under the most trying circumstances, Sir Henry Campbell-Binnermin had stunk to his post and done his duty to his country, would support in a very whole-hearted fashion that tribute to a thoroughly honest Englishman. (Applause). THE soura AFRICAN STORE 3 SCANDAL.

Mr. J. HowEs remarked that the exposing of the scandals of the present Government was something we had got thoroughly used to. (Hear, hear.) As scandal followed scandal with lightening-like rapidity they in- creased id bulk, and if the present Government remained in office much longer, it would he almost im- possible for any Government in the world to out-do it in jobbery and robbery. (Hear, hear.) Some time ago when the Prime Minister violated a Pledge made in reference to the fiscal question Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman at once called the attention of the House of Commons to the fact and asked whether Mr. Balfour in the face of our colonial friends wished to pledge us too return to protection. Mr. Ballot" refused to face the music and put forward a subordinate to meet the case brought against him. They would remember the seeds which took place when the House of Commons refused to hear the second in command. The Warrington Pro- gressive Labour League, ever on the alert, at once framed a resolution condemning the action of Mr. Balfour and sent copies of the resolution to the Prime Minister, Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman and Mr. Robert Pierpoirtt, M.P. He quoted that to show the kind of work the League was doing. (Applause.) The Liberal party did not want to live upon

THE- BLUNDERS OF THE PRESENT GOVERNMENT They wanted to discuss those questions of such grave importance which Mr. Crostield had placed before them that night. (Applause.) They, however, also desired that night to express their opinions concerning the recent scandals in reeard to South African affairs and the way in which the Government at the present moment proposed to deal with the question. (Hear, bear.) It was discovered after the war was over that the representatives of the British Government in South Afr‘ea had under their control an immense quantity of food for cattle and other military stores, together with a number of cattle which were wanting food. A drought occurred and there was a scarcity of food. Any ordin- ary man under those circumstances would naturally have either taken his goods to the people who wanted them or else brought the people to his goods. (Hear, hear.) These, however, were extraordinary men and did not deal with matters as an ordinary individual would have done. Instead of feed- ing their cattle with the food they possessed they brocteld in a number of friends whose names cquld not be decently pronounced on an English platform— (applause)—and who were in the habit of making con- tracts with the representatives of the Government. They then sold the goods to those German and alien Jews,and the moment the stuff had been sold commenced to buy it back. It was then found that the goods were not only, sold but sold very cheap and were not only ' bought back but were bought back at a very high price. One or two names came out at the investigation which he thought would be remembered for many years to come.

div.head: ONE WAS COLONEL MORO AN
div.p: ONE WAS COLONEL MORO AN

who had a brother. It was discovered that that brother was associated with the company whirda bought the goods from the Government officials and then sold them bath again. Colonel Morgan was frightfully indignant and declared that he could meet every charge which had been brought against him. In this country wa were always ready to believe every mar, innocent until he was proved guilty but if the Government believed Colonel Morgan why did they not give him the chance of proving his innocence? (Applause). Why did not Colonel Morgan take action himself and demand a court martial? The Government would be forced to grant one and the charges could be fully inquired into. (Applause). Some persons mgcle a nice sum ont of the transactions to which he had referred and at the investi- gation it was shown that some of these people made about £2,000 a day out of the sale of oats alone,although ho did not believe they ever handled the oats. They must have seen then because they discovered that some were damaged and sent in an impudent claim against the Government for damages, and an official at once wrote out a cheque and handed them a large 'sum of money. He desired his hearers to understand that the war was undertaken to put down the corruption of Kruger's government, though he doubted whether a war ever made £2OOO out of Kruger's government. (Applause). Two years ago Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman called attention to a similar scandal which the Government had since hushed up with reference to the operations of

THE COLD STORAGE COMPANY. These South African companies were all the same, but one week they were the Cold Storage Company, the next the Dead Heat Company, and the next something else. (Hear, hear.) Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman pointed out that between April Ist, 1893 and June3lst 1901 this company paid a dividend of 30s. in the £ and placed £1,000,000 to a reserve fund and were making £4,773,000 out of a single transaction. The men in- terested in that company were all patriots who called anyone who was against the war" Pro Boer "and sang "Rule Britannia" though with difficulty as they could only sing in broken English,and would have continued to sing so long as they plundered the people who by their bone and muscle had brought aboutlthe prosperity of the English nation. (Applause). Wnen Sir HearyCampbell- Bannerman made his disclosures the Government said he was traducing British officers, bathe Government stipu- latedthat in future, in the buying and selling of stores, the stores should not be sold to the same company, meaning thereby to exclude compinies with _

A:PREPON-DEMANCE: ISILELITISH NAMES on the list of shareholders. A contract was then entered into and the stores were sold to 4 man named Meyer. It was now discovered that there were two men named Meyer and that when they talked about one it was not the one whom the Government meant. It was a difficulty to know which was the right MD. There would probably have been 22 Meyers had they been wanted. (Applause.) Meyer immediately amalgamated with the old company although it was declared in the contract that he should not be allowed to do so and the same gang teak over the nem lob which had had the old job. There was no breaking through the Israelitish people in South Africa and ever since the Jameson raid we had been supporting alien millionairs at the expense of the British nation and at the sacrifice of the lives of British soldiers to the eternal disgrace of the present Government who were responsible for the death of 36,000 brave men whose lives were wasted in order that those filthy aristocrats shauld get Chinese labour at Is. per day. (Applause.) The blue book showed that we had been plundered not of thousands but of millions of pounds and that the plunder was still going on. What we wanted to know was who was going to be punished. (Applause.) The Govern- ment came before the Hausa of Commons and sugge3tecl that a committee of the House should further investigate the matter. That meant that a committee would be appointed by the Governmint upon which would boa majority of their own followers. Such a committee could only sit while Parliament was sitting and Parliament woulil rise in Aagust and not sit again until February of next year. The effect of such a pro- posal avas,therefore, that no investigation worth speak- ing of could tb.ke place before next year. Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman protested and the Prime Minister asked for 24 hours to further consider the matter, and that night had consented to 'a Royal commission being appointeito go into the matter. A Royal Com- mission was better than a Parliamentary Committee,but 'what was really wanted was that two justices with Sir William Butler should try the men implicated upon the evidence already produced. Tlaose men might or might not be guilty, but as Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman, , had said we wanted to get at the resppnsibiiity of those who held high offices. Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman asked that the House of Commons should be allowed to discuss

THE RESPONSIBILITY OF TfiE GOVERNMENT for allowing those swindles to go on. Mr. Balfour asked "does the hon. member want to have it discussed before the inquiry, is ended? If so I think it would be most unjust and unfair." 'Sir Henry Campbell Banner- man replied "the Prime Minister misunderstands my point. There are two branches to the discussion. The first is the guilt or innocence of these individuals who have done certain things and then there is the question, of far greater importance, of the responsibility of those in authority who allowed these things to go on." We wanted the House of Commons to discuss the liability of the Government and to see how far the Government was implicated. Mr. Balfour said he had already relieve(' the officers interested of their dnty. though that must not be regarded as an imputation of censure upon them. Mr. Balfour indignantly asked whether the members of Parliament thonght any member of His Majesty's Government`, should be censured. The man in the street thought there were a great many. We wanted to thrash out that question and if that reso- lution were passed that night it would be sentnp to Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman, to the Prime Minister and to Mr. R. Pierpoint, and if other towns took the same action we would soon let the Government see that we wanted these scandals stopped as speedily as possible. (Applause.) These men had.

_ _ MADE MILLIONS OF POUNDS OUT OF TAXES upon oar tea and sugar.it was not enough that our soldiers should have died for them ; it was not enough that we should have destroyed two Republics for them ; it was not enough that we should have destroyed the prosperity of that part of the world for them • it was not enough that we should give them Chinese labour at Is. per day to the exclusion of the Britisher, but we must tax our food in order that those aliens should be made rich. The sooner we were rid of the Government which allowed such things the better. (Applause.) The Britisher who could tolerate those things did not deserve to have a vote. (Applause.) That night he asked them to strengthen the bands of Sir Henry Campbell-Banner- man in his endeavour to have that matter thrashed out in the House of Commons, and to bring about an investi- gation as to the criminality of the men who were impli- cated. (Load and continued applause). The result was carried unanimously. THE MIAMIAN THANKED.

Mr. CROSFIELD said he was sure it gave great plea- sure to everyone present-to see his friend Mr. Osborne, one of the most thorough, earnest, and genuine pro- gressives in Warrington, occupying the chair at a meeting of such great importance, and it was his very pleasing duty to propose that they accord to Mr. Osborne a very hearty vote of thanks. He saw sure it was a great satisfaction to Mr. Osborne, as is was to them all, to see the awakening of public spirit and interest in public affairs that was taking place in Warrington where a certain stagnation in such matters had, he was afraid, held sway for too many years. All the signs were good and he was sure it was a great satisfaction to the chairman as it was to the rest of them. (Applause.) Mr. J. A.J. MORTON seconded and the vote was heartily agreed to.

div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH
OF WARRINGTON.
WEEK ENDING JUNE 17th, 1905. Daring the week, the following births and deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, 49, deaths, 21. The excess of births over deaths was 23.

The birth-rate was equal to 36.8. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 15-8 per 1,003 against 169 the average of the previews 4 weeks and against 16•7 the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 3•0 per 1,000, against 31 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 6-0 the corresponding period of 1901.
The ages of mortality were:- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—np. Total. 7 4 3 1 5 1 21.
The deaths included-3 from measlos,l from croup, 1 from enteric fever, 4 from phthisis, 1 from lung diseases, 11 from all other causes.
The following cases of infectious disease have been reported- during the wee:. :—Scarlet fever, 2 cases: memb. croup, 1 case ; erysipelas 1 case; phthisis, 6 cases.

Total number of patients in hospital, week ending June 17th, 1905, 36. • METEOROLOGY.—The Roan temperature was 60 Fah and therefore 9 degrees higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 75E., was recorded on the 12th inst., and the minimum temperature 46F., on the 11th inst.
The rainfall measured 1.13 in. The general direction was S.E.

A RUSSIAN SOLDIER'S ESCAPE. There are thousands of Russian refuges soldiers its London at this moment. They come direct to " The Jews' Free Shelter," where their cases are investigated. Let us sit at one of the long deal tables at which mem- bers of the Committee are cross examining the applicants for guidance and assistance, receiving money, making out tickets, and dispatching the refugees to various parts of the world. A squarely-built man of about thirty, pale, haggard, and with a hunted look in his eyes, comes forward. He tells his story. He is a builder of wooden houses. He had served his time, and had been horns but for a few , weeks, when he was ordered to rejoin. He talked the matter over with some fellow-reservists. They made up their minds to escape. They sold their possessions, got together a little money from their friends, and started. . There were six of them, and they got into a train. After travelling a long time they came to a station at which the carriage was entered by soldiers, who dragged four of the company out. The men% were charged with being deserters. Two of the compaay remained in the train, the man standing now at the table was one of them. But they knew their turn would come, so they scrambled out on the other side of the line and ran for their lives across the country. A party of soldiers started in pursuit. The men reached a river and leapt in. The soldiers fired and killed one. The man at the table swam to the opposite bank and made good his escape. 1 For many hours he went on and on in his wet clothes, shivering with cold, his limbs benumbed. He endured the most terrible privations, but at last be. reached the frontier, got into Germany, and with the money concealed about him purchased a ticket to London. IHe stands before as in London to-night, waiting to know where the commitees can send him for the roubles which he still has left. He receives a ticket for a ship 1 leaving for Canada, drops a knee in the Russian manner of salutation, and goes forth gleefully into the street to think out the tuture in the London lamplight. —Geo. 14 Sims in "Pearson's Weekly."

div.head: DISTRICT MEETING OF CHEMISTS.
div.p: DISTRICT MEETING OF CHEMISTS.
Address by Mr. Rymer Young, J.P.

At a district meeting of Chemists and Druggists of the West Riding, held at the Grand Central Hotel, Briggate, Leeds, on Monday, June 19, Mr. Rymer Young, of Warrington, who for the second time has been elected vice-president of the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain, gave an address on the claims of chemists and druggists to public recognition. Repre- sentatives were present from all the principal towns in the West Riding, and among the audience were Alderman Dunn, of Shipley; Mr. T. Fairley, Leeds Public Analyst; Dr. C 'moron, Medical Officer of Health ; and Mr. J. C. Malcolm, Coroner for Leeds. Discussing the meaning of the word chemist, Mr. Young said the popular acceptation of the term was not a correct one, and that misapprehension was the basis of the large amount of injustice from which the calling suffered. So long ago as 1852 the Legislature separated from the region of., loose description the term "pharma- ceutical chaipfst." and elevated it to the rank of a legal professional title, to be attainable only after examina- tion and registration. The reason for the establishment of a privileged class was to create a legal differentia- tion between the incompetent and the competent, the ignorant and the systematically trained, so that the priblic might discriminate, and not be misled by the un- scrupulous, who are always ready to appropriate that which they have not earned. Sixteen years later—in 1868—the Legislature made the words chemist and druggist," "chemist," and " druggist," definite legal titles, to be applied only to individuals who were registered as the statutory compounders, dispensers,and retailers of poisons. Thus Parliament placed a specific and professional meaning on the word "chemist," which invested it with a wholly different status from the ordinal.; names attached to non-technical and non•scientiflc trades. The ordinary citizen, perhaps, did not realise what was the nature of the examinations which a chemist had to pass. In the first place, there was a preliminary educational test, coin- pris;ng English, Latin, modern foreign languages, arith- metic, Euclid, and algebra. Then followed a three years' ' period of pupilage and strenuous preparation, both practical and scientific, for the qualifying examination, for which there was an entrance fee of ten guineas. Taking into consideration the cost of papilage, college and entrance fees, the'title " chemist ' represeaterl a a capital expenditure of from £l5O to £2OO, whila during at least four years the student was spending money and earning none. There are at the present time nearly 16,000 such chemists in Great Britain, many of them struggling under hours and conditions of labour and remuneration that an unskilled man would refuse to swept. Nevertheless, in spite of these facts, the chemist is being constantly lashed as a " monopolist " by unexamined and unregistered per:ons who, under the wgis of the Companies Acts, exploit his title. In 1980 it was decided in the courts of law that a company was not a" person," therefore could not be controlled by the Pharmacy Act like an individual. Thus, an individual possessing no qualification whatever Is liable to a penalty if he calls himself a chemist, but if that same indi +ulna!, together with six others as ignorant of the art of pharmacy as himself, combine together and form a company, there is nothing to pre- vent them calling themselves chemists and trading as such. The Pharmacy Bill which was now before Parlia- ment had for one of its objects the placing of companies on the same footing as individuals. Mr. Young con- cluded by referring to the services which arecontinually being given to the public by chemists in refusing to sell potent substances to suspicious persons, in detecting unusual doses in prescriptions, in discovering incom- patibilities, and saving the patient from badly propor- tioned ingredients. He contended that the registered man had fulfilled his duty to the State, and might reasonably ask the representatives of the people to do their best to rectify an anomalous condition of affairs.
