div.head: " FELO-DE-SE " VERDICT.
div.p: " FELO-DE-SE " VERDICT.
Warrington Wire Weaver's Suicide.
THE CORONER AND THE JURY.

The unusual verdict of " Felo-de-se " was returned by a Warrrngton jury on Monday in the case of John Rawlinson Savory (21),tivire netting weaver, Sharp- street, who committed suicide on Friday morning by hanging himself. The inquest was opened on Saturday but was adjourned because the Coroner declined t) accept a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane." The only witness on Saturday was Eliza Ann Savory, deceased's widow, who said she last saw deceased alive at 9.40 on Thursday night when he left home to go to work, as he was on the night turn. She got up at nine o'olock on Friday morning but did not see deceased. She thought nothing about that, as deceased sometimes went for a walk before retiring to bed. At 11.30 she went into an outbuilding and found deceased hanging by the neck from a cord attached to a beam. Deceased was a jovial man and she had never heard him threaten to take away his life. They had been married about four mouths. So far as she knew, deceased had no reason whatever to commit suicide. '

The Coroner pointed oat that the law presumed every person to be of sound mind until the contrary was proved. Before they could return a verdict that deceased committed suicide whilst of unsound mind they must have evidence to support it.ln this case,there was an entire absence of evidence to show that deceased's mini was anything but sound, and he could only direct the jury to say that Savory feloniously killed himself. It was the popular idea that when a person took away his life he must be of unsound mind. That, however was,not sound reasoning for they might just as well say that a man could not kill his parent if he was of sonnd mind.

Sergeant Barlow (Coroner's °facer) said he had fully investigated the case. Deceased, it appeared, was seen playing with some children at the back of Sharp-street at eight o'clock on Friday morning- His brother left him at 7.30 at the works and he was then jovial and in the best of health and spirits. . .

After the jury had deliberated in private for about a quarter of an hour, the foreman (Mr. Dale, Sankey- street) said that with the present evidence they could come to no other conclusion than that the deceased took away his life in a temporaay fit of insanity. The Coroner : lam very sorry, but I cannot receive that verdict at your hands. I won't receive it either. There is no evidence to justify it. The Foreman : The other alternative is that we must have additional evidence from the foreman of the works where deceased was employed, and others. The Coroner: We had better adjourn the inquiry then. lam not saying it in any angry or hostile way, but I have no right to receive a verdict from you that is totally against the evidence. The inquiry was adjourned until Monday morning for the attendance of additional witnesses.

div.head: ADJOURNED INQUIRY AND VERDICT.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED INQUIRY AND VERDICT.

THE CORONER AND "ASHAFILE VERDICTS." At the adjourned ininiry on Monday, deceased's widow stated that decessed had never shown any signs of insanity or of having a weak mind. About twelve months ago he was out of work, and witness was told that he then threatened to take his life. Deceased kissed witness and her mother before going out on Thursday night. She thought that was curious, as it was a very unusual thing for deceased to do. The Coroner : The ways of some married people are very strange. In answer to the foreman of the jury, witness said she had never known deceased to hat on horses. Deceased's mother said she last saw him alive on Wednesday when he was in good health and gay spirits. He bad always been a very jovial man, and there was no insanity in the family. Thomas Barnes. foreman of the netting department at Messrs. Rylands' works, said deceased had worked there for the last seven years, and was one of the merriest of men. When witness last saw him on Saturday morning he was in the best of moods. Deceased had lost a great deal of work through illness, and witness thought prob- ably that had preyed on his mind. Still he did not believe deceased to be of unsound mind.

Robert Savory, brother of deceased, said deceased had always been of a cheerful temperament and witness never had any reason to suspect that he would take his life. Ho last saw him alive at 7.30 on Friday morning when he appeared to he in his usual health and spirits. Deceased had been rather low financially; it appeared as if everything went the wrong way with him. Annie Crump, 65, Birchall-street, said that at 7.45 on Friday morning she saw deceased playing at ball with some children and he appeared to be in his usual jolly mood.

Mary Mercer, 75,Sharp-street. said that at her invita- tion deceased had a cup of tea in her house on Friday morning and he was in good health and spirits—in fact he was so jovial that witness asked bim if he was "going cracked." About twelve months ago decer.sel was out of employment. Ile seemed very despondent and told witness that if he did not get work soon, he shonld drown himself.

William Cryan, 1, Annie-street. also stated that deceased appeared to be just as usual on Friday morning During this witness's evidence it transpired that before hanging himself, deceased had chalked on the wall " Ntanchester cup—Airship--nap." The Coroner: And Airship won. (Laughter.) That was hardly a sign of insanity. Sergeant Barlow stated that he had failed to elicit the slightest evidence that deceased had shown signs of insanity. The Coroner directed the jury at considerable length. He said he made no complaint about having to hold an adjourned inquiry, tor the reason that he thought it would clear the atmosphere in South West Lancashire in regard to these cases of suicide. The jury must not think for a moment that be was moved by any spirit of hostility towards them, and he was sure they did not entertain any such spirit towards him. Mr. Brighouse proceeded to define the legal position, as interpreted by Sir John Jervis in his book. The opinion general ob- tained that the man who committed suicide must be non COMpos mentis. This very argument used in extenuation, stated Sir John, was in fact an aggravation of the offence. If tenable it would excuse every criminal equally with a snicide,and would apply more forcibly in proportion to the enormity of the crime. Mr. Brighouse also read extracts from a treatise by Dr. Wynne Wescott, one of the London coroners, to the same effect. Suicides, continued Mr. Brighouse, were on the increase. That might be attributed to various causes,but it was a very grave question whether the mis- placed kindness of jurymen in returning verdicts of suicide whilst of unsound mind " had not something I to do with the increase. When jurymen on very slight I evidence or on no evidence in some cases were prepared to say that 3 man kad taken away his life whilst I of unsound mind, the act itself did not seem i repugnant to those who were living and it was an incen- tive to others to do the same thing. Juries ought not to return these "amiable verdicts," but verdicts accord- ing to the evidence. To his mind the returning of an amiable verdict was something that tended to make other people take theiralives when they otherwise would not do so. If the jury liked to return the same verdict that they arrived at on Saturday he would register it and sign it. He had fulfilled his duty by telling them the law on the subject. In order to come to the conclusion that deceased was of unsound mind the jury should be satisfied that at the time he took away his life he was in such a state of mind that if instead of taking away his own life he had taken the life of another, the jury if they had been sitting at the Assizes would have said that he did not appreciate the difference between right and wrong, and ought not to be hanged for the offence. The jury having deliberated for a few minutes, the Foreman said that having heard the additional evid/nce they had changed their opinion. If the evidence had been forthcoming on Saturday, the decision would have been quite different. They were quite satisfied that it wailC case of " Felo-de-se." The Coroner : That is a very sensible verdict.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases. ME9DAT.--BefOre Alderman Hutchinson (in the chair),
Messrs. W. Richardson and C. Jackson Holmes.

EXPENSE TO THE RATEPAYERS.—Edward Hill, last from Bilston, was charged with running away from the borough ore September 17th, 1897, leaving his two children chargeable to the common fund of the War- rington Union.—Mr. Shearer said the prisoner went away eight years ago, and his children had cost the borough £1.50. One of his children was still in the Union, but the other ous was discharged in 1901. The prisoner surrendered at Bilston.—Superin,tendent Monaghan said the prisoner had been brought up before for neglecting his family.—Hill was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour. HER 31ST APPEARANCE.—Mary McDonald, of no settled abode, was charged with having boon a rogue and a vagabond and found sleeping in an outbuilding early that morning and having no means of subsistence. Sergeant Smith proved the case.—Superintendent Monaghan said that made the prisoner's 31st appear- ance.—Prisoner, who said she was sleeping on her mother's premises, was discharged. WANTED ATBIRKENHEID.—MiIes Burke, a stranger surrendered himself at Warrington on Monday. on a charge of having stolen a horse and cart from Birken- head.—He was handed over to the Birkenhead police.
TIT E R CTNCORN S ENSATION. -BOY COM M ITTED TO AN
INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.

_ At Runcorn, on Wednesday, Frederick Walker (10) pleaded guilty to the attempted murder of Ethel Clatley aged three, or. May Day. He was committed to the Chester Industrial School until sixteen, and for a further two years will be under the supervision of the managers of the school. His father was ordered to contribute half-a-crown per week towards his mainten- ance.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday June 24, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday June 24, 1905.

Penketh Parish Council on which authority Bro.Houghton holds a seat. A procession was formed and the Grand Master was escorted to Penketh where the inhabitants, assembled in full force, cheered him with the utmost cordiality. There was a crowded gathering in St. Mary's Mission school (the Druids' lodge room) where a meeting of welcome and congratulation was held. Dr. Murray, chairman of the Parish Council, presided and Ve attendance included the Vicar (Rev. J. R. Jones), Mr. James Dodds, Mr. J. G. Withinshaw, Bros. James Plumptoo, N.G.A., and Whitfield, L.S. (of the Penketh United Lodge). The CHAIRMAN offered the heartiest congratulations to Bro. Houghton on the honour which he had attained and said they all knew that for years the new Grand Master had devoted himself most assiduously to the work of the Order. It WAS certainly a great honour to the Penketh Lodge that one of their number should have been chosen for the Grand Mastership. (Applause): Bro. HOUGHTON, who was very pordially received assurred the gathering that be would not do anything to tarnish the high office, but on the contrary he Loped that his conduct as Grand Master would rebound to the credit of Penketh. It was common knowledge, even amongst his village friends, that for some time he had been passing through a very severe trial. He was sure it was a source of great pleasure to them all to know that he had come out of it spotless. (Applause.) While the trouble had been hard to bear, he had all along been encouraged by the knowledge that he bad not committal a single wrong. (Applause). He had been exonerated from every disgraceful charge that had been made, and now he stood at the head of the Order. (Applause). Short congratulatory speeches in support of a vote of thanks to Bro. Houghton were then delivered by N.G.A. James Plumpton, L. S. Whitfield, and Mr. J. G. Within- shaw.

Mr. JAMES DODDS said he rejoiced to be permitted to join in the congratulations to their dear friend and neighbour on the great honour which had been con- ferred upon him by his Order. He rejoiced more than all that Bro. 'Houghton had come through unscathed from the terrible attacks of which he had told them. There was nothing more important in our public life and in public societies than that the men at the head should be men of probity whose characters were not only right but believed to be right. Disgrace- ful attacks had been made on Bro. Houghton and he (Mr. Dodds) was proud, and he was sure every person in Penketh was proud, that Bro. Houghton had come through the attacks in the manner in which he had. He (Mr. Dadds) was proud to be associated with him not only as a neighbour, but as an honourable man of high character. He had never had the slightest doubt as to how Bro. Houghton would come out in the matter, and Bro.Houghton knew it. The hoped the new Grand Master would live long to show what gpod men were, and to be associated with them at Penketh, and that he might have health to carry out the duties of the office in such a way as would be satisfactory to himself, his family, and all associated with him in Warrington and else- where. (Applause.) The Rev. J. R. Jones said they had assembled to con- gratulate a strong, brave man who had come out of the battle victorious. (Applause.) He had had the chain of office placed upon him as being deserving of the Grand Mastership, and he (the speaker) thought that at the end of the year that chain wottld be handed on clearer and brighter still, as having been worn by an honest man who was not afraid of public inquiry (Applause.) Bro. Houghton was the representative of a society whose motto was justice and fair play and, trusting in God, they believed that all true men were victorious in the end. (Applause.) The vote of thanks was passed with cheers. On the proposition of Mr. H. J. Maintop seconded by Mr. T. S. STEEL thanks were accorded to Penketh Tannery Band for their services . _ _
„ A similar compliment to the chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: DRUIDS' GRAND MASTER.
div.p: THE DRUIDS' GRAND MASTER.
BRO. DAVID HOUGHTON'S HEARTY RECEPTION.
Speeches at Warrington and Penketh.
" TERRIBLE AND VINDICTIVE CHARGES."

• Bro. David Houghton, the newly-elected Grand Master of the Order of Druids, had a splendid reception on retnrning to Warrington from the Crewe delegtion on Saturday evening. This is the first time in the history of the town that a Warrington friendly society official has attilined the dignified and responsible position of Grand Master, and it was therefore doubly fitting that Bro. Houghton 'should be heartily congratulated upon the honour which was practically unanimously conferred upon him. The Grand Master arrived at Rik Quay Station at 4.45 and a number of leading friendly society officials were in waiting to greet him. A pro- cession was formed and, headed by the Penketh Tannery Brass Band, proceeded through the main streets to the Lion Hotel. Bro. Houghton, who wore his gold chain of office, rode in an open carriage, and was accompanied by Bro T. S. Steel, hi solicitor, and P.P.G.M. of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity), Bro. Hinton, of London, D.G.M. Miller, of Crewe, D.D.G.M. Usher,of Crewe (all of the Order of Druids). At the Lion Hotel a congratulatory meeting was held and was largely attended. Amongst those present were :—D. S. Thomas Dickenson and D.G.M. Thomas Wright (National Independent Drder of Oddfellows), D.G.M. Clough and D.D.G.M. Alcock, (Grand United Order of Oddfellows), H.S. ;Peter Edgar (Ancient Order of Shepherds), and P.D.C.11. William Bullock, (Order of Foresters). • The CHAIRMAN said they were all delighted to know that Bro. Houghton had overcome the great obstacles that had been placed in his way and that he had been elected to such a high and honourable position. (Applause.) The office he now held was unique for Warrington for, although there were many friendly societies in Warrington, they had never had the honour conferred upon them previously of seeing one of their number elected Grand Master. He need not go over the difficulties Bro. Houghton had had to face during the past few weeks. He (Mr. Steel) knew a great deal of them, and he had been extremely sorry and pained to know that there were brethren in a Friendly Society who would do what had been done to prevent Bro. Houghton attaining that position. (" Shame.") It was abominable that such tactics should be used. He had known 13r0. Houghton for some considerable time and had always hada great regard for him not only as a friendly society member, but as a man. Throughout the difficulties and trials Bro. Houghton had had to contend with, his (the speaker's) confidence in him had not abated in the slightest. (Ap- plause). The charges which had been made against him were paltry and unfounded—(hear,hear)—and they were simply reaped up with an object. He was sure all the friendly society representatives present would be agreed that Bro. Houghton was deserving of the confidence reposed in him and that he would never do anything duriug his term of office to disgrace that position. They all wished him every possible success and happi- ness. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN announced that the members of the Order of Foresters were having their annual picnic, but a telegram had just been received from Bro. Llewellyn Davies, secretary,offering the heartiest congratulations to Bro. Houghton. Several congratulatory speeches were then delivered. BM. THOMAS DICEF,NSON characterised the opposi- tion to Bro. Houghton as very cruel, and said they were all delighted that he had come out at the top of the tree. (Applause). Bro. PETER EDGAR said that despite the charges made, he had remained faithful and true to Bro. Houghton, believing that he would clear himself. He much regretted that certain brethren bad acted as they had dons, for it did not tend to that spirit of brotherly love which he desired should permeate friendly society work. (Applause). Bro. W. Witiotre (Order of Rechabites) paid a tribute to Bro. Houghton's abilities as a friendly society leader and regretted that the present unfortunate dispute had clouded what should have been a brilliant reception. Such an honour would probably never fall to Warring- ton agaio.and he was sorry a more united receptiou had not been accorded to Bro. Houghton. (Applause). Bro. WILLIAM BULLOCK (Foresters) expressed the hope that Bro. Houghton's success would lead to greater unity among the local friendly societies. (Ilear,hear). Bro. OXLEY (Grand United Oddfellows) offered a few words of congratulation. Bro. C. HALEY (Order of Shepherds) said that from the beginning he had confidence that Bro. Houghton would emerge from the ordeal with flying colours. The Order of Druids had conferred a great honour upon itself in electing him Grand Master. Bro. EZRA EDEN (District Treasurer of the Order of Druids) said he was proud to congratulate Bro. Houghton on bringing such an honour to the Warrington district. He had worked with Bro. Houghton for four years and he did not think there was a more honest or con- scientious servant in England. It had grieved him (the speaker) ler a long period to see such charges brought against Bro. Houghton, and he was pleased to have been slightly instrumental in helping him to disprove them. (Applause.) Bro. GEanori JOLLEY (formerly district treasurer of the Order of Druids) also spoke. Grand Master DAVID HOUGHTON was warmly received on rising to reply. He was, he said, fully sensible that the high honour which had been conferred upon him was equally an honour to all the friendly societies in Warrington. While he had to uphold the dignity of the office and of the Order, he also felt that the dignity of every friendly society in Warrington was in his keeping, and that any stain on his office would reflect on them. He proposed to make his year of office as memorable a year as any which had preceded it. (Applause). He had cleansed himself of the terrible charges which had been brought against him, but he had never had anything to fear. He was thankful that at the conference he was able to treat the accusations with silent contempt, and out of his opponents' mouths he was proved to beinnocent. (Applause.) He could hardly realize, continued Bro. Houghton, the vindictiveness and !maliciousness of the charges brought against him. Certain of his opponents told him that he would never wear the Grand Master's chain in Warring- ton—that it would be torn from him. He was, however, proud to be wearing it that day. (Applause.) He wanted now to express his thanks to Messrs. Belibington, Eden, Buckley, Jolley and Steel for the way they had backed him up. It was not for himself that he had been fiehting—it was for the money of their members. It was found that the investments of the society were not in order. There was an inquiry—and he himself had to guarantee the necessary money before the Registrar would come down—and the result was that they had now £2,470 of their registered funds invested according to the rules. (Applause). Now he had another fight on for the children this time. There were 1,800 members of the lfamily funeral fund, and the question was —where were their funds invested? He intended to find that out. (Applause.) He had actually been threatened at a district meeting that his wife and children should be turned on to the high road nt Penketh and that the hedge should be their shelter. (" Shame.") They were, however, still at home. (Applause). At the Crewe delegation he expressed the hope that the day would not be far distant when the cloud would be brpken. He did not mean to convey the impression that he was wishful to patch the matter up at any price—certainly not—(applause). He was hoping to achieve the end he was fighting for, and that then the cloud would be broken and they would bask in the sunshine of prosperity. When the suggestion of compromise was mentioned to his solicitor, Mr. Steel: replied " Until you are restored in the eyes of your fellow townspeople and purged of every charge against you, we will not listen to reconciliation, but it shall be a fight to the finish." (Applause.) The result of the trial at Crewe was that he stood before his Warrington friends not the blackguard that he was alleged to be a fortnight ago, not the expelled thief that he was called, but as spotless and high-minded a man in friendly society matters as ever trod the streets of Warrington, (Applause). Bro. Houghton stated that he had also been the victim of anonymous letter attacks,such a communication sent to the Postal Authorities causing his books at Penketh to be audited without warning whilst he was away from home, because it was thought he was a defaulter. As a result of the investigation, however, he stood higher in the estimation of the postal authorities to-day than ever he stood before. (Applause.) Bro. Houghton con- cluded with a promise that there should be no reconcilia- tion until the children's fluid had been restored to its former position. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding, con- cluded the meeting. The Grand Master afterwards entertained a large gathering at tea. RECEPTION AT PENKETIL

div.head: SPEECHES BY THE GRAND MASTER, REV. J.
div.p: SPEECHES BY THE GRAND MASTER, REV. J.

R. JONES, AND OTHERS. The inhabitants of Penketh, where Mr. Houghton holds the office of postmaster, were naturally delighted that such a high honour should be conferred upon one of of the most esteemed residents in the village, and arrange- ments were speedily set on foot to accord the Grand Master an enthusiastic reception. The scenes witnessed on Saturday evening will Tank as memorable in the history of Penketh. On arrival at Sankey Bridges Bro. Houghton, who was accompanied in his carriage by Mr. T. S. Steel, was met by the Penketh Tannery Brass Band, the officers and members of the Penketh United Lodge of the Order of Druids, which Bro. Houghton was instrumental in forming, and members of the

div.head: OFFICIAL WELCOME AT CREWE.
div.p: OFFICIAL WELCOME AT CREWE.

An official welcome was extended to the new Grand Master at a largely attended meeting of Druids held under the auspices of the "Loyal Britannia" Lodge, Crewe at the Angel Hotel. Bro. W. Boyden, N.G.A. of the lodge, presided, and he was supported by the Grand Master (Bro. Houghton), and several of the delegates who had attended the A.M.D.

During an interval in the musical programme, Bro. R. J. MELLOR moved a resolution of congratulation to the new Grand Master, and in the course of an able speech referred to the great service which Bro. Houghton had rendered to the order for many years I past. He was one of the stalwarts in Druidism, and had rightly earned the honour conferred upon him by the Delegation. (Applause.) Certain charges had recently been brought against him by some of the mem- bers of the Warrington District, but he had cleared himself of those charges, and to-day he stood higher in the estimation of the Order generally than ever before. (Loud applause.) The resolution was seconded by Bro. ARTHUR BILLINGTON, who heartily joined in congratulating Bro. Houghton upon attaining the highest office in the order, and expressed the hope that his year of office would result in considerable progress for the order The health of Bro. Houghton was then drunk, with musical honours. The GRAND MASTER, in replying, thanked the Crewe ' brethren for the warmth of their reception, and especially for the admirable way in which they had stood by him during the past few months. He believed he had in Crewe the most since,ro friends that he could claim in Druidism, and he regarded it as a great com- pliment to be asked to pay his first official visit to the "Loyal Britannia" Lodge. (Applause.) Evidence was not wanting of the success of the order inthe Crewe Equaliad District and he hoped and believed that one result of the visit of the A.M.D. would be to fire them with still greater enthusiasm in seeking, to promote the interests of their noble institution. (Applaus3.) Bro. Rauxuu, of Stockton-on-Tees, responded to the toast of the visitors, and in the course of his remarks, paid a very high compliment to the new Grand Master. Referring to the charges which had been preferred against Bro. Houghton by a certain section of the Warrington District, Bro. Parker said that be came to the A.M.D. having no knowledge what- ever of the circumstances of the case, but after perusing a large number of documents, which were placed at his disposal by Bro. Houghton, and hearing the discussion at Wednesday's sitting of the Conference, he was per- fectly satisfied that there was not the least justification for those charges. (Applause). If it be any consolation to their Grand-Master, he might tell him that it was his (the speaker's) intention to make it known through- out the North of England that Bro. Houghton was fully deserving of the confidence which the delegation had reposed in him, and he tfelt sure that in his hands the dignity of that high office would be thoroughly upheld. (Loud applause). Other speakers joined in hearty congratulations to the Grand Master, and in wishing him every success during his year of office.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

As was only to be etpected, disaster :narked the eliminating trials of the French competitors for the Gordon-Bennett race, two of the vehicles, according to reports just to hand, being smashed. Apparently through taking one of the many curves too sharply, Henri Farman's car ran off the track and disappeared down a ravine, providentially first throwing the driver and mechanicien into the branches of an adjacent tree. NE. Girardot's raceralso came to grief at a corner and was shot thence into a field. In both cases drivers and mechaniciens were severely shah; but are understood not to be severely injured.

to bear in mind in this connection is that every car soldi by them will not only be thoroughly over- hauled by competent workmen before being offered to the public, but will have a written "character " con- cerning its actual condition signed by Mr. R. E. Phillips, the well-known expert, so that even the unmechanical person, when dealing with this Company, may be certain that in every case the vehicles will be worth the price asked for them.

As a rule, there is considerable risk attached to buying? second-hand car of unknown history. Even a practical motorist, unless he be something of an expert, may readily be deceived, whilst the admitted novice generally falls an easy prey to the unscrupulous dealer. Yet, in thh end, such business tactics bring their own reward, for ill news travels apace, and those who have been victimised are not slow to publish the history of the transaction abroad, even if they take no legal proceedings in connection with the matter. It is a worldly-wise maxim that calls honesty the best policy ; but there is no doubt of its truth in commer- cial dealings. The man who deals honestly with his customers does not only ensure that customers future trade, but is also practically sure of the support of his client's many friends.

div.head: POLICE BUILDINGS.
div.p: THE POLICE BUILDINGS.
APPLICATION TO BORROW MONEY OVER-SPENT.
Inquiry Adjourned.

As we briefly stated in our last issue, Colonel W. R. Slacke;R.E., conducted an inquiry at the Town Hall last Friday on behalf of the Local Government Board into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £4,506 for the purpose of defraying expenditure in excess of the amount 'authorized to be borrowed under the Corporation's Act of 1899 for the provision of police buildings. The Town Clerk explained that the total cost of the new buildings, including the site, was £28,026 15s. 3d. The loan originally authorized was £.25,000, the excess being £3,026 15s. 3d. Taking from that the amount represented by surplus land, materials, 3cc., the excess was left at £2,606 7s. 9d. To this £2,261 6s. was to be added for additional parade room accommodation, which made the tali excess now applied for £4,867 13s. 9d. The application was opposed by Councillor Pemberton and others.

The Inspector expressed dissatisfaction with the plans submitted to him, stating that they did not show what was really required. They mist be sent back to show what was really done and proposed to be done, together with an explanation as to why alterations were made when the Home °Moe had approved of the plans, The Inspector then visited the police buildings. When the inquiry was resumed the Town Clerk said he would have a statement prepared showing the various items the Inspector required. It would be a difficult matter, but not insurmountable.

Controlllor Pemberton asked if the figures of the original tender for the police station could be given. The Town Clerk : £19,483. The Borough Surveyor said that when the scheme was sent out for competition, the amount was tied down to £16,000. Unfortunately, at the time the building was erected, the building trade was in an inflated condition, and the lowest tender received was £19,485—a matter of £3,009 more than had been contemplated. Mr. Gough: Was not a mistake found in the tender for the contract?

The Borough Surveyor: When Mr. Davenport's tender was acoepted it was for £18,486. He however, found out that he had made an error and threw up the contract. The committee then accepted the contract at 21,000 higher, but it was still, £l,OOO less than the next lowest tender.

The Inspector: He righted an error? The Town Clerk: Yes. The error was quite palpable. It was a mistake in the addition. In the course of further discussion Councillor Pemberton said there had been a great deal of feeling in the town about this work. There had been a lot of extravagance and it had been most difficult to get any information about things excepting at public inquiries The Inspector: Well, the Surveyor has promised to send me the information you ask for and you can see the statement.

Councillor Pemberton: lam a member of the Town Council, and I wished to get these figures so that I could put my views before you, but I could not get them, being told that the account was not yet settled up and the figures could not, therefore, be obtained. I think members of the Council ought to have some other method of obtaining information they are entitled to rather than having to come here.
The Town Cler; : Who did you ask for the informa- tion? _
Councillor Pemberton: The Borough Surveyor for one.

The Borough Surveyor: I don't remember it. Councillor Pemberton : Another thing I think ought to be inquired into is the question of old materials. Mr. Hindle (represent:rig the architects) said his firm had all the papers connected with the work and they would be pleased to give the figures. Councillor Pemberton : I think there has been money expended which should not have been, and in my opinion the Locol Government Board ought to refuse to great this loan.

The Inspector : You object to the loan on the ground that money has been improperly expended. Councillor Pemberton : do; and also on the ground that the architects' specifications have been exceeded. The Town Clerk : I deny there has been any extra- vagance or that any money has been improperly expended. Councillor Pemberton : lam prepared to prove it to the Board. Materials have been used that were not in the specification and were not necessary for the building. Ultimately the Inspector adjourned the inquiry until July llth in order that further details might be submitted.

Councillor Pemberton : Can I have to access the figures I have spoken of. The Inspector : I cannot say as to'that, but I should think that as a member of the Council you should have an opportunity of seeing the statements prepared before they are submitted to me, The Town Clerk : Councillor Pemberton is never refused any information. _
CouncillOr Pemberton-(warmly) : That is quite un- true, and I must strongly protest against it.

"The high-powered tri-car has,undoubtedly come to stop," reiterated a believer in motor cycles of mbderate b.p, when he saw that writer hopelessly out of the London to Edinburgh Whitsun ride at one Of the con- trols, but still battling with a comatose tri-car that refused to budge an inch.

St. Peter's Church. At this church on Sunday the annual choir sermons were held, the preacher, morning and evening, being the Rev. C. F. Cross, vicar of Stratton. A special musical service was held in the afternoon conducted by the curate, the Rev. D. R. James. Miss Pollie Houghton sweetly rendered "0 Divine Redeemer" and " With verdure clad," while Master Jack Greaves was heard to advantage in " Angels, ever bright and fair." The anthems rendered by the choir ware" Praise the Lord, omy soul "and" Praise thb Lord, 0 Jerusalem." Tho treble solo was taken by Master Reddish and the tenor solo by Mr.W.Booth. At the evening service the choir sang special settings by Simper to the Haanifleat and NIIIIC Dimittis. The organist was Mr. F. Webster who accompanied the solos, and also gave an organ solo 4' Offertorie." Collections were in aid of the choir fund and a satisfactory"surn was realized. Hill Cliffe Baptist Chapel.---Summer Anniversary. This anniversary was celebrated on Sunday when , many friends from a distance attended. In the morn- ing there was a floral service, when the children brought their floral offerings, and these were displayed in front of the corarnunionitable. Mr. B. Lloyd Jones presided Hymns were suns and Miss May Isherwood also sang "Saved by grace "in an effective manner. The address was delivered by the Rev. C. L. Stowe and was upon "Wasted flowers." There was a good congregation. In the afternoon the chapel was filled. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. A. Spurgeon Hollinshead, of Nelson, who spoke upon the "Greatness of God." An anthem "Come unto Me" was well rendered by an augmehted choir, under the leadership of Mr. J. M. Muir. As usual tea was provided in the schoolroom for those who had•come from a distance. In the even- ing the chapel was crowded, and Mr. ffellinshead again preached, his theme being "Inquire at the word." The chapel choir rendered very sweetly an anthem entitled "Teach me, 0 Lord." The Pastor, the Rev. J. S. Hughes, took part in the evening service and the collec- tions and donations for the day, amounting to nearly £23, were considering the holiday season and the unfavourable weather, regarded as good. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. , An open meeting of this Society was held on Sunday last, when there was a large gathering to hear Mr. Frank Lord, of Manchester City Mission, who paid the Society a second visit. The Rev. John Yonge presided, and was supported by Mr. Farrar, the hon. secretary.—Mr. Yonge said he was pleased to see such a large gathering, which:bore testimony to the good done by this movement. He commended to them the words of ope of the greatest preachers that ever liyed : "I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ." When they saw what that grand gospel had done for the speaker at that meeting,and many others like him, they rejoiced, and he hoped Mr. Lord would tell them of the good work of the Manchester City Mission. Mr. Yonge then introduced Mr. Lord who was received very heartily. Mr. Lord said he was glad to meet them again, and to bear testimony to the powar of Jesus, to save to the uttermost. He had been serv- ing the evil one all his life, he was brought up in dark- ness and sin; his sin brought misery to his home, h" God found him, and caused him to go to one of the Rev. Collier's mission services, and there he gave hire - self up to Christ. The Missioners found him work and now his life was happy, and his wife shared with him the real joys of life. Many illustrations Mr. Lord gave of wicked men being brought to light, even from some of the darkest places in Manchester. The meeting was greatly impressed bY Mr. Lord's address and cheered him heartily as he sat down. Messrs. Cook's Quartette Party sang very sweetly " The Beautiful Shore." Mr. If. Beswick and the Secretary took part in the meeting. Me. W. H. Payton, Mus. BAC., presided at the organ.

div.head: Husband's Callousness.
div.p: A Husband's Callousness.

An epidemic of tragedies has broken out at St. Helens, judging from the large number of C 8903 brought before the magistrates on nday, and a further one which has since been recorded. A FATAL DISPUTE.

A sad story was told before Coroner Brighonse as to a dispute ending in the death of the married woman, named Maria Pilkington (37), of 31, Hardy-street, andl the committal of her brother Edward Ryan (33) for trial one charge of manslaughter. Ann Ryan. mother of the parties, detailed how her daughter—the deceased woman Pilkiogton—was living at her house, apart from her husband. Her son—the prisoner, Edward Ryan—also lived there. At midnight on the 9th inst. they were all more or less intoxicated, and "an argument " sorung up between the brother and sister about supper. The mother said she did not nOtice precisely what transpired. Constable Spencer said that as soon as he reached the house, Mrs. Ryan said : "The murderer has been breaking the furniture and laying on his sister." Mrs. Pilkington got up from the floor, and, pointing to her brother, said : The murderer has been striking me with this," and she held uplaolog with irons on the sole. All the parties were drunk' said the ()Meer. Evidence wits tendered showing that the woman died last Wednesday night, and Drs. Unsworth and Bellew, who had made a post-mortem examination, Haid that death was due to blood poisoning from two wounds on the head. A blow from an instrument like the clog produced would cause the incised wound, and a fall would cause the contused wound.
The jury, after a brief retirement, returned a verdict of "Manslaughter " against Ryan, who was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.
ATTENIPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.

John Goulding, a labourer, of .:16:,—EUr.—s't;i3e.t, was charged at the Police Court ivith attempting to murder his wife Ellen, by cutting her throat with a razor, and he was also charged with attempting to commit suicide. About half-past nine on Sunday night, said Chief Constable Ellerington. Police Constable Lewis saw prisoner's wife in the street asking for a doctor. She was bleeding from a wound in the throat, and after- wards discovered that Goulding bad jumped into the canal. When arrested he said,"l wish I'd wither head off." When formally charged with attempting to murder his wife and to commit suicide, be replied, Right ; lam sorry I've not done it. You can book that.' Prisoner was remanded for a week. FATIIER-IN-LAW WOUNDED.

A serious stabbing affair was also before the magis- trates ; John Greenhalgh, a young labourer, of 70, Silk- stone-Street, being charged with unlawfully wounding his father-in-law, John Davies, by stabbing him on the bead with a pocket knife. It was stated that prisoner married prosecutor's daughter last September, but the parties had rnt lived happily together, and a short time ago Mrs. Greenhalgh returned to her parents' home. On Saturday night last prisoner visited Greenhalgh's house and tried to force his way in. He used threaten- ing language, and in the conrss of a struggle, it is alleged, prisoner pulled out a pocket-knife and struck his father-in-law a blow on the head with it. Prisoner was committed for trial at Liverpool Assizes

NIARRERD WOMAN'S ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. A remarkable story of domestic unhappiness was unfolded by Chief Constable Ellerington in stating the details of a charge against Leah Stockton, a young married woman, of 19, Bold-road, Sutton, of attempting to commit suicide.

The prisoner's husband had repeatedly taunted and tormented his wife, and this preyed so much upon her mind that she swallowed some liniment which her husband had got for his arm. She had expressed her sorrow for what she had done, and her husband now promised to look better after her. On that understanding the Bench allowed her to go. LABOURER'S THROAT CUT. At an early hour on Monday morning the police were called to the residence of Alfred Walker, a labourer, of Peter-street. St. Helens. Walker was found in a front apartment with his throat badly cut, and he was removed to Plyidence Hospital. It is supposed that the wound was self-inflicted.

_ - DROWNING CASE SEQUEL. A ectnel to a recent drowning ogee at St. Helens WAS seen at the local police court on Monday, when Thomas Briers, licensee of the Victoria Vaults, Pocket Nook, WAS snmmoned for permitting drunkenness and for supplying drink to a drunken nerson.—About a week ago a railway signalman named Kelly was found'drowned In the canal. He bad been seen entering and leaving Brier's house, and it was alleged that he was there per- mitted to get intoxicated. The defence was that Kelly was perfectly sober while in defendant's house, and that he was in that condition when he left to go home. He would have to pass along the canal bank after leaving the house.—The magistrates, after a lengthy hearing, imposed a fine of £5 and costs upon the defendant.

div.p: Cpciing Gossip.
BY THE CLUBMAN.
i The Catering Difficulty.

A question of great interest to all cyclists, which will probably never be satisfactorily settled, is whether the rider gets better catered for as an individual or as a member of a club. Discussion has always centred largely round this topic, which is just as much to the fore now as it has been any time since cycling began, and, of course, riders all answer it according to their individual experiences. Some have unfortunate stories to tell of large club gatherings at which insufficient provision has been made, which they contrast unfavourably with enjoyable and satisfactory results attained on runs where the party consisted of only two or three. , On the other hand, some clubs seem to be always fortunate, and always go to the right places, where every on is catered for satisfactorily and plentifully. The truth is that satisfaction or the reverse in regard to club parties is principally dependent upon the officers and the manner in which they are supported by the members. If thc officers do not trouble to make adequate arrange- ments beforehand, and the members do not give notice of their intention or otherwise to attend a run, a large club party will always run the risk of unsatisfactory catering, especially if members turn up at the last moment, who have not notified their intention to be present, or, on the other hand, if they stay away after promising attendance. It is the duty, certainly, of every club member to do everything that he can to make' the work of the officials easy, and to notify , his intention to be present at a club run; and having once agreed to attend, the engagement should religiously be kept, for only in this way can satisfactory catering for club parties be ensured. If club runs are not satisfactorily catered for, members will, of course, prefer
'ACTORY GATHERING
The Lighting-up Question Again.

The question of the desirability of carrying rear- lights on cycles is, it seems, being satisfactorily solved by many cyclists for .themselves, by the simple expedient of attaching a lamp-bracket to the front fork of the cycle. There are many ways of carrying out this idea, some lamp-brackets being attached to the front hub spindle, while others are clipped to the front fork itself. The right fork is preferable to the left, as being more easily visible when the cyclist is being overtaken; and the lighting obtained when the lamp is mounted in this way is really much more. satis- factory, because the light is thrown directly upon the road; but care needs to be taken when bicycles are left in inn yards and stables, as a lamp so attached is more liable to damage than when fixed in the regular place,at the head of the machine.

div.head: Cycling Holidays.
div.p: Cycling Holidays.

By all accounts the practice of taking cycling holidays in the form of long tours is not growing as steadily as in the earlier days of the pastime. A much better, and perhaps more enjoyable, way of Spending a cycling holiday which is increasing in favour is the practice of touring from a base. Headquarters are selected in a fairly central spot within reach of a number of places that cyclists might wish to visit. Each day a different destina- tion is fixed upon, and the rider returns at night to the base to finish the day, and to sleep. When these points of interest are exhausted, the rider can move on to another base and repeat the process. When a cycling holiday is managed in this way, the base can very often be a small village where good accomodation and plentiful, if simple, fare is obtainable- The trouble, of course, in many cases is to find the village. Some little time since, the writer spent an extremely enjoyable holiday of this kind in the South of England, making the village of Hellingly, in Sussex, the touring base. From this little village innumerable places of interest can be visited, all on first-class roads, and through most delightful scenery. Tunbridge Wells, Peven- aeY, Eastbourne, Hastings, and Brighton were ,all visited from this base, and we found really very comfortable quarters at the local C.T.C. hotel at very moderate charge. The map will reveal many other equally convenient spots situated 10 or 12 miles from our southern watering-places at the junction of well-known main roads. In a general way cyclists pass through these places without giving them second, thought, but they are liable to furnish admirable headquarters for a holiday tour from a base. From such the cyclist will always depart with regret at
;ANT HOLIDAY.
The Revival of Cycling Club Life.

among CIRO alum ILLznrahe mscanceb these efforts are being • strongly backed from outside sources. I notice,, for instance, that at the recent great race 'meting for the benefit of the N.C.U. held at the Crystal lb race, the New Hudson Company provided two of the most important prizes for competition, one consisting of a splendid silver cup, and the other of a handsome silver salver, and I understand that a number of gold and silver medals are being presented by this enter- prising company to.cycling clubs in different parts of the kingdom, No, doubt other firms who have had an exceptionally good year will not be slow to follow their exampl, which cannot fail to prove of the greatest adv:-.1.1.,gu in bringing about sustained interest in cycling 'among the recently formed clubs.

Only a few months ago writers in the cycling press were in many cases sadly bewailing, the decadence of club life. The present season, how- ever, has shown a very strong revival both in the formation of new clubs, and in increased activity among old ones. Very considerable efforts are being made at the present time to ensure sustained interest in, club life among newly formed clubs. 1 bear of efforts to initiate racing prize funds, of the, provision of ehal'enme cup.: and trophies /11111111111 a 111111•1111111111111 h,

div.head: Speed Work ori the Road.
div.p: Speed Work ori the Road.

Many newly formed clubs seem to require a little guidance in regard to the competitions which they are arranging to take place on the highway. It is, perhaps, more natural for a young club to go in for road work than for holding a race meeting on the track with all its attendant expenses; at the same time, it must not be forgotten that the authorities will not tolerate a crowd of racing cyclists scorch- ing along upon highways that are already con- gested. Competitions on the road should therefore take the form of time trials under strict conditions, the course to be not less than 25 miles, the competitors to be started at intervals, strict timing arrange- nients being enforced, and the semblance of racing always being avoided.

div.head: CHESHIRE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: CHESHIRE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

Creches or Infant Schools? • A meeting of the 'Cheshire County Education Com- mittee was held at Crewe on Monday. Mr. C.E. Thorny- croft was re-elected chairman of the committee, and Dr. William Hodgson deputy chairman., Dr. Hewitt moved the following resolution :—"That it be an instruction to managers of all schools in the county not to admit pupils to the schools under five years of age, and that this be reported to the Board of Education for their sanction." He did not believe in bending babies to school. Members of the committee would not send their own children to school under ten. The presence of infants under five in their school inter- feied with the education of children of older years. Mr. J. M. Yates, ICC.' said that they had had chil: dren of 21 years coming to the school in which he was interested, and some of these children came very Con- siderable distances. He thought it would be better if ladies who understood the principles of kindergarten would take these children into creches. Colonel Dixon (chairman of the County Council) said it would be impossible to form creches all over the county. He was strongly in favour of Dr. Hewitt's motion. Some of these little children had to travel a long distance to get to school, and not only was this prejudicial to their health in wet weather, but they sat lon benches for long periods in school, which caused them to have" round backs." The Rev. J. Grant Bird said he had had some expert- of schools where children had been admitted at an early age, and he was bound to say that from an educational point of view the results were very good. Children thus trained had much greater opportunities than those who remained at home until later age. He had also seen all immense physical improvement in these young 1 children through going to school. If they bad creches It would be far more expensive than the admission of the children to school. At school these young children had the advantages of healthy playgrounds and plenty of light and air. Dr. Hodgson said it was perfectly true that the mortality statistics of the population of the country was greater in the case of children under five, but it. ! had not been proved that the schools were responsible 1 for that. It was certainly true that schools did propagate infectious diseases, that that was one of the arguments for the exclusion of these young children ; but, he did not believe that they would get rid of the diseases in the homes of the children, especi- qlly in populous centres, if they excluded the children i from schools. The resolution was the result of a sudden temptation to effect economy, but while there was a great deal to be said in favour of it, there vi as a great deal. more still to be said in favour of the present system. If they shut the schools to them, the children would ho in the streets. They could not establish creches up and down the county. He thought the sub- ject was one that really ought to be inquired into by a Royal Commission or a Departmental Committee. It was a big question, and parents had a right to have it fully discussed before it was settled. rilderman I'. Besley moved an amendment asking for a report on the accoMmodation for infants and the opinions of the various districts. On being put to the vote the motion and amendment were both negatived.
The Examiner, Saturday, June 24, 1905.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
TEE CONGREGATIONAL UNION SECRETARYSHIP.

General relief is felt in Congregational circles that without undue delay the successor to the late Mr. Mitchell in the Secretariat of the Con- gregational Union has been appointed. The Union has been particularly unfortunate with the deaths of its two former Secretaries, and a delay ' in making a fresh appointment would have been an additional misfortune to the Union. The choice of the Committee has fallen on the Rev. R. J. Wells, of Havant. Mr. Wells is, to alarge extent, an unknown man, but golden opinions are entertained as to his qualities an-1 possibilities. He is on the sunny side of fifty, in the prime of life, and possesses the experi- ences gained by twenty-three years in the Ministry. Mr. Wells, in addition to serving the Congregational Chureli at Havant, has been Secretary of the Congregational tinier) of Hampshire, and an active worker in connec- tion with the Free Church Council, ind hll who have come into ebntact with him say that he 'till make an ideal Secretary.

div.head: METHODIST CONTERENOES.
div.p: METHODIST CONTERENOES.

The Conferences of the Methodist bodies COlild rather thickly just now. Tlagreatest of all is the Wesleyan Conference, which meets it) July, and over which the Rev. C. FL Kelly k to preside. This is not the first time that Mr, Kelly has presided over the Wesleyan Confer- ence, and he is also an ex-President of the National Free Church Council, so that the meetings should be di4.tinguit‘hed by a notable Chairrinuisbip. Primitive Metho,:ilts bold their Conference in Scarborough. The Rev. J. E. Butt, after 17 years' service as a Missionary in South Africa, was elected to the Presidency by a unanimous vote. The Methodist, New Connection Conference was held at,Leeds, under the Presidency of the Rev. F. H. Robinson.
LOYALTY AND THE IPEE cHtn-curs.

It is gratifying to note that although the Established Church has almost a monopoly of State favours, the Free Churches are occasion- ally recognised in Royal functions. A few Free Church leaders were invited to the Coronation Ceremony in 'Westminster Abbey, and now several were honoured by receiving invitations to the Garden Party in connection with the marriage of Princess Margaret of Connaught and Prince Gustavus Adolphus. Among those who were invited were: Mr. Geo. Cadbury, Rev. John Clifford, M.A., D.D., Rev. J, Monro Gibson, M.A., LL.D., Revr B. F. Horton, M.A., D.D., Rev. Charles Kelly, Rev. Thomas Law, Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., Mr. R. W. Perks, M.P., and Mr. J. Compton Riekett, M.P., D.L.

div.head: 'DL HORTON'S CONVENTIONS.
div.p: 'DL HORTON'S CONVENTIONS.

The Conventions that Dr. Horton has been holding in connection with his Presidential Campaign for the National Free Church Council have been highly successful, and have created a wonderful interest throughout the country. The meetings at Llandrindod Wells were marked with all the fire and enthusiasm of the Welsh character. Dr. Horton has now gone on to Lowestoft, repeating his three days' meetings there, and afterwards is covering the Northern Counties in a three days' Convention at Sunderland, from July erd to 6th. The Rev. B. J. Campbell, M.A., is preaching the Convention sermon on the Tuesday evening (July 4th), and amongst those taking part are Rev. Dr. Townsend, Rev. Thomas Law, Rev. W. H. Findlay, M.A., Mrs. Charlotte Benham, Rev. Dr. Clifford, and Rev. J. E. Rattenbury. Dr. Horton, of .courso, presides over all the meetings, and also preaches the following Sun- day in two Methodist Churches in the town.

div.head: FOREIGN MISSION CRISIS.
div.p: FOREIGN MISSION CRISIS.

The position of affairs—as regards finance-- in connection with several of the great denominational Missionary Societies might well be called critical; the Baptist Missionary Society is just now faced with a important crisis. With a repeated deficit of over £:10,000 upon the year's accounts, they am o now confronted with the offer of eleven young men —two of them fully 9ualified medical men— for service in the Mission Field, whilst the call from all fields is for reinforcement. An appeal has been sent to all the Baptist Churches, pointing out that the income of the Society must be increased at least £15,000 per annum, or it will not be possible to accept the eleven candidates.

div.head: BAPTIST IVORLD CONGRESS.
div.p: BAPTIST IVORLD CONGRESS.

We are on die eve of historical gatherings in London when Baptists from all parts of the world meet in a Great World Conference. These meetings are fixed for July 11th to 18th. The hospitality of the London churches is being taxed to its utmost to provide accommodation for the numerous delegates from abroad. Some 500 are corning from the -United States and Canada to London. The only deputation to be received during the course of the meetings is one from the National Free Church Council, headed by Dr. Horton, the President. Dr. Maclaren, the venerable preacher, is to preside over this World Congress, and the gatherings should. be of historic interest.

div.head: RUNCORN BETTING CHARGES.
div.p: THE RUNCORN BETTING CHARGES.
County Full Back Fined.

At Runcorn, on Monday, the adjourned charges of gaming and betting preferred against several prominent Runcorn men, amongst whom was Samuel Houghton, the well-known Rugby footballer, were gone into. The cases caused a deal of interest, and in conse- quence the court was again crowded, As will be remembered, at the last hearing two cases of permitting gaming with dominoes preferred against Samuel Houghton for allowing his licensed premises, the Egerton Arms, to be used for the purpose, were dis- missed. DR. HORTON ON THE ATONEMENT.

Although it is generally supposed the study of theology is not popular, the issue and sale of many volumes on different phases of theo- logy show that really the interest of those who compose the Churches can always be reckoned on when really valuable contributions are pro- duced. Dr. Horton has a reputation as a writer equal to that he enjoys as a preacher, and his latest little volume on the Atonement, under the title "Does the Cross Save ?" has met with art eager welcome. It is published by the National Free Church Council.

div.head: VERSATILE CHARACTER COMEDIAN.
div.p: VERSATILE CHARACTER COMEDIAN.

James Halen-ood,a young fellow whose cards describe him us "Erie Palma, the original American versatile chin acter comedian," was, at Newton-le-Willows, re- manded on a charge of stealing two gentlemen's rings, three breast pins, a pair of field glasses, and a stamp album, from IS4, Crow-lane, Newton-le-Willows, the property of John Edward Quirk and Walter F. Hunt, clerk at the General Post 0 lice, who lodge at the skive address. Prisoner's merlins operandi, it was alleged, was to obtain lodgings on the strength of his " poles- sional" cards, and rob the occupants of the house he lodged at. He was among the crowd at the Manchester Racecourse when Police-constable Hughes discovered him. Inquiries by the police show that this " original Ametion "is wanted at Barnsley, Leeds, Ireland, &c. for similar offences.

div.head: " Vaccinated Veal."
div.p: " Vaccinated Veal."

Sir,—Owing to some startling admissions made in the House of Commons, there has been a deal of discus- sion up and down the country as to the suitability of offering for sale the carcases of calves which have been used for the production of vaccini lymph. As this latter process is carried on at the Pathological Laboratory. Crofton Lodge, Runcorn, perhaps a brief description from an official report will be of interest. The calves are selected when about three months old, and after the abdomen has been carefully scraped and shaved. from 50 to 70 incisions are made with a lancet, into which, the virus is rubbed. From 10 to 14 days elapse until the vesicles ripen and the calf is again operated on, the scabs being removed and the underlying fluid drawn off. The beasts are then killed and accord- ing to the President of the Local Government Board, "sold in the ordinary way, over 1,000 such being dis- posed of in London last year." Many dozens of animals are similarly treated at the above-named institution in Runcorn and, as a matter of public importance, I should like to know if any carcases are sold in the district and if so, how many per annum? Personally I consider it disgusting that they should be offered as fit for human food and 1 think in justice to the public all butchers should be forced to let their customers know what they are purchasing, by labelling it" vaccinated veal." Owing to the importance of the subject I append my name in full.—l remain, yours &c., F. GREENE, The Lodge, Allerton, 17th June 1905.

div.head: National Extravagance and its Effect on Industrial Progress.
div.p: National Extravagance and its Effect on Industrial Progress.

Sir,—Mr. Edgar Speyer in an address lately delivered before the institute of Bankers in London illumines the question of national finance in a way that merits the attention of all wily take an interest in the country's well-being. ThilMdress has received the commenda- tion of the best financial papers, and many of our lead- ing economists, Although the subject may by many be thought dreary I venture, because of its importance, to bring before your readers such parts as can be made clear in a letter and which will be of special interest to the many who have of late interested themselves in what is known of the Fiscal Question. Mr. Speyer finds ample reason for the compamti;e stagnation of our trade for the last ten years, as evidenced by the slow growth of our ex- ports, in national, municipal and individual extravagance this extravagance having grown out of all proportion to the income or profits necessary to meet it.

NATIONAL EXPENDITURE. Comparing the decades 1886 to 1895, and 1896 to 1905, the national expenditure in the latter decade increased £538,000,000, nearly 60 per cent, and this mostly of an unproductive character. Eliminating expenditure of a productive nature Mr. Speyer finds that while the unproductive portion in the 1886-1895 decade, as com- pared with its predecessor increased only 3•6 per cent., the decade 1895-1905 shows an increase in unproductive expenditure of 71 percent. It is true that the latter period included the South African war. Deducting this the increase is reduced to 45 per cent. While the war expenses may be looked upon as exceptional it does not affect the question as far as the withdrawal of national capital is concerned, and its consequent effect upon trade. Some critics have pointed out that Mr. Speyer's division or what is productive, and what is unproduc- tive expenditure is somewhat arbitrary, but it must be remembered that the writer is viewing the question entirely from the point of view of national capital, and takes no account of such questions as are raised when we consider the ultimate effect on the nation, of expenditure, say on education. •

div.head: MUNICIPAL EXTRAVAGANCE.
div.p: MUNICIPAL EXTRAVAGANCE.

Making a similar comparison in municipal expendi- ture over like periods, and comparing the same decades we are told the increase in municipal expenditure amounts to £533,000,000 or 72.5 per cent. Again it might be said that in the whole municipal expenditure has been wisely spent. This may be so from some stand- points, but Mr. Speyer sees in it a withdrawal of national capital from the channels in which it has hitherto been used to develope international trade.

div.head: INDIVIDUAL EiTRIVA.GANCE.
div.p: INDIVIDUAL EiTRIVA.GANCE.

Turning to'siiiis'it-e-M-Mr'.--S.:;;:ei-fiTd-;:i-hat in com- paring the decades ending 1893 and 1903 our consump- tion of spirits went up 15.8 per cent., while our population only increased 10 per cent. The consumption .of tobacco increased 309 per cent., against the 10 per cent. increase of population. The increased value of private dwelling houses, as charged for inhabited house duty went up 30 per cent. and so on with several items of expenditure. In summing up this section of his address Mr. Speyer says :—" The consequence of this general extravagance has been that our imports have been largely increased, while our exports have remained relatively stationary. The result has been that the balance of our imports over our exports has been more than doubled since the later eighties. I do not think we need go to our fiscal system to find any other scapegoat for this state of things. The reason seems to be perfectly obvious we have been spending too much money. We have been burning the candle at both ends." It may be necessary to explain to those who have not thought out the question of national exchange, and national investment, the connection between this lavish expenditure, and our balance of trade which Mr. Speyer says is " perfectly obvious." In the sixties, seventies, and eighties the quantit?of capital invested in the Colonies and Foreign Countries by Great Britain was very large. These investments were the outcome of the national savings, they did not go out of the country in the form of cash, because no country can build railways, bridges, S:c., with soverigns, but went in either increased ex- ports or what is the same thing reduced imports, thus Vie balance of trade was kept low. When we entered the nineties, and national, municipal, and individual extravagance became rampant we had less savings to invest, and our experts ceased to grow. This view finds confirmation from the income tax returns on foreign investments, which although incom- plete for the purpose are sufficiently accurate to gauge the general drift. Taking three representatives years we find as follows :

Annual income from Foreign Investments. 1880-1 £29,951,000. 18904 55,488,000. 1900-1 60;131,000. We see therefore that in the eighties our investments increased in the ten years in their interest yield 2G millions, in the last decade the increase was only live millions.

In the eighties the average excess of imports over exports was about 93 millions, in the nineties the average excess was 118 millions. It may be suggested that putting our savings in ioreign countries is no better than investing the money at home. This is perfectly true, and we too often for- get it, but the point Mr. Speyer makes good is that the capital we were saving, and sending out in exports for foreign investments, we have of late spent at home in extravagant and unproductive ways, and the only trne way to right the financial and commercial difficulty is to retrench on our unproductive expenditure, and invest the savings. If I may venture to add anything to Mr. Speyer's paper, I would point out there are indications that there is already some improvement,the latest retuins indicate that the excess of imports over exports is not increas- ing, and that we have again something saved to invest abroad, which is having the effect of increasing our exports, and consequently as far as they are concerned increasing th 3 employment and general prosperity of the country. Peniceth, June 21st, 1905.

div.head: Havdock Assault Case.
div.p: A Havdock Assault Case.

John Picton, New Boston Farm, Haydock, was summoned at the Occasional Court on Tuesday for unlawfully wounding Thomas Berry, Haydock Old-lane, on May ah.—P.C. Kelly prosecuted and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.—lt was alleged that on May 25th Thomas Berry's boy was seen on a coal and refuse tip in the occupation of Picton. Picton ran after the boy and upon catching him dragged him through an at field and was very violent with him. Joseph Berry, the boy's uncle, and Thomas Berry, the boy's father, came up and asked Picton to let the boy go as he was hurting him. He refused, and Thomas Berry then tried to get the boy free. In the struggle an fell upon a gate, Picton having his head cut. When they gat up, Picton struck Berry a violent blow on the head with a heavy stick, rendering him unconscious. The result was that he had to be attended by a doctor and was not fit to work even now.—After hearing evidence the magistrates reduced the charge to one of common assault. —Picton stated that he had to strike Berry in self defence. He charged the two Berry's with assaulting him.—The magistrates dismissed the case against Picton, being of the opinion that the two Berrys had committed an assault on Proton, and Thomas was fined ss. and costs and James 10s. and eoSfg. A ease against the boy,for committing damage to Picton's oats was dismissed,

div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.

Hickman-- Hensball. There was a very pretty wedding at Latchford Wesleyan Church on Thursday, the coatractiug parties being Miss Helen Beatrice Henshall, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. R. G. Henshall, Norwood, Grappenhall, and Mr. Frank Hickman, son of Mr. William Hickman, 13, Arplerstreet, Warrington. ,Both the bride and bride- groom are well-known and esteemed in Warrington and great interest was taken in the wedding, a large congregation assembling. The service was choral and included the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," the psalm "God be merciful unto us" and the anthem "0 perfect love" (Barnby) vrhich were exceptionally well rendered,. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ and played a choice selection of music including the air " Andantino " (Schubert) air " Candi& Rosa" (Spohr), "Wedding March (Men- delssohn) and "Bridal March" from "Lohengrin" (Wagner). The officiating ministers were the Rev. John Gunnell and the Rev. Joseph Manning. The bride, who was given away by her father, looked charming inn dress of ivory chiffon taffeta trimmed with Spanish lace and real orange -blossom. She wore a tulle veil and spray of orange blossom and carried a lovely shower bouquet of white roses and orange blossom. She was attended by three bridesmaids : Miss Mabel Henshall and Miss Gertrude Henshall (sisters of the bride) and Miss Ettie Worsley (Hasling- den). Their dresses were of white pin head muslin trimmed with Valenciennes lace, and they 'wore white chip hats trimmed with tulle', pink and white roses, and eau de neil silk strings. They carried shower bouquets of pink roses. Mr. George Clay, of Gravesend, discharged the duties of best man. After the ceremony a reception was held at Norwood, G-rappenhall, the residence of the bride's parents, and a large number of guests attended. Later in the day the newly-married couple left for London en row, for Paris and Switzerland, where the ' honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling r dress was a white serge costume with silver buttons, with a hat of pale blue straw trimmed with forget-me-nots. The marriage took place at Bold-street Wesleyan church on Wednesday, of Miss Ruth Jones, eldest daughter of Mr. E. C. Jones, 105, Liverpool-road, and Mr. Andrew Barber, of Manchester, youngest son of the late Mr. J. Barber:Kirkcudbright. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of Duchesse satin, enabroidered by her mother, and a veil worked by her mother. She carried a lovely, shower bouquet, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were the Misses Minnie Jones, Lily Paikin, Ada Jones, and Jannett Barber. The first two named wore dresses of cream satin, with white lace bats, and carried baskets of flowers. The other bridesmaids wore dresses of silk aeoline trimmed with Paris lace, and Paris hats trimmed with blue. They carried bouquets of pink roses. The officiating minister was the 'Rev. J. Manning. Mr. W. H. Payton was at the organ and played suitable selections of music, giving an excellent interpretation of Mendlesshon's "Wedding March." The reception was afterwards held at the Cairo-street • schools and later in the day the happy couple left for Oban where the honeymoon is being spent. Cricket. Warrington had exceedingly hard lines in not registering a couple of League points at the expense of Earlestown on Saturday. It is no exaggeration to say that Warrington proved much the superior eleven, and their opponents may indeed account them- selves fortunate in narrowly averting a crushing defeat, Taking first turn at the wicket the Warring- ton batsmen carried all before them and when the total had reached' 205 for the loss of 4 wickets the captain declared. Everything pointed to a splendid victory for Warrington for with their sacra at 145 the Earlestown men had lost nine wickets. G. B. Leigh, however, whipped in and played out time, with the result that when the time limit had expired, the position remained unaltered, and Earlestown had just saved the situation.

E. A. Connor, the Warrington captain, was the hero of the match. He gave a really magnificent display with the bat and was not out with 133 to his credit. Beyond a chance at the wicket at 48, not a single faulty stroke marred his innings, and his chief hits were twenty-f mrs. A brilliant performance !

Alf Thewlis, the ex-professional, shared with Connor the credit of taking the Warrington total to such a substantial figure. He made 50 in grand style and gave no chance weatever, with the result that he was able to carry out his bat. He hit five boundaries.

With two hours and a quarter in which to save the match, Earlestown made a bad start, for with wily six runs on the board Barr was bowled by Mason. Crawley however, made a fine stand and ran up 40 before he too fell a victim to one of Mason's deliveries W. H. Crowther gave the home team very valuable service, and compiled 32..
