Warrington second were victorious in their League match with Earlestown, the match being chiefly inter- esting. for the splendid stand made by E. Pierpoint and D. Plinston. The display of each player was highly creditable, Pierpoint making 81, while Plinston com- piled 58. Pierpoint made no fewer than 14 boundary strokes, and Plinston was responsible for eight fours. The Warrington innings closed for 186, and in reply Earlestown made 132, F. Valentine contributing 55 in faultless style. W. Bennett and W. Ashton were the most successful bowlers, the former capturing four wickets for 26 runs, and W. Ashton five for 49. F. Reade secured five Warrington wickets for 24 runs.

Sankey Wire Mill visiterKnotty Ash and triumphed a majority of 17. F. Taylor batted well for the victors, his innings realizing 23 runs. Gleave and R. Cook were in splendid form with the ball, and took five wickets for 18 runs and four for I runs respec- tively.

The pretty village of Arley was the scene of an exciting encounter, the Park eleven beau; defeated by Crosfield's by the margin of one run. 'T here was no very high scoring on either side, Dutton (19 not out) heading the list for the winners.
Latchford Baptist 2nd made a very poor show against Weston who baat,thern by a majority ot 47 with two wickets to spare. Not ons of Vie Baptists had the satisfaction of attaining doable figiares.

Cheshire Lines Engineers had an ea;y task in dis- posing of Bewsay Wesleyans. The scoring was 1)w, as is evidenced by the fact that W, Hill (12) gave the best display. Duckw3rth and Daeley bowled most effectively their respective analyses being :—Duck- worth, 9 ovars, 4 msidens, 8 runs, 7 wickets ; Daeley, 9 avers, 6 maidens, 7 runs, 2 wickets.
Monks, Hall and Co., defeated All Saints' Mission, Hayward.(l4) being the most successful batsman.

Golborne-street Baptists met doughty opponents in the MersPy eleven but managed to gam the victory by a single run. Woodhead (19) batted in fine style. -- Bowling. As I anticipated with regard to the championship prize offered 1y Mr. E. England no difficulty has been found in according with the wishes of the donor with regard to the throwing open of the competition to all clubs' in the town. The Warrington and District League committee have even improved upon Mr. England's suggestion and have invited four repre- sentatives from each club to compete—the players to be the most expert trundlera connected with the clubs. It is hoped to be able to hold the competition on the Corporation green and this also should be arranged without difficulty.

There is a prospect of a novel in.tin beirig held shortly on the Cemetery green, it having been decided to organize a handicap open to the wives and lady friends of the members of the club.No doubt the ladies will greatly appreciate the innovation.

The members of the Cemetery Club spent an enjoy- able evening on Thursday, when they held a smoking concert at their headquarters, at which opportunity was taken to present the prizes won in connection with the opening main. Mr Kay, chairman of the club committee, performed this office, and in doing so urged the members to strive to give a better account of themselves in the League matches—an injunction which all promised to carry out. During the evening songs were given by Messrs. J. Draper, Princep and Humphreys, Mr. R. Anderton acting as accompanist.

To-day marks an interesting stage in the hiatory of local bowling as it will witness the opening of the first municipal bowling green to be ;:established in the town. Situated in Victoria Park the green is in splendid condition and should during the season be the means of affording pleasure to a large number of trundlers who are not associated with the other greens in the town, and will also test their capsbilities as bowlers as it has one of the highest, if not actually the highest crown of ary green in the town. An excellent pavilion has been erected and a sufficient number of:serviceable woods have been provided. The establishment of the green is in the nature of an experiment and it now remains for War- rington workingmen to show that they appreciate the provision by taking advantage of it.

WARRINGTON WORKS COMPETITION. Two more matches were decided on Saturday in the second round of the above competition, and in one a sarprise was occasioned by the defeat of Richmond's team which it was generally expected would claim the honours of the game. The men from Longford how- ever made a splendid struggle and thoroughly deserved to win. Their start W 0.3 far from encouraging as the first game placed them in arrears to the extent of 7 points. Matters did not improve as the result of the next two games which increased Richmond's lead to one of 18 points. Against J. Failey, T. Atherton made a very poor start and allowed his opponent to run to 11-3, and then to 14-5. He however added four more points to his score before the game ended in his opponents favour.

The third Longford player also took some time in finding the run of the green and allowed R. Bennett to eury the score 6-1. T ve doubles and a single, with a single to Bennett placed Holloway on m3re even terms and four ends later lie had drawn within one of total of Richmond's representative the score being 10_9. The majority of the points then went to Bennett who won 15-10, Longford were not particularly pleased with the prospect, but Atherton raised their hopes by reducing the Richmond's lead by 7 points.

The first point in his game with P. H.ankinson went To-day two matches will be played, and in each the against him. Equal play followed and the pair peeled home team should win. Fegnhead will entertain the at 5 and 6 and again at 8, when Atherton ran home, Horse and Jockey team while the ex-champions will Hankinson not recording another point. visit Sankey.

Atherton's example was ably seconded by A. Vernon who in his game with J. Pemberton held the lead throughout. The next game had a great bearing up -sn the match as it gave the Longford men the lead by 3 points, the totals standing at 72-69. Ford was the man whose failure proved fatal to his side, and against E. Clare he gave a very poor account of himself. ' Longford naturally rejoiced at the turn which the game had taken and their delight was increased by the next game. J. E. Harrison proving too strong for T. Coopor and winning by 15-9: N. Field- ing occasioned the leaders some uneasiness and at first it appeared as though he was to wrest from them the advantage which they held.

Starting with a double and two singles he went to 8-2, Simister then awakened to his position and. after some splendid trundling peeled at 8-8 falling behind again immediately, afterwards and being defeated by 1540 the Longford lead thereby being reduced to one of 4 points. It followed that the interest of a large crowd of spectators was fully aroused and their enthusiasm was not abated as the result of the next game. W. Sirnister opened well against J. Finnigan ,and in twelve ends led by 6 points. Finnigan then raised the hopes of Richmond's team and by some excellent trundling peeled at 14. The last point wai hotly contended but the game rested with the Longford player Though at the outset A. Jordan obtained a useful lead A. Scott recoiled the sixth victory for Longford by 15-7, and Longford led by 13 points. T. Jones endeavoured to stem the tide of disaster, and after his game with S. Radcliffe 11 points separated the teams. W. Ployd was faced with a big task in order to give his side the victory. The task proved beyond his strength and Longford qualified for the third round by a margin of 12 points.

Thewlis and Griffiths team were never given a chance by Whitecross (No, 1) team who from the beginning to the end held the upper hand. The game between G. Ball, sen. and T. Ellison aroused the greatest amount of interest both players being old opponents and figuring prominently in the War- rington and District League fixtures. Ellison opened with two doubles, but a few ends later Ball peeled at 6, and again at 7. The next point went to Ellison, when with a double Ball took the lead. Ball was playing a good length and placing his woods well. Ellison was defeated by 15-8. Another inter-, eating game was that between F. Dean and A. Lingard. Dean opened in an unusually good manner, and totalled eleven before his opponent opened his score. Then Lingard had a turn and placed 8 points to his credit, whilst Dean remained stationary. Dean recorded a single, but three ends later Lingard peeled 11, taking the lead immediately afterwards by two points, though a double and a single to Dein lost him the game.
Two more matches will be played this afternoon in connection with the second round of the competition
OTHER MATCHES.

The Liberal Club had their revenge• on Saturday when they entertained the Saracen's Head players, and won by an aggregate of 74 points. On the home and home matches they are however in arrears to the extent of 9 points, being beaten away by 83 chalks. On Saturday out of 20 singles the Liberal won 13, and in the double ten victories were recorded in their favour.
when Rylands Netting will meet the Corporation team, and Rylands (No. 2) will meet Fletcher's.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. Saturday did not witness any unexpected develop- ment in connection with the League. The matches which wera decided had the ending which was expected except perhaps in the case of Penketh Park's engage- ment. The wooden spoonists were entertained by the League leaders and visions of broken records were general, Penketh Park having throughout the season shown extremely poor form whilst their opponents have proved themselves to be the most powerful combina- tion connected with the competition. ——

div.head: EDUCATION 10MNIITTEi. Business of the Next Meeting.
div.p: EDUCATION 10MNIITTEi. Business of the Next Meeting.
The monthly meeting of the Education Co.rnmittee will be held at the Town Flail on Nionday evening, when the business to be transacted will include the follow- ing :

div.head: PUPIL TEACIIERS AND VIZ TUNAS.
div.p: PUPIL TEACIIERS AND VIZ TUNAS.

TJae School Man tgement Committee has resolved that the Director shall enquire and report to the Committee at their next meeting as to what arrangements, if any, could be made for obtaining the admission of the male and female pupil teachers in the service of the Com- mittee to the baths at reduced charges- PHYSIC-it ISTRUCTION.-OFFER TO THE GYMNASIUM COMMITTEE.

This question has orilt-v-O-CCions bean considered by the School Management Committee, with the result that it has been decided to make the following offer to the Gymnasium Committee :—(a) of £3O per annum for the use of the gymnasium by the teachers of the Secondary, Trinity National and Warrington British schools on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday in each week from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., on Wednesday from 9 a.m. to 4.30 p.m., and on Satutday morning from 9 to 11 o'clock, for the instruction of the scholars of those schools in physical exercises; and (b) of £2O per annum for the use of the gym tasium and for the services of the gymnasium instructors in connection with the evening classes proposed to be formed for certain teachers in the Borough. PUPIL TEACHEEtS' SCHOLARSHIPS.

The School Management ,Committee recommends that in future, the preparatory pupil teachers' scholarships offered by the Committee be only awarded after the pro- duction of a satisfactory certificate of health.

div.head: PERMISSION TO C-LOSE SCHOOL REFUSED.
div.p: PERMISSION TO C-LOSE SCHOOL REFUSED.

At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee, a further application was submitted from the managers of the St. Peter's school, for permission to close that school on the 6th October,l9os, for the purhose of hold- ing the annual sale of wors in connection with St. Peter's Church, and it was resolved that the desired per- mission be not granted.

SALARY INCRE ISE, It is recommended that the year enceng the 13th June, 1905, be counted as a year of service to Mr. Thomas F. Hughes, assistant School Attendance Inspector, and that his salary be increased from that date from 255. to 275. 6d. a week, in accordance with the committee's scale.

div.head: BEAMONT SCHOOL.
div.p: THE BEAMONT SCHOOL.

A notification dated the 9th May, 1905, from the Board of Education—conveying the approval of that Board of the plans for the erection of the "Beamont " Council school as providing accommodation for not more than 360 boys, 360 girls, and 360 infants—total 1030, for a manual training centre for 30 scholars, and a cookery centre for 13 scholars at practical work and 541 at demonstration—was submitted at the meeting of the Sites and Buildings Committee. It was resolved that instructions be given to the architect for the "Beamont" Council school to provide for the artificial lighting of the school by electricity instead of gas; that, in connection with the material to be used for the playgrounds at that school, the Surveyor be authorised to visit certain premises in Manchester and some schools in Birmingham at which different kinds of material are used for paving, and be requested to report to the committee upon the matter at their next meeting.

div.head: SCHOOL IMPROVEMENTS,
div.p: SCHOOL IMPROVEMENTS,

A Sub-Committee, consisting of the Chairman of the Committee and Mr. R. T. Fairclough, was appointed to consider, and, if possible, approve the plans to be submitted by the Managers of the St. Ann's National school for the improvements and alterations to bP carried out at that school.

div.head: TECEINICAL INSTITUrE SCEIOLARSEIIPS,
div.p: TECEINICAL INSTITUrE SCEIOLARSEIIPS,

The Education Committee at its next meeting will be recommended to award scholarships, tenable at the Technical Institute next session, to the following stu- dents, who were in attendance at the undermentioned Evening Continuation schools last session. These scholarships are awarded on the result of an examination which was held in April last. They will entitle the holders to free admission to the Technical Institute, together with the necessary text books for an approved course, for a period of one year, and will be renewable for not more than three years in all, pro- vided a favourable report is received each year from the principal of the Technical Institute, viz : Ha rail ton-s tree t.—J ohn Bretherton, Joseph Chatterton Oswald Edwardson' Samuel Hayes, John W. Hudson, Thomas Massey, Harold Plinston, Joseph Bennett, Charles E. Walker. Heathside.—Ernest F. Baker William Battersby, Reginald B. Dixon, Sydney T. 'lnce, Samuel Jones, Arthur Makin Harry Mason, John E. Pardoe, Alfred Whitehouse, Harry Shaw, Henry Hazeldine, Walter Whittaker, Clifton Billington. Warrington British.—Charles Armstrong, William Downing, Arthur Gardner, Thomas Hill, George Keel- ing, John Massey, Robert B. Mellor. Arthur Milne, George Monks, Annie Dobson, Margaret Gatley, Ann Gleave, Hetty Gleave, Hilds M. Heywood, Carrie Hill, Gertrude Hill. Annie Jackson, Kate Kilgallon, Clara Mason, Elsie Throssell. Wycliffe British.—Margaret Hawthorne, Flossie Law, Kate Rigby, Annie Robertson, Janet Sparks, Alice Wright. This forms the first step in the Scholarship Scheme to which we recently crew attention. Many of the successful scholaas left the day school at the earliest possible age, and, after spending a session or two in the Evening Continuation school, have brought themselves to such a level that they are now able to proceed to the Technical Institute and compete with scholars who have remained at the day school for a year or two longer than they have had the opportunity of doing. The next examination for these scholarships will be held on the evenings of Monday March 26th,Wednesday March 28th, Tuesday April 3rd, and Thursday April sth In next year, and deserving scholars in the Even- ing Continuation schools wilt have a further oppor- tunity of passing on to the Technical Institute.

LOCAL CHURCHES. Welsh Church Anniversary. Successful services in celebration of the anniversary of the Welsh Church, Crosfield-street, were held last week-end. On Saturday evening a service was held in the church when the Rev. John Hughes, of Liver- pool, preached. For the Sunday services the Church workers had been fortunate in securing such a well- known preacher as the Rev. Wynne Davies, of Bangor, (late of Liverpool). Many Warrington people will recall with pleasure Mr. Davies's previous visits to the town in connection with the annual Eisteddfod where he has acted as conductor of the meetings, and large congregations assembled to hear him on Sunday. In the morning the rev, gentleman conducted the usual , service in Welsh in the church. The afternoon and evening services were held in the Parr Hall. Mr. John Taylor, L.D.S., presided at the afternoon gathering andl in the course of a short address expressed his sympathy with the Welsh revival and hoped it , might spread to Warrington where there was great I need of it. The Rev. Wynne Davies spoke on "The Welsh Revival," pointing out that in the course of his work at Bangor, ha had come into personal contact with Mr. Evan Roberts. The evangelist was not selfish and wrapt up in himself, but very amiable and took a greet interest in all kinds of athletics. Mr. Davies commended the revival, and gave several instances of its remarkable effects. An enjoyable musical programme was submitted. Mrs. Booth very feelingly sang "Hear ye, Israel," and the Apollo Quartette Party was heard to advantage in " Rock of Ages." At the evening service there was an attendance of over 1,000. The Rev. Wynne Davies preached on the words "In the beginning God." He impressed upon his hearers to 'place God at the beginning of everything in their lives. IMany Christians, he said, saved their souls and got to Heaven but their lives were lost because they did not Ide vote them to helping others. He asked ihis hearers to save their lives as well AS their souls. In appealing for a liberal offering, Mr. Dawes said the members of the Welsh Church were only I a small band but they were doing a good work quietly. The church was a home for Welshmen away from their native land. Miss Carrie Hastings gave a solo in a very creditable manner and the Quartette Party sang "Come unto me" (Handel). Mr. A. Trow ably presided at the !organ at both services. The amount of the collections is regarded as very satisfactory,

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

Owing to dull weath'er in the earlier part of the day, only a dozen members of the Warrington Cycling Club turned out for the ran to Winsford on Saturday. On arrival at the Cheshire salt town they found that there were so many visitors that they could not be catered for, so they rode on to Middlewich for tea. A very pleasant time was spent.
On Tuesday evening about half-a-dozen members had a spin to Little Leigh.
The Enal of the first bowling main was decided on Wednesday evening, and resulted as follows :-1, R. Davies; 2, A. Stagg' ; 3, George Smith.

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.

Warrington will decide their next League fixture on Tuesday evening when Everton will be the visitors to the Corporation baths. The second team will try con- clusions with South Hill, and the Works squadron championship races will be commenced.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE.
div.p: THE NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE.
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON BRANCH.

The members of the Warrington Branch of the National Service League held their annual meeting at Appleton Hall on Saturday. Formed two years ago the Branch,the first to be established in the country, has progressed steadily and a considerable increase in the number of members is recorded. There was a large attendance at the annual meeting which was held in a marquee which had been specially erected in the well appointed grounds at Appleton Hall. Mr. T. H. Lyon presided and amongst those also present were the Countess of Dunmore, Hon. Mrs. F. Lyon Mrs. Florence Lyon, Hon. J. and Mrs Cross, Rev. Canon Willis Major Roome Mrs. Edelsten, Mr. T. C. Horsfall (Mancl ' iester), Rev. E. 'Roes, Rev. and Mrs. Evans, Miss Massey, Miss Broadbent, Miss Crosfield, Mr. and Mrs. H. Roberts. Rev. T. A. J. Ridpath, Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross; Mr. F. W. Monks, Mr. Shoe, (Secre- tary of the League) Mr, William Richardson, Mr. T. May, and Captain Crosfield (hon. secretary of the Branch). MR. H. -LYON AND TRUE PATRIOTS.

Mr. Lyon remarked that he remembered the inauguration of the volunteer system 46 years ago and witnessed the review of 30,000 volunteers two years later in Hyde Park. The move- ment was ridiculed but he had the greatest respect for the Volunteers and hoped that in future they would be better treated than they had been in the past. If the National Service movement were not carried to a successful issue we would have to pay for the upkeep of a double army and a double navy. If we liked to sit down to that we could do so. Mr. Lyon concluded by showing how no one seemed to want to join the army, stating that there were at the present time some 4,000 officers short.

ADDRESS BY MR. SHEE. • Mr. Shoe moved the adoption of the annual report , and statement of accounts. They would agree, he ' thought, that the position of the branch was most . satisfactory. Two years ago the branch had a i membership of 40, whereas the membership that day I was well over 400. He thought that success was largely due to the energetic hon. secretary, the ladies com- mittee under the able leadership of Mrs. Edelsten 1 and to the principle which they all had at heart. I (Hear, hear.) It must be a great scource of satisfaction 'that Branches of the League were being started in Man- chester and Liverpool and other important centres and that considerable enthusiasm was being shown in the movement which was started at Warrington. (Applause.) After three years people might ask "what is the good of it all? Is the I.4sagne making any real progress ?" iHe had the greatest satisfaction in answering that question in the affirmative. The League had Imade substantial progress and people now recognized , 1 that it was a living force which had come to stay. Mr. ' J. i Balfour n a very long and able speech professed to have analysed the possibility of the invasion of this !country, professing at the same time to take the most ',unfavourable hypothesis. Ctiticism by experts had I shown that instead of taking the most unfavourable , I Mr. Balfour took the most favourable hypothesis. In taking the idea of a helpless fleet of transports attempt- ing to land troops in England Mr. Balfour did ' not consider the vary real probability of our having, in case of war, to deal with two Powers. (Applause). The only way to maintain peace was for us to prepare for war. During the last year two or three very important facts had been brought to light which must have impressed strongly upon us, the need which there was for the national reform proposed by the League. There was the report of the Physical Deterioration Committee, which showei that if the physique of the nation was not deteriorating it was distinctly not improving. The greatest example was afforded by Japan which when called upon sent out a strong array, self reliant and which gave an example to the world of patriotism, self-devotion and magnificent efficiency. (Applause.) Many reasons were given to account for this but the true reason was that about 35 years ago the Japanese adopted the principle of National Service. With regard to the physique of our nation only- a few days ago the army medical report was issued which showed the material of the men who we expected to fight our battles. In 1903 the strength of the army was 242,000 and of these 183,000 were at some period during the year in hospital through sickness. There were 11,256, or 47 per 1,000 constantly non effective I through sickness. Sixty-two men were discharged from ;the army for weakness of intellect. For the defence of ' England it was necessary that we should have a navy 1 strong, well trained, and highly efficient, and a long service army for foreign police and garrison duty. Behind this it is necessary we should have a nation trained in the use of arms. Penketh Park's position is indeed hopeless, and this is to be regretted, as it will considerably detract from the interest of the competition, the destiny of the wooden spoon being assured. Last season there was quite an interesting fight to avoid the occupancy of the foot of the Leaorrue table, and the holding of that unenviable distinction was not decided until the end of the season, when it was taken by the Liberal Club. Interest will this season be bentred solely in the com- petition for the leadership, which promises to be unusually close.

The Cemetery Hotel team has, so far been unaccountably off form, and they on Saturday fell easy vicunas to the dexterity of the Horse and Jockey men of the Longford green. Their start was far 'from encouraging. E. Taylor, and T. Harrison, on paper are well matched but the Cemetery man was off colour and was very easily beaten. J. Wood was also far from up to the mark and his opponent further increased the Jockey Lead. J. E. Harrison did make a better fight but he also met more than his match in G. Higham.

Ellison stopped what might be described as the rot which had set in and considerably reduced the home teams lead by defeating P. Wells 15-6. CT. Ball, jun., brought about a further \ reduc- tion, as after allowing Holbrook to early on take the lead he ran out winner 15-10. The Jockeys were, however, not to be denied and T. Wells; after having been in arrears uP to the 12th end further improved their position to the extent of 5 points. It. Bothwell and J. Bolton peeled at four when Bolton carried his score to 10 and then to 13-8, a double giving him the victory by 15-8. T. Humphreys per- mitted the sixth defeat for the visitors, losing to W. Mees 3-15. J. Allison suffered the same fate as the majority of his colleagues and the position of the Cemetery club was absolutely hopeless. In the last three games they lost ten more points and were beaten to the extent a 44 points—the severest reverse they have maintained since the inauguration of the League,

Fearnhead journeyed to Sankey and did not exactly return with flying colours. Prior to the match they entertained but small hopes of victory and probably their regarding the match as a foregone conclusion had something to do with the surprising extent of their defeat, They gave a very poor account of them- selves and never once looked like winning, being 46 points in arrear after the last game.

Ild should be sorry if any military men took exception to what he was going to say, but he was glad to think especially in the light of recent revela- tions there were only 62 idiots found in the British Army. (Laughter.) How many more there were left he should not like to hazard a guess. With reference to the voluntary system, it was said, " Let that system have a fair show," but why did we not help to get a. fair show for it? How much did those people who criticized the proposals of the League do to assist the voluntary system to which they attached so much im- portance? (Hear,hear, and applause.) At its inception the voluntary system was treated with contempt, and the whole service had been starved, literally starved, from that day to this. Another objection urged was that universal training was all very well in its way, hut it was compulsory training that was objected to. What about compulsory vaccination, compulsory education, compulsory payment of rates, compulsory citizenship, and a thousand other compulsory things which were in- tended for the benefit of the individual, the community and the nation? And if it was necessary for the pro- tection of the homes and the firesides of this great nation that our youth should be trained in military matters by all means let them do all they could to bring about the issue at the earliest possible moment. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Lyons for their kind hospitality. (Applause.) Captain Crosfield seconded. He thanked all present on behalf of the committee, members and associates, and especially the honorary members for the able manner in which they had backed up the committee during the past year. It was gratifying to hear from the General Secretary that the example of Warrington was stimulating other towns to form branches of the National Service League. (Applause). He wished also to heartily endorse Mr. Lyon's remarks about the Volunteers. It was going absolutely the wrong way about to reduce them and to throw cola water on them. (Hear, hear.) Until we had compulsory service we wanted as many Volunteers as possible, and we should make them as efficient as possible. Mr. Shee put the resolution to the meeting, and it was heartily agreed to. An excellent tea was afterwards provided the cater- ing of the Winmarleigh Cafe Company giving the greatest satisfaction. During the proceedings excellent musical selections. were given by Mr. R. H. Pearson's band, which also played for dancing which was freely indulged in. Croquet and howling also received a fair share of attention and the visitors spent a very pleasant evening

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. Annual Meeting of the Warrington and District Association.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. Annual Meeting of the Warrington and District Association.

The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Association was held at the Patten Arms Hotel on Thursday evening, Quarter Master Sergeant J, P. Hollins presiding over a fair attendance. In his annual report the HON. SECRETARY (Mr. T. P. Bradshaw) pointed out last season the area of the Asso- ciation was divided into five divisions, and the number of clubs in each division was as follows, viz. Warring- ton 15, Cheshire 5, St. Heiens 1, Widnes 2, viz., 2, making a total of 25 clubs compared with 36, the previous season, being a decrease in membership of 11 clubs. Out of that number 12 clubs entered for the "Observer "Challenge Cup, as against 18, the previous season. This competition continued to prove agreat source of attraction to the followers of the Association game, the matches being well patronised, particularly in the semi-final and final ties. The gate receipts in the final match nearly beat all final tie receipts, the sum takenat the two matches amounting to £64 149. The final of last season must be put down as the most stubbornly interested in the history of the com- petition and both teams were to be complimented on their efforts to capture the cup. As neither side gained the advantage after a re-play, it was decided that Warrington Albion and Sutton Commercial should be loint holders. He was pleased to report a decrease in the number of miscon- duct cases, only 25 being dealt with as against 74 last season. Refereeing in the district showed a marked improvement which it was hoped would be maintained. Financially the Association was in a sound position having a balance in hand of £36 6d. 7d. as against a Is. 7d. last season. The report and statement of accounts were Passed after some discussion.

The officers were re-elected as follows :—President, Councillor J. Fulton Smith • treasurer, Mr. R. Hind, secretary, Mr. T. P. Bradshaw; chairman, Quarter Master Sergeant J. P. Hollins ; auditors, Messrs. W. 0. Smalley and J. T. Bibby. The Executive Coramkttee was elected as follows :—Warrington, Messrs. Small' Titmas. Bibby, Foulkes, Banks ; Cheshire division, r• R. P. Booth.

div.head: EARLESTOWN WESLEY GUILD.
div.p: EARLESTOWN WESLEY GUILD.

On Saturday last, -the-a-b-ove " Guild" numbering over 50 took part in a ramble to Winwick. The weather had been very showery in the morning, and it had been expected the programme would not be carried out. However, from 2 p.m. the numbers kept increasing so that by 245 there was quite a fair muster, and a start was made. The party who was under the conductorship of Mr. George Clarke, "Ramblers " Captain set off via Fairclough-street and Wargmve- road, along the "Mesuas." A brief stay was made just to take a glance at the Old Hall near Newton Bridge, and proceeding along Mill-lane until they reached the spot where rests the famous "Bloody Stone," here halt was called, and the leader had a very attentive hearing whilst he read the various theories, and traditions or historical facts relating to the interesting obiect they were then sursoundingand also referred to points of interest in Wargrave and Newton. A move was then made along the Warrington-road, the partY, turning into Hermitage-lane. In passing along it haa been intended to have decended into the dell, to view the old ' " Well," but a barrier had been erected for although the party had a very peaceffil mission, and a useful instrument in times of war, in the shape of a barbed wire fence, effectually prevented its accomplishment. However, another halt was made, and seated along the roidside, the party of "Guilders " listened to further references to various interesting items, including "Fierce Fights at Red Bank. in Crornwellian days," "Gallows," Croft, "St. Osivald's Well," which later on was found also barred against visitation by the public ; it could onlY be opened at a distance and from the roadway. Turning, back, the party made their way towards Winwick, and at 5 p.m. full justice was done to tea provided at "Rose Cottage." After tea, time was spent in various ways, including rose cultnre, photography, visiting the ancient church, &c., and at 6.30 the journey was resqmed—past the Asylum and on to the Vulcan, where an open-air service was held, conducted by Mr. A. W. Glover. Soloe were nicely sung by Mrs. Williams, Mims S. E. wa- king, and Mr. A. Drills, and a recitation was rendered very effectively by Miss M. Watkins. An earnest addresg was given by Mr. George E. Warburton. A large audi- ence gathered, and were very attentive, the service being very impressive. The weather, which at the start , had been rather cloudy, was all that we could desire, and a most enjoyable rambling excursion was concluded about 9 p.m.

The Duke of Devonshire has' intimated his intention of supporting a scheme providing homes for aged and deserving at Eastbourne, by giving a site, on terms equivalent to a donation of £5OO. The institute is to be carried on on the Danish system. Mr. James Sexton, of Liverpool, presided on Wednes- day evening at one of the Parliamentary committee rooms over a largely attended private conference of Labour representatives on the subject of the Govern- ment Bill, concerning the unemployed. The three bodies represented at the conference were the ParliamentarY Committee of the Trade Union Congress. the executive of the Labour Representation C:mmittee, and the executive of the Federation of Trade Unions. Mr. heir Hardie, Mr. John Burns and other Labour members of Parliament were present.
